He points out the quays where his boat stopped. Samir returns from washing his hands and sits down. "Save me some bread. I have a thing or two to say about the road as well." You stay at the house that night and leave with the paper in the morning.
ev.alexandria.welcome.gate.leave: "Thank you both. I'd like to look around the market first."
ev.alexandria.welcome.gate.leave_result:
Samir points down the lane with his chin. "Go left, then turn right at the red awning. Those stalls stay open late." The host calls for the crate. Samir waves, lifts it, and carries it into the house.

Back on the main street, the scales at the quay have been put away and the market lamps are coming on.
ev.alexandria.welcome.gate.tears: "My purse is running low. May I ask you about the road first?"
ev.alexandria.welcome.gate.tears_result:
The host opens the door. "Come in and eat. We can talk about the cost of the road afterwards." Samir leaves your bag against the wall and goes to wash his hands.

After the meal, the host draws the port and the water seller's shelter outside the land gate. "You can ask about boats heading inland. If the sailing doesn't suit you, look for a grain caravan at the shelter." He sees your hand around your purse and waits until the trader goes for more water. "I have twelve silver for this part of your journey. When you get to Cairo, find yourself a meal first."

Samir returns, spots the shelter on the page, and laughs. "That water seller talks a lot. He'll tell you a dozen stories, but his directions are good." He folds the page and hands it to you. You stay at the house that night and leave with the paper and the fare in the morning.
ev.alexandria.welcome.gate.title: Samir Shows You a Door
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.aid: "I'm short of money. I'll accept your help with the fare."
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.aid_result: The host places twelve silver at the corner of the paper and rests a finger on the road out of the city. "Ask about boats first. If the sailing is late, find the caravan. Keep your money close; the quay is crowded." Samir folds the paper into quarters. The trader moves his cup aside so you can put it away.
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.body:
Samir sets an empty bowl beside the table and the host brings out bread. When you sit down, a trader moves his cup to make room for your bag.

The host has travelled to Cairo. He draws the port and the water seller's shelter beyond the land gate. "Ask about boats tomorrow morning. If you travel by land, look for the grain caravans at the shelter." The trader rubs a peppercorn between his fingers. "Ask the boatman how many times he'll unload on the way. If the boat waits, you wait with it."

Seeing your purse, the host offers twelve silver for the next part of your journey. He turns the paper towards you and waits for your answer.
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.decline: "Thank you for the meal. I'd like to see the market and the boats."
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.decline_resul: The host walks you to the door with a drying cloth in his hand. Samir is returning to the quay and goes with you as far as the end of the lane. He points right. "See the red awning? The market is just beyond it."
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.food: "The meal is plenty. Please keep the money and tell me more about the road."
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.food_result: The host puts the money away and marks two places on the paper. "Ask about boats at the quay and caravans at the water seller's shelter. See what's leaving tomorrow, then choose." The trader leans over and draws a crooked little boat beside the port. Samir laughs.
ev.alexandria.welcome.meal.title: The Host's Table
ev.antiochia.entry.body:
The cart ahead of you stops on the bridge into Antioch. Its driver calls back, "Give me room! One of the boards has lifted." A mule holds up a hoof, unsure where to put it. The silk on its back brushes the rail; below runs the Orontes.

The bridge keeper pins the loose board with a stone and asks the driver to move half a step. A ferryman at the bank has put his hook into the water; he seems to have a problem of his own. People in the queue crane their necks as the mountain shadows reach the city wall.

The keeper notices you. "Wait until this cart is clear if you're crossing. If you need directions, ask me here. We don't need another person stopping on the bridge to work out where to go."
ev.antiochia.entry.choice.look: Stay and find out what has stopped the carts
ev.antiochia.entry.choice.pass: Ask the bridge keeper for the way out of town
ev.antiochia.entry.title: Arriving at Antiochia
ev.antiochia.two_names.body:
Inside the gate, a merchant from the coast holds a small packet of dried beans. He stops the gatekeeper. "The bridge over the Orontes—is that the one here? Somebody asked me to bring these to a soup stall beside it."

The gatekeeper pauses at the river's name. "We call it the Asi. The bridge ahead is the one you're after. What's written on your paper?"

The merchant spreads a creased sheet on a stone bench. It shows a bridge and a row of food stalls. The river's name is written large, but water has blurred the recipient's name. The merchant would rather ask again than hand the beans to the wrong person.
ev.antiochia.two_names.choice.guard: "Could you show us the bridge? I also need the road to Tarsus."
ev.antiochia.two_names.choice.maps: "I've just crossed that bridge. Let me see the map."
ev.antiochia.two_names.result.guard:
The gatekeeper asks a companion to watch the gate and takes you to the bridge. The soup seller lifts the lid of his pot. As steam rises, the merchant recognises the stall drawn on his paper. He passes over the beans. The seller tests a handful in his palm. "That will last me a few days."

Back at the gate, the keeper shows you where travellers for Tarsus gather. The merchant folds his paper and mutters that he will write down the river's other name before he loses another morning to the same search.
ev.antiochia.two_names.result.maps:
You turn the paper towards the river and recognise the low row of food stalls by the bridge. The merchant comes with you. The soup seller smiles as soon as he sees the beans. "My brother remembered at last. Last time he promised loudly enough and came back with nothing."

The merchant hands over the packet with relief. On the way back he says he came from Tripolis and tells you which caravan takes travellers that way. The gatekeeper has learned the river's other name too.
ev.antiochia.two_names.title: Two Names for the River
ev.axuma.entry.body: At the edge of Axuma, a young woman is shifting water jars away from a sun-warmed stone monument. Her father, a priest, watches her work with a small copper coin in his palm. “Will you tell our visitor why you keep that?” she asks him. He shows you the worn letters and says that kings once struck coins here; some travelled across the sea, while others remained in local hands. “Can this one still buy bread?” you ask. “My daughter says it can buy a story,” he replies, “and then she makes me carry her jars.” She laughs and explains that travellers have been taking the wrong track beyond the stones and arriving after the water seller has closed his shed. She points to the main road with her chin. “If you go now, take the broad turn by the fig tree. If you stay, help me put these jars in the shade before the afternoon heat gets to them.” The priest slips the coin away and picks up the last jar himself.
ev.axuma.entry.choice.pass: Ask the priest for the next road and continue
ev.axuma.entry.title: The Water Jars at Axuma
ev.axuma.parchment.body: At the church door, a reader has spread two loose manuscript leaves on a clean cloth. The wind keeps turning one over. His nephew pins the corners with pebbles and says, “You told me to carry them separately. I did. Now you say they belong together.” The reader shows him the end of a line on one leaf and its continuation on the other. “I should have shown you this before you went across town,” he admits. They must return the leaves to an elderly copyist whose eyes are tired; he wants the nephew to know their order before they leave. The boy asks you to hold the cloth while he reads the join aloud. He stops at an unfamiliar word, and the reader pronounces it slowly. The boy tries again and gets through the sentence. “She'll ask you, not me, which page comes first,” the reader tells him. The nephew looks at you, waiting to hear whether his answer sounds right.
ev.axuma.parchment.choice.help: Help carry the leaves to the copyist
ev.axuma.parchment.choice.stay: Stay and practise reading with them
ev.axuma.parchment.result.help: You carry the cloth while the nephew keeps the leaves from lifting in the wind. At the copyist's house he tells her which page comes first and shows her the joining line. She thanks you both, then asks him to read it once more at a slower pace. Word of the help reaches the reader at the church.
ev.axuma.parchment.result.stay: You spend the day at the copyist's house. She gives the boy a clean scrap to practise on and lets you try the same line; whenever either of you rushes, she taps the table. At supper she shares lentils and warm bread. You leave rested, with the two leaves safely back in order.
ev.axuma.parchment.title: Two Pages at the Church Door
ev.axuma.site_gap.body: A water seller near the old stones holds a large jar against the light. A hairline crack runs from its rim, and his niece is already kneading clay to seal it. “If I fill it now, it will leak all the way to the road,” he tells you. She sets a smaller jar beside him. “Use this one for the travellers today. I can mend the large one after we close.” He worries that the smaller jar will run dry before the next caravan. You ask where he draws water. “From the spring beyond the southern rise,” she says, “but the road to Dongola continues farther west. People confuse the two forks.” She takes a piece of charcoal and marks both paths on the flat side of a broken tile. The uncle tries to take it from her with wet hands; she makes him dry them first. Then she asks if you can hold the jar steady while she binds the cracked rim.
ev.axuma.site_gap.title: The Water Seller’s Cracked Jar
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.body:
At the Nile, a water carrier and his daughter are arguing over a lunch basket. She wants to take it to her uncle on Rawda Island, where he records the river's level. The carrier has just filled two heavy jars and does not want her to board the ferry alone.

"Leave it here. I'll go when I've delivered the water," he says. The girl holds the basket tighter. "You said that last time. Uncle waited until dark and his food went cold."

Seeing you search for the road, the carrier sets down a jar and points to the landing. "Go through Fustat by the river, then on into Cairo. If you want the island, wait for that small boat to come back." The girl asks the boatman when he is leaving. He promises to wait a little longer.
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.choice.look: Help the carrier deliver his water and stay by the river for a night
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.choice.pass: Ask for the road into town and continue
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.title: The Lunch Basket by the River
ev.badashan.a.body:
At a highland stone market, the broker Farid is arguing gently with his sister over a lapis lot. She says the wrapping has rubbed through on one corner and wants him to reduce the price. He says the stone itself is sound. You ask to see the parcel opened, and they place it on felt where the light reaches the blue surface.

Their mother, who knows the road down from the Kokcha valley, arrives with the porter’s tally. ‘You forgot the extra mule,’ she tells Farid. He checks the figures and admits she is right. His sister points to a yellow fleck in the lapis and asks whether you recognise it. Farid says miners call it part of the stone’s natural pattern; he warns the porter not to knock the parcels together.

The family has a full merchant lot of lapis for 135 silver. You can spend a day learning how they examine and record it, buy the lot and hear which way their carriers go toward Balkh, or ask the mother about the mountain approaches toward Taican and Kashmir.
ev.badashan.a.choice.ask-mines: Ask about Taican and Kashmir mountain approaches
ev.badashan.a.choice.buy-lapis: Buy the lapis merchant lot for 135 silver
ev.badashan.a.choice.walk: Spend a day learning how the stones are checked
ev.badashan.a.title: The Blue Stone Ledger
ev.badashan.b.body:
A clerk is writing visitors’ names when his niece asks why the same valley appears under two spellings in his books. He takes down an older volume and says the travellers who gave him the names spoke in different languages. A court messenger waits nearby with a document that needs a careful copy before he can leave.

The clerk reads out a local family’s claim that its rulers descend from Alexander and the daughter of Darius. His niece asks whether the written claim proves every name in the line. ‘It tells us what they say about their family,’ he answers. The messenger asks them to finish his copy before debating the past. You help hold the pages flat while the clerk writes.

The niece wants to learn how to greet the people bringing stones from the hills. The clerk can teach you a few useful words for 2 silver; he also knows a licensed broker offering one uncut balas ruby for 135 silver. You can spend a day hearing the family account, pay for the language lesson, or buy the stone.
ev.badashan.b.choice.buy-ruby: Buy the uncut balas ruby for 135 silver
ev.badashan.b.choice.learn-tongue: Pay 2 silver for a few local phrases
ev.badashan.b.choice.listen: Spend a day hearing the family account
ev.badashan.b.title: The Clerk’s Different Names
ev.badashan.bluepigment.body:
At a small workshop, a painter is grinding a pinch of blue pigment while his daughter holds a bowl of water. She wants to colour a wooden panel for her grandmother, but this batch has turned too pale. Her father asks where she put the darker powder. ‘I used it on the border,’ she says, showing him a row of careful blue marks.

A neighbour comes to borrow the grinder and offers another pinch of pigment. The painter thanks her, then asks his daughter whether she wants a darker panel or would rather keep the colour she has made. She looks at the border again: ‘Grandmother will know I painted it.’ You ask how the blue powder reaches the workshop. The neighbour says stone dealers bring it down from the high valleys, and the painter shows you how he keeps different batches apart.

You can spend the day helping the girl finish the panel and carry it to her grandmother, or stay for a short demonstration of grinding and mixing the colour before you travel on.
ev.badashan.bluepigment.choice.finish: Stay a day and help finish the panel
ev.badashan.bluepigment.choice.learn: Watch how the painter mixes his blue
ev.badashan.bluepigment.result.finish: You help finish the panel and carry it to her grandmother. The older woman holds it near the light, recognises the border at once, and thanks you for coming with her granddaughter. The family speaks well of you afterward.
ev.badashan.bluepigment.result.learn: The painter lets you feel the difference between a coarse grain and a fine one, then shows how little water the powder needs. You write down the method while his daughter returns to her panel.
ev.badashan.bluepigment.title: The Colour in the Bowl
ev.badashan.entry.body:
A stone dealer at the Badakhshan market has his son count the bundles on a felt rug. The boy puts a blue lapis parcel beside a box of red stones, and his father moves it back. ‘Those belong on separate pages,’ he says. A visiting buyer asks why. The dealer opens his ledger: one party carried the blue stones down from the high valleys; another brought the red ones.

The son asks whether he may write the buyer’s name. ‘When she agrees to a price,’ his father says. The buyer examines a stone and asks to see it in daylight. You hold the edge of the felt while they take the box toward the doorway. The dealer asks where you have travelled from. When you answer, he names a lodging house used by people on that road.

The boy comes back and reads the figures aloud, stumbling over one line. His father lets him correct it. You can mark Badakhshan and go on, spend a day listening to the stone traders, or visit a nearby place of worship and meet its caretakers.
ev.badashan.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the stone traders
ev.badashan.entry.choice.shrine: Visit the nearby place of worship
ev.badashan.entry.title: The Stone Dealer’s Ledger
ev.balc.a.body:
By an older wall in Balkh, mason Farid is sorting loose stones for a neighbour’s doorway. His niece Mina holds two pieces with the same flower carved on them. ‘They belong together,’ she says. Farid sets them side by side and finds that one is a different thickness. ‘They may have stood in different places. Bring the level before we build either into the door.’

You ask who made the carving. Farid does not know; his father told stories of earlier houses here, and he has repaired this lane all his life. Mina asks whether people will still see the flower when the stones are set. ‘If we turn one toward the street,’ he says. A caravan woman passing with a basket mentions that her family has sent workmen from Samarkand before. She can speak about that road when her delivery is done.

Farid asks you to help measure the doorway. Mina finds a small carved fragment that cannot bear weight; her uncle says you may keep it if you want to remember the work. The woman returns from her delivery and waits while Mina holds up the level.
ev.balc.a.choice.explore: Spend two days measuring and hear the Samarkand road
ev.balc.a.choice.fragment: Keep the carved fragment Farid set aside
ev.balc.a.choice.listen: Hear Farid’s family stories of the lane
ev.balc.a.title: Stones Beside the Old Wall
ev.balc.b.body:
In a caravan inn, the keeper’s son Yunus is checking two ledgers that got wet at the trough. One belongs to a lapis trader from Badakhshan, the other to a woman taking cloth toward Samarkand. ‘You put my pack number under his stones,’ she tells him. Yunus finds the mark and apologises; he had copied it while a camel pushed against the table. The lapis trader laughs and moves his chest away from the water.

You ask why the traders do not simply mark the chests again. The woman says a seal shows who paid for carriage, and a new mark would require another witness. Yunus calls his mother from the kitchen to compare the old ink. The trader opens his chest: one full lot of lapis costs 135 silver. He also has a single uncut balas ruby for the same price. ‘Buy if you like,’ he says, ‘but let her sign first.’

His mother confirms the pack number. The woman with cloth is ready to show you the two roads when Yunus returns the ledgers, and he brings a clean sheet for your notes.
ev.balc.b.choice.lapis: Buy the lapis lot for 135 silver
ev.balc.b.choice.ruby: Buy one uncut balas ruby for 135 silver
ev.balc.b.choice.talk_traders: Ask the two traders about their roads
ev.balc.b.title: The Innkeeper’s Two Ledgers
ev.balc.c.body:
On a low hill outside Balkh, an old keeper is sheltering a small shrine lamp from the wind. His grandson has brought fresh oil but left the wick at home. ‘I thought there would still be one here,’ the boy says. The keeper asks him to cut a strip from the spare cloth. When you offer your knife, the boy takes it carefully and gives it back with the blade clean.

You ask whose shrine it is. The keeper says families from different roads have named it differently for many years; his own family tends the lamp because his mother asked him to. ‘Did she tell you the old stories too?’ the boy asks. ‘More than I can remember,’ he replies. A woman visiting the hill sets down a small dish of incense, pays for oil, and asks whether she may rest until morning. The keeper shows her a sheltered place beside the wall.

He offers you the same shelter if you want to stay a night. The boy lights the new wick and waits to hear whether you would rather sit with them at dusk or come back at dawn.
ev.balc.c.choice.chant: Listen to the keeper at dawn
ev.balc.c.choice.offering: Pay 2 silver toward oil and incense
ev.balc.c.choice.sleep: Stay a night by the shrine
ev.balc.c.title: The Keeper of the Hill Shrine
ev.balc.entry.body:
At the toll station outside Balkh, a clerk is trying to dry a page on which three caravan names have run together. His daughter Laila has set a flat stone on one corner, but the wind keeps lifting the other. ‘If I write over it now, Father, the next man will swear he paid twice.’ The clerk asks her to fetch an older list. You hold the page while she looks.

You ask which road is easiest to provision. The clerk points to his store of empty water jars. ‘That depends on the wells and the season. Ask the drivers before you leave.’ Laila returns with the list and notices that one caravan carried a sealed lot of jade. A merchant behind you says he still has one to sell for 135 silver. She asks whether the mark beside its name means it came through Samarkand. Her father says the driver can answer that when he comes back.

As the ink dries, the clerk invites you to stay and learn how the toll records work. Laila wants to show you the family’s small collection of old stones after her work is done. The jade merchant lays a sample beside the register. Laila turns the page away from it before the ink can stain the stone.
ev.balc.entry.choice.customs: Stay two days to learn the toll records
ev.balc.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day with Laila and the old stones
ev.balc.entry.choice.market: Inspect and buy the jade lot for 135 silver
ev.balc.entry.title: The Toll Clerk’s Daughter
ev.balc.mentor_closure.body:
At the inn, copyist Nadir is making a road list for a driver whose younger sister will travel alone for the first time. The driver wants every well recorded. Nadir asks him which ones he has visited this season. ‘Three of them,’ the man admits. His sister, who has been listening, points to a blank space and says she knows someone at the fourth. Nadir writes her name beside it and asks her to describe the place herself.

You ask whether he keeps old lists. He brings out a stack, some carefully revised and some crossed through. ‘This list is from last year; the fourth well has a new keeper now,’ he says, then asks you what you have seen in Balkh. You tell him about a person you met, and he asks one more practical question about that meeting. His sister brings tea for the driver, who now wants to check every mark.

Nadir invites you to hear how he gathers accounts if you have a day to spare. The driver’s sister waits to see whether you will ask her about the fourth well.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Nadir about the next road
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: Nadir asks which loads you carry and points out where a water stop matters most. The driver’s sister corrects one well name from her own memory. You leave with a useful introduction to their way of keeping road accounts.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay a day and listen to the full account
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day at Nadir’s table. He compares the driver’s list with two older copies and has the sister write the fourth well in her own hand. When you leave, he promises to show you another page if you return.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank Nadir and take your leave. The driver and his sister are still debating how to spell a village name. Nadir lets them finish before he dips his pen again; you hear the sister win the argument as you step outside.
ev.balc.mentor_closure.title: The Copyist at the Inn
ev.balc.threadspool.body:
In a yard behind the market, rope maker Hana is teaching her son Idris to wind a long line around a wooden spool. A neighbour needs it to draw water from a deep well; Idris has tied one end with a knot too large for the iron ring. ‘Try it against the ring before you finish the whole length,’ Hana says. He pulls the knot through, and it catches exactly where she expected.

You ask whether the line is too thick. Hana says the fibres are sound; the knot needs to sit closer to the end. Idris asks why she had him make it before showing him. ‘You remembered the one for the cart,’ she says. ‘This well uses a narrower ring.’ He laughs, unties it, and lets you feel where the twist is tight. Their neighbour arrives with the ring and a bucket, eager to try the rope before evening.

Hana offers to pay you 0.8 silver if you stay and help finish several spools for her orders. Idris can also show you the well test now; he holds the iron ring steady and waits for the new knot.
ev.balc.threadspool.choice.watch: Watch Idris test the knot at the well
ev.balc.threadspool.choice.work: Stay a day helping Hana finish the spools
ev.balc.threadspool.result.watch: Idris ties the new knot against the narrow ring and draws up a bucket. The line passes smoothly. Hana asks you to feel the twist once more; you record the simple test and the family’s work in your travel book.
ev.balc.threadspool.result.work: You spend the day winding and testing the ordered ropes. Hana pays you 0.8 silver after the neighbour hauls a full bucket without the knot catching. Idris sets the finished spools in a dry corner and promises to label their different rings.
ev.balc.threadspool.title: The Rope Maker’s Spool
ev.baldacum.a.body:
At an old palace wing by the river, a keeper named Yusuf is clearing silt from a narrow water channel. The courtyard has been repaired more than once, and he knows which stones belong to which stretch of work. His granddaughter has brought a basket for the loose tiles. ‘Only the broken ones,’ he tells her. She holds up a whole blue tile and asks why it lies beside the ditch.

‘Because someone set it aside when the water ran too high,’ Yusuf says. You ask where the channel reaches the Tigris. He points through two courtyards and says the same river carries cargo south toward Basra. A metal merchant is waiting at the gate with another full bundle of Damascus steel, priced at 146 silver; he has come to use the dry path through the yard.

The girl puts the whole tile back where her grandfather can find it. Yusuf asks whether you will walk the channels with him, look at the merchant’s steel, or sit while he finishes the work and talks about the old rooms. He lifts another stone and finds water still moving beneath it.
ev.baldacum.a.choice.explore: Spend two days following the old water channel
ev.baldacum.a.choice.listen: Stay a day with Yusuf and hear about the courtyard
ev.baldacum.a.choice.treasure: Buy the steel merchant’s bundle for 146 silver
ev.baldacum.a.title: The Old Palace Water Channel
ev.baldacum.b.body:
In the Baghdad market, a weaver named Mariam is checking a brocade length for a customer. Her apprentice has left one gold thread loose near the edge. ‘I can mend it here,’ the boy says. She asks him to show her where he would begin. He touches the wrong row, and she puts a needle in his hand before pointing to the back of the cloth.

A money changer next door offers fruit syrup while they work. He tells you a pepper seller is waiting for word from Hormuz, while dates arrive from Basra by river. You ask whether his coins from those places look alike. He lays two on the table and says he weighs each before entering a value in his book.

Mariam’s full merchant length of brocade costs 135 silver. The apprentice finally finds the loose end and asks her to hold the cloth still. ‘Now you can mend it,’ she says. The money changer pushes a cup toward you and tells him to make the stitch before the drink warms.
ev.baldacum.b.choice.brocade: Buy the full brocade length for 135 silver
ev.baldacum.b.choice.sherbet: Stay a day and talk over fruit syrup
ev.baldacum.b.choice.spices: Ask where the pepper and dates travel from
ev.baldacum.b.title: The Weaver’s Missing Thread
ev.baldacum.boatplug.body:
At a small landing, a boatman has pulled his boat onto the bank to mend a leak. His daughter brings a wooden plug her grandfather shaped, but it is too wide for the hole. The boatman asks her to fetch his knife. ‘Grandfather said to cut the edge, not the middle,’ she replies, guarding the plug in both hands.

You help hold the hull while he works. A neighbour waiting to cross asks when the boat will float again. ‘When my daughter says the plug fits,’ the boatman says. She rolls her eyes, then presses the piece into place and checks whether it sits level with the planks. You ask where the neighbour is going. She has a bundle of letters for family on the far bank and can wait until the repair is sound.

The boatman offers to pay you 1 silver if you stay the day and help test the hull. If you are leaving soon, he can instead show you how the plug is cut and sealed; his daughter has already laid the knife and cloth beside the boat.
ev.baldacum.boatplug.choice.learn: Watch how the plug is cut and sealed
ev.baldacum.boatplug.choice.test: Stay a day and test the repaired hull
ev.baldacum.boatplug.result.learn: The boatman pares the edge while his daughter presses the cloth into the gap. You record their repair method as the neighbour sits on the bank reading one of her letters again.
ev.baldacum.boatplug.result.test: You spend the day helping the family test the hull in shallow water. When the plug holds, the neighbour brings her letters aboard and the boatman pays you 1 silver. His daughter says she will tell her grandfather his wooden plug worked.
ev.baldacum.boatplug.title: The Boatman’s Wooden Plug
ev.baldacum.c.body:
In a tea house, an older storyteller has set out three scraps of paper. Each records what a family told him about the siege years ago. One speaks of a broken riverbank, another of a gate crowded with people, and a third of someone carrying a small chest out of a burning house. He asks his daughter to read the names aloud so he does not mix the families up.

‘That one was my mother’s neighbour,’ she says. You ask whether the storyteller has checked the dates. ‘As far as the records let me,’ he answers, ‘but one man’s grandfather changed the story each time he told it.’ A listener at the next table points out that his family remembers a different gate. The daughter offers him a blank page rather than arguing.

A dealer beside the storyteller turns an old coin over and says he will sell it for 2 silver. The daughter has two days of visits planned with relatives whose accounts are still missing. The storyteller holds the blank page toward the listener and asks for the first name.
ev.baldacum.c.choice.record: Spend two days helping record their accounts
ev.baldacum.c.choice.search: Buy the old coin for 2 silver
ev.baldacum.c.title: Three Accounts of the Siege
ev.baldacum.entry.body:
At the Tigris landing, a boatman and his sister are arguing over a wet cargo list. She handles their family’s accounts; he left the paper under a water jar while unloading. Now one line of numbers has blurred. ‘Tell me which bundle it was before I write anything,’ she says. He points to a stack of cloth and swears it was the smallest one.

A clerk from the customs desk comes over to check the count. The boatman asks him to wait while his sister compares the list with the marks on the bundles. You hold the top sheet out of the spray. A merchant beside them is selling a full bundle of Damascus steel for 146 silver; he wants the clerk to finish so he can load it before dark.

You ask who knows the city’s streets and older stories. The sister says the river workers know the landings, the merchants know the markets, and an old keeper near a former palace wing will tell you how the water channels were laid out. She finds the blurred number on the third bundle and taps it with her finger. ‘There. Write that one down.’
ev.baldacum.entry.choice.customs: Spend two days clearing your cargo at the customs desk
ev.baldacum.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day hearing the river quarter’s stories
ev.baldacum.entry.choice.market: Buy the Damascus steel bundle for 146 silver
ev.baldacum.entry.title: The River Landing at Baghdad
ev.baldacum.geomancy_court.body:
You find the sand-reader and his daughter at the courtyard gate. She has set the tray on a low stool, where the wall protects it from the river wind. A neighbour is waiting with a question about a missing parcel. The reader asks which shop last saw it, and the neighbour names two; his daughter writes both down.

‘Should we make a figure first?’ the girl asks. ‘After we know what he is asking,’ her father says. The neighbour checks his own delivery slip and realises one shop was closed that day. You ask whether he wants to go there now. He says he will ask the open shop first, then come back if the parcel still cannot be found.

The tray is ready for your own question. The reader remembers the figures you learned and offers you the stylus. His daughter smooths the sand at the edge, leaving a clean place for you to begin.
ev.baldacum.geomancy_court.choice.cast: Lay out the sand figures for your question
ev.baldacum.geomancy_court.title: A Question at the Courtyard Gate
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.body:
A traveller from farther east has set a calendar on a low table near the river market. His niece is copying dates while he helps a boatman decide when to fetch cargo. The boatman wants a single lucky morning; the traveller asks instead when the boat can actually sail. ‘The pilot says three days,’ the boatman replies. ‘Then start with those three,’ the teacher says.

The niece asks whether she should mark the river’s water level beside the dates. Her uncle nods and turns the page to show you the four pillars he uses in his own method of reading a birth time. You ask whether a traveller can learn it without abandoning the road. He says the full course takes twenty-one days and costs 100 silver; his sand-reading colleague teaches a different ten-day course for 80 silver.

The boatman returns with news that his pilot has moved the loading time. The teacher has his niece change the calendar entry before he answers your question, then invites you to sit at the table.
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.choice.ask: Ask how he chooses dates around a boat’s schedule
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.choice.learn: Pay 100 silver and study four pillars for twenty-one days
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.choice.learn_geo: Pay 80 silver and study sand-reading for ten days
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.title: The Travelling Calendar Reader
ev.baldacum.mentor_geomancy.body:
A sand-reader works in a courtyard near the river market. His daughter is pressing the corner of a cloth over the tray while he marks a row of dots in fine sand. A gust gets beneath the cloth and erases one line. ‘I told you to move indoors,’ she says. Her father replies that the light is better here, then accepts her help in finding a sheltered corner.

You ask what the figures mean. He draws one set again and has his daughter count the marks before he names it. She corrects him when he misses a dot; he laughs and gives her the stylus. A boatman comes to ask about his southbound trip, and the reader first asks when the vessel is ready. ‘After the rope is mended,’ the man answers.

The reader offers a ten-day course for 80 silver, beginning with how the figures are made. His daughter leaves room at the edge of the tray for you to try one before deciding. The boatman waits nearby for his own turn.
ev.baldacum.mentor_geomancy.choice.ask: Ask to see one figure made
ev.baldacum.mentor_geomancy.choice.learn: Pay 80 silver for the ten-day sand-reading course
ev.baldacum.mentor_geomancy.title: The Sand Reader’s Covered Tray
ev.basora.dateboat.body:
When you return to the landing, Samir is arguing with the boatman over a count. His aunt’s basket is safe, but a second basket has no mark. Nura is busy tying up the jars and asks him to settle it before the boat leaves.

‘If it goes without a name, no one will know who should be paid,’ Samir says. He asks you to stay while he opens the baskets and counts their contents. The boatman offers a small wage for the time. A vendor nearby has fresh dates and cool water if you would rather get on with your journey.

You ask Samir whether the second basket came from the same garden. He looks at its contents: one layer of dates is softer than the rest, which makes him think two loads were stacked together. The boatman says his younger brother tied the rope at dawn and may have covered the mark by accident. Nura calls across the landing for the boy to come and look; he is still unloading jars. Samir offers him a piece of charcoal to write the name clearly once they find it. The vendor brings a cup of cool water for Nura, who has been lifting jars all morning, and tells her to sit for one moment before the tide turns.
ev.basora.dateboat.choice.count: Stay for the day to count the baskets
ev.basora.dateboat.choice.eat: Buy dates and water for 0.6 silver
ev.basora.dateboat.result.count: By dusk, Samir finds the missing mark beneath a knot in the rope. The boatman pays you 0.6 silver for the day. Nura puts the basket aboard with its owner’s name facing up.
ev.basora.dateboat.result.eat: You pay 0.6 silver and sit by the canal with dates and a cup of water. Samir calls out the final count from the boat; this time Nura nods at once. You feel ready to travel again.
ev.basora.dateboat.title: The Unmarked Basket
ev.basora.entry.body:
The canal reaches the Tigris between date groves and low houses. At the landing a woman named Nura counts jars onto a boat. Her son keeps calling out numbers before she does, and she makes him start again whenever he skips one.

‘The jars are for my sister downstream,’ she tells you. ‘She sent the boat up for them, and now everyone wants to leave before the tide turns.’ She leaves a space on the bench for your pack while she checks the last rope. From here, river craft carry dates and cloth toward the Gulf; the road inland returns toward Baghdad.

Her son Samir checks the last jar against a scratched list and asks why his aunt needs so many. Nura says she is taking them to families who bring dates to her yard, and several of their old jars have cracked. ‘Will she send us back the empty ones?’ he asks. ‘Only if you remember to tell her which belong to whom.’ You ask whether the boat will return tomorrow. The boatman says he must watch the water first; Nura tells Samir to write the owners’ marks on a dry board so the boatman can read them. The boy runs for charcoal and comes back before the last jar is loaded.
ev.basora.entry.choice.rest: Stay the day and rest by the canal
ev.basora.entry.title: The Basra Landing
ev.berrhoea.entry.body:
The citadel rises above the streets of Aleppo. At a covered stall below it, Safiya is laying out sheets of paper. Her father has written the prices on a scrap, but rain has blurred one number. She holds it up to him.

“If you cannot read it, ask me,” he says. “I am asking,” she replies. He laughs, gives her the price, and makes her write it again in larger figures. She says the writing is for him too: last week he sold two sheets at the old price and then wondered where the money went.

Safiya asks where you are headed. Travellers leave names of towns at her stall when they buy paper for letters. She has heard of routes from Aleppo to the northern coast, although she has never gone that far. She shows you the nearby water place and offers to take a day to walk the streets with you if you have time.
ev.berrhoea.entry.choice.look: Spend a day seeing the town with Safiya
ev.berrhoea.entry.choice.pass: Thank Safiya and continue through the streets
ev.berrhoea.entry.title: Safiya’s Paper Stall
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.body:
At the edge of a busy lane, Nadwa ladles lentils from a clay pot. Her son Harun watches the bread oven next door. Nadwa promised to save his grandmother a bowl, and he has put a small wooden spoon beside it so nobody serves that portion by mistake.

Harun's grandmother used to cook here. She now sits at home with a sore knee and sends him back whenever the soup needs more salt. “She could tell from across the lane,” Nadwa says. Harun insists that he can tell too, takes a careful taste, and asks for a little more.

Nadwa offers you a bowl for the road. If you stay to help prepare tomorrow's pot, she can feed you and let you sleep indoors. Harun says his grandmother will inspect the soup either way.
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.choice.buy: Buy soup and bread for 0.8 silver
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.choice.stay: Stay a day to prepare the next pot
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.result.buy: You pay for soup and bread. Harun carries the reserved bowl to his grandmother before taking yours from the pot. He returns to report that she approves of the salt, though she wants the bread warmed longer next time. You eat on the road and regain some strength.
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.result.stay: You spend the day washing lentils and carrying water for the next pot. In the evening Harun brings his grandmother over on his arm. She tastes a spoonful, tells Nadwa it is good, and then quietly asks you to warm her bread a little longer. Nadwa gives you supper and a place to sleep. You leave the next morning rested.
ev.berrhoea.lentilpot.title: A Pot of Lentils
ev.bethleem.entry.body:
Beside a hill road in Bethlehem, Yona sweeps ashes from his oven into a clay bowl. Pilgrims passing through sometimes sit by his hearth. His daughter Lina has just taken out a tray of small loaves. The edge of one is black.

“I said only yesterday that I'd watch the fire this time.” Lina turns the loaf over, trying to hide the burnt edge.

Yona picks up the wooden peel. “The back of the oven is hotter. See which loaves the travellers take first? Always the ones near the front. We'll eat this one ourselves and bake another tray for them this afternoon.”

Lina asks whether he burned loaves as a child. Yona says that the first time he watched an oven alone, he spoiled a whole basket. His mother showed him how to turn the tray halfway round. The next day he had bread he could sell. Lina looks into the oven and draws a circle in the dust with the peel, a reminder to turn the tray later.

Yona sees you resting nearby and asks whether you will continue along the road or wait for the next baking.
ev.bethleem.entry.choice.pass: Ask Yona about the hill road and continue today
ev.bethleem.entry.choice.rest: Rest by the oven for a day and try Lina's fresh bread
ev.bethleem.entry.title: Bethlehem
ev.bethleem.stool.body:
Outside a small house on the slope, Hanna sets a low stool on level ground and tries to rock it. It stands firm. Her son Ishaq crouches beside her and measures two of its legs with his fingers. “Will it stand as well at Grandmother's?”

“On this level ground,” Hanna says. “Your grandmother's doorway has old stone slabs. We'll take it there and try it.”

Ishaq says his grandmother's knees trouble her. She stands to knead dough and has to stop several times before a meal is ready. Hanna has been making the stool for days, and he kept asking her to hurry. Now that it is nearly finished, he worries it will rock on the stones at her door.

Hanna puts a small wooden shim in her pocket. “I'll adjust it when we get there. You can walk up the slope with us, or stay here and help me smooth the rough edge first.”
ev.bethleem.stool.choice.deliver: Carry the stool up the slope with Hanna and Ishaq
ev.bethleem.stool.choice.sand: Stay at the house and help Hanna smooth the stool's edge
ev.bethleem.stool.result.deliver:
You and the family walk up the slope to the grandmother's place. On the old stone slabs, one leg does lift slightly. Hanna takes the shim from her pocket and settles the stool. Ishaq holds his grandmother's hand as she sits. She runs a hand over the seat and says she can now take her time kneading dough.

On your way back, Ishaq shows you where the hill road joins the way to Jerusalem. Next time you visit, he says, he will bring bread his grandmother made herself. You add Jerusalem and that road to your map.
ev.bethleem.stool.result.sand:
You and Ishaq sand the edge until it no longer catches on a hand. Hanna feels along the grain and asks her son to sit on the stool. He says it is steady, then jumps up. “Grandmother gets the first proper turn.”

Hanna carries it away and promises to tell you whether it needs a shim on her mother's stone floor. The neighbours hear that you helped them finish it and greet you when you pass.
ev.bethleem.stool.title: A Small Stool on the Hillside
ev.bochara.battuta_a.body:
Near an old school wall in Bukhara, a melon seller is helping her father patch the shade over his stall. Some of the nearby buildings were damaged in earlier wars and rebuilt in stages; this wall remains, and local children use it to measure how tall they have grown. Her father recalls a family story of these lanes after an earlier war, when some houses needed rebuilding. The seller asks whether this wall stood then too. He says older neighbours remember it standing.

An older neighbour joins them with a story he heard as a boy: the conqueror, he says, began as a blacksmith in Khotan. The melon seller interrupts. ‘My father heard another version. Tell it as a story, not as his life.’ The neighbour laughs and admits he cannot name the first teller. He does know the caravan road to Samarkand; he has sent fruit that way.

You ask about the wall, the road, and the melon slices drying beneath the shade. The seller offers to show you where the old school stood, the neighbour can spend the day tracing the Samarkand road with you, or you can pay a little for a piece of melon and eat it while they finish the roof.
ev.bochara.battuta_a.choice.melon: Buy a piece of melon for 0.4 silver
ev.bochara.battuta_a.choice.ruins: Spend a day with the seller by the old school wall
ev.bochara.battuta_a.choice.tale: Hear the neighbour’s tale and the Samarkand road
ev.bochara.battuta_a.title: The Old School Wall in Bukhara
ev.bochara.entry.body:
At the edge of a Bukhara cloth yard, a dyer is helping his daughter count the rolls that will leave with the next caravan. The girl lays out six, then calls her father back: one has a loose outer cord, and she will not put it on the cart until he checks the cloth. He laughs and unfastens the cord. ‘You caught it before I did.’

A neighbour arrives with a cup of water and asks whether they have room for her bundle too. ‘If your son brings it before the drivers finish loading,’ the dyer says. She asks you where you came from. When you name a road, she points to a lane with places to sleep and says people who have crossed that way often gather there at supper.

The daughter finds the cloth uncut but asks for a fresh wrapping. ‘This roll is yours to watch,’ her father tells her. ‘Count it once more tomorrow morning.’ She asks whether you intend to go on today. You can leave after marking Bukhara on your map, or stay a day by the yard, rest, and listen while the drivers arrange the next load.
ev.bochara.entry.choice.rest: Rest by the cloth yard for a day
ev.bochara.entry.title: The Cloth Yard in Bukhara
ev.bochara.recipe.body:
A baker named Hamid has room for one more tray in his oven. His sister has brought dough for her household, but a caravan driver asks him to bake his bread before the wagons leave. Hamid looks at the heat and says both batches will fit if he moves the coals. His sister wants him to eat something first; he has worked since dawn.

‘You promised me the first tray,’ she reminds him. ‘I did,’ he says. ‘You also told me not to send a traveller away hungry.’ The driver puts down his sack. He can wait while Hamid’s bread finishes, but he must return to his wagon before dusk. You ask who will watch the oven when Hamid goes for water. His young nephew raises a hand, then admits he cannot yet tell when the crust is done.

Hamid gives the boy a small piece of dough to practice with. You can stay for the day and help the nephew turn the trays, earning a little pay from Hamid, or buy a warm piece of bread now and eat while his sister takes the next turn at the oven.
ev.bochara.recipe.choice.eat: Buy a warm piece for 0.4 silver
ev.bochara.recipe.choice.work: Stay the day and help with the trays
ev.bochara.recipe.result.eat: You pay 0.4 silver, eat the warm bread, and feel better for the road. Hamid’s sister takes the oven fork while he drinks his water; the driver settles down to wait for his batch.
ev.bochara.recipe.result.work: You show the boy how the edge of the bread changes colour. When his aunt’s tray is ready, he calls Hamid over before lifting it. Hamid pays you 1 silver for the day and lets the boy take the first finished piece home.
ev.bochara.recipe.title: The Baker’s Shared Oven
ev.cabul.bellstrap.body:
In a caravan yard, a leather worker is fitting a new strap to a mule’s bell. Her younger brother thinks the old strap can last one more journey. She holds it against the light and shows him a thin split near the buckle. ‘If it breaks on the pass, we will be searching for this bell in the snow,’ she says.

The mule driver from the cobbler’s yard arrives with his repaired boots and asks whether his animal is ready. The leather worker tells him to walk the mule while she listens. The bell rings once, then falls silent because the new strap twists against its mouth. You ask whether a shorter loop would help. Her brother fetches a knife and waits for her to say where to cut.

She can pay you 0.8 silver to stay the day and help test the caravan’s bells, or show you the quick check she uses before each mountain stage. The mule nudges the driver’s sleeve while everyone listens for the next ring.
ev.cabul.bellstrap.choice.learn: Learn how she checks a bell strap
ev.cabul.bellstrap.choice.test: Stay a day and test the caravan bells
ev.cabul.bellstrap.result.learn: The worker shows you the split by the buckle and the twist that muffled the bell. You write down the two checks; her brother fixes the loop while the driver walks the mule once more.
ev.cabul.bellstrap.result.test: You help test each bell and the worker pays you 0.8 silver. The brother trims the new strap where she marked it; at last the mule’s bell rings clearly across the yard.
ev.cabul.bellstrap.title: The Mule’s New Bell Strap
ev.cabul.entry.body:
At a Kabul lodging yard, a cobbler is measuring a mule driver’s worn boots. His daughter holds the new felt against the old sole and says they need another strip of leather. The driver wants the boots before his caravan leaves, but the cobbler says the stitching will pull free if he rushes it. ‘Your feet will be the ones inside,’ he reminds him.

You ask where the caravan is going. The driver names the road toward Taican and the northern mountain approaches. His daughter points out that travellers also reach Kabul from the south and east; she has repaired boots from more than one direction. Her father sets the felt by the warm brazier and asks her to fetch the stronger thread.

The driver tries to stand on the old sole and feels its edge lift. ‘Fine, finish it properly,’ he says. The cobbler shows you a place to sleep beside the yard. His daughter returns with thread. Her father finishes the last seam, and the driver tries the boots on before offering to share his supper.
ev.cabul.entry.choice.rest: Rest a day at the lodging yard
ev.cabul.entry.title: The Cobbler’s Door in Kabul
ev.cabul.site_gap.body:
At the cobbler’s stall, the mule driver has come back wearing the repaired boots. He says one foot feels tighter than the other. The cobbler’s daughter asks him to loosen the upper strap and walk across the yard again. He does, and the left sole no longer lifts. ‘That was the part I worried about,’ she says.

You ask how they make a felt boot warm enough for the mountain road. Her father shows you washed wool, dampens a small layer, and rolls it between his palms. He points to the leather beneath the sole, where stones would wear through the felt. The driver wants to know whether this pair will last until Taican. The cobbler says it depends on the path and asks which pass the caravan plans to use.

The driver draws a line in the dust, then sees the cobbler’s daughter shake her head. She knows a better branch where the mule has firm footing. Her father hands her the stick to redraw it for you both.
ev.cabul.site_gap.choice.interact: Watch the cobbler make and fit felt
ev.cabul.site_gap.choice.route: Ask her to trace the road toward Taican
ev.cabul.site_gap.title: The Felt Boot at the Pass
ev.cacanfu.entry.body: Boats laden with silk crowd the wharf at Cacanfu. A broker spreads a waterway map on his counter and points to the side channels. “These waterways join the route to Cambaluc. Send the silk north by boat; near the capital, other merchants can take it onward without loading it all into carts.” A weaver nearby works gold thread into silk and laughs: “Light gauze hates damp. Keep it above the dry silk rolls when you load the boat.”
ev.cacanfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cacanfu.entry.title: Concerning the Cities of Cacanfu and of Changlu
ev.cachanfu.entry.body: When you leave the castle, and travel about 20 miles westward, you come to a river called CARAMORAN, so big that no bridge can be thrown across it; for it is of immense width and depth, and reaches to the Great Ocean that encircles the Universe,—I mean the whole earth. On this river there are many cities and walled towns, and many merchants too therein, for much traffic takes place upon the river, there being a great deal of ginger and a great deal of silk produced in the country. Game birds here are in wonderful abundance, insomuch that you may buy at least three pheasants for a Venice groat of silver.
ev.cachanfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cachanfu.entry.title: Concerning the Great River Caramoran and the City of Cachanfu
ev.caffa.entry.body:
At Caffa, the road reaches the Black Sea. Arslan has stopped his cart near the shore to let his horses drink. His granddaughter Sada is brushing sand from a leather bag. She says it was clean when they left home; Arslan says she has opened it six times since then to count the dried apples inside.

“There are still eight,” she tells him. He asks how many there were in the morning. Sada looks at you before answering: ten. Arslan breaks one apple in half and gives her a piece, saying she can count that as one or two, whichever makes her happier.

They have travelled from the open country beyond the shore. Arslan knows where the carts gather before setting out again and shows you a path between the houses and the water. He offers you a place beneath his shelter if you need to recover from the road.
ev.caffa.entry.choice.pass: Thank Arslan and continue through Caffa
ev.caffa.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day at Arslan's shelter
ev.caffa.entry.title: The Road Reaches Caffa
ev.caffa.leathercut.body:
Arslan has spread pieces of leather beside his cart. He is cutting a pair of boots for Sada, who claims her feet grew during the journey. She puts both feet on the leather and asks for extra room at the toes.

“You said that before we left,” Arslan says. Sada says the road has been long. He measures again anyway. A larger bundle of finished leather, brought from inland, is tied beside the wheel for sale. Arslan also needs someone to sort and wrap the smaller pieces before the next cart goes out.

Arslan sets the full leather lot on a dry board. Sada watches him cut the last boot piece, then points to a small offcut he promised she could keep. He asks her to wait until the buyer has checked the whole pack.

You ask why she wants the offcuts. ‘I am making a cover for my little sister’s knife,’ Sada says. Arslan reminds her that the blade must be wrapped separately until she learns to stitch the sheath. She asks whether you can show her how to make the first hole without tearing the leather. Her grandfather gives her an awl and points to a scrap that is safe to practise on. The cart driver calls from the road, asking when the remaining small pieces will be ready to load. Arslan says after the boot work is settled, and asks Sada to keep the awl away from the finished leather.
ev.caffa.leathercut.choice.buy: Buy Arslan’s bundle of leather for 120 silver
ev.caffa.leathercut.choice.work: Stay a day and sort the leather for a wage
ev.caffa.leathercut.result.buy: You pay Arslan and take the bundle of leather. He checks the ties before letting you lift it. Sada watches him cut the boots; after he has left extra room for her toes, she gathers the offcuts to make a small pouch. You carry the purchased leather onward.
ev.caffa.leathercut.result.work: You spend the day sorting and wrapping the smaller pieces. Arslan cuts Sada's new boots between bundles. By evening she can walk in them without her toes pressing the front, and she shows you a pouch made from the scraps. Arslan pays the agreed wage. You leave the next morning, after Sada has run around the cart twice to test her new boots.
ev.caffa.leathercut.title: The Leather for Sada’s Boots
ev.caffa.mentor_runes.body: On the quay a northern trader casts runes for the steppe road inland.
ev.caffa.mentor_runes.choice.ask: Ask what Raidho names on this quay
ev.caffa.mentor_runes.title: Runes at Caffa
ev.caffa.site_gap.body:
Beside the water, Rena and her brother Matvei are moving bundles of furs onto wooden slats. Matvei sets a bundle on the bare ground; Rena lifts it again. The bottom of its wrapping is already damp.

Their mother packed the furs before they left the steppe, sewing a different coloured thread into each bundle so the family could tell which belonged to whom. Matvei knows the colours but keeps forgetting to lift the bundles clear of the ground. Rena says their mother would notice that too.

A boat going along the coast toward Trebizond may carry some of the bundles. Rena can tell you where to ask about the crossing, or would welcome help putting the last pieces safely above the wet ground.

‘Mother stitched the red thread into mine,’ Matvei says, turning a pack to show you. Rena checks the seam and replies, ‘Yes, and she told you twice to keep that side dry.’ You ask whether the ship to Trebizond has space for all their cargo. Rena says they will learn when the captain weighs the load; she has not promised the family more room than she has. Matvei lifts the wet pack onto the slats and asks if it can still travel. His sister feels the lining, finds the fur dry inside, and tells him to leave it open to the air until the boatman calls. She hands you the next bundle by its dry handle.
ev.caffa.site_gap.choice.cargo: Help Rena lift the last fur bundles
ev.caffa.site_gap.choice.route: Ask Rena about the Trebizond crossing
ev.caffa.site_gap.result.cargo: You and Matvei lift the last bundles onto dry slats. Rena checks the coloured stitches and finds every package in its place. When their mother returns, Matvei shows her which ones he stacked himself. She thanks you, and the family tells neighbouring carriers who helped protect the furs.
ev.caffa.site_gap.result.route: Rena points along the Black Sea coast toward Trebizond and tells you where the boatmen gather. Matvei reads the coloured stitches aloud as he counts the bundles for the crossing. You mark Caffa, Trebizond, and the route over the water on your map, then leave them to finish the loading.
ev.caffa.site_gap.title: Fur Bundles by the Shore
ev.caiju.entry.body: Caiju is a small city towards the south-east. The people are subject to the Great Kaan and have paper-money. It stands upon the river before mentioned. At this place are collected great quantities of corn and rice to be transported to the great city of Cambaluc for the use of the Kaan’s Court; for the grain for the Court all comes from this part of the country.
ev.caiju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.caiju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Caiju
ev.cail.a.body: You stand upon the quay where all the ships from the west make land — from Hormos and Kis, from Aden and all Arabia — their decks heavy with chargers and with other wares for sale. Grooms and brokers press close about the gangways, and the smell of salt, tar, and horseflesh hangs upon the air.
ev.cail.a.choice.ask_routes: Ask the shipmasters where their vessels touch next
ev.cail.a.choice.buy_charger: Buy an Arabian charger from the Hormos merchants
ev.cail.a.choice.watch_landing: Stand a day upon the quay and watch the horses come ashore
ev.cail.a.title: The Horse Quay
ev.cail.b.body: King Ashar, the eldest of the five brother-kings of Maabar, keeps great state upon the harbour concourse. He favours merchants and foreigners, and wears upon his person a great store of rich jewels; the crowds that gather for the horse-fairs bring immense business to his city.
ev.cail.b.choice.buy_cotton: Buy cotton cloth in the harbour market
ev.cail.b.choice.hear_brothers: Listen while the brokers speak of the five brother-kings
ev.cail.b.choice.wait_audience: Wait two days upon the concourse in hope of seeing the King pass
ev.cail.b.title: Ashar's Harbour Concourse
ev.cail.battuta_a.body: From the sea you first see the mountain of Serendib standing like a pillar of smoke, nine days before you make the land. The king of Ceylon grants you leave to visit the blessed foot of Adam, and sends you with four Jogees, who make the pilgrimage every year, four Brahmins, and fifteen men carrying provisions. Two roads climb the peak: the easy way of Mama, and the rough way of Baba, by which alone the pilgrimage is counted made. On the hard road, iron pins hold ten chains in the rock; the last is called the chain of witness. At the summit, in a hollow of the stone, lies the foot-mark, eleven spans long.
ev.cail.battuta_a.choice.baba: Climb by the way of Baba
ev.cail.battuta_a.choice.foot: Watch the pilgrims at the foot-mark
ev.cail.battuta_a.choice.ruby: Buy a ruby the islanders sell
ev.cail.battuta_a.title: The Pilgrimage to Adam's Peak
ev.cail.entry.body: Cail is a great and noble city, and belongs to ASHAR, the eldest of the five brother Kings. It is at this city that all the ships touch that come from the west, as from Hormos and from Kis and from Aden, and all Arabia, laden with horses and with other things for sale. And this brings a great concourse of people from the country round about, and so there is great business done in this city of Cail. The King possesses vast treasures, and wears upon his person great store of rich jewels. He maintains great state and administers his kingdom with great equity, and extends great favour to merchants and foreigners, so that they are very glad to visit his city. This King has some 300 wives; for in those parts the man who has most wives is most thought of. As I told you before, there are in this great province of Maabar five crowned Kings, who are all own brothers born of one father and of one mother, and this king is one of them. Their mother is still living.
ev.cail.entry.choice.battuta: Ask of the traveller who climbed Adam's Peak
ev.cail.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.cail.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cail
ev.cairo.caravan.body:
In the eastern caravan yard, two sisters sort dates into small baskets. The older one picks out the softest fruit; her sister slips a few back in. The older girl sees her and rolls up her sleeve. "You have your own share for the road."

Their mother is travelling with a caravan to visit family in Petra. The younger girl wants a few good dates in every basket. Their mother is indoors sewing a waterskin and has no idea what the girls are debating.

Another group in the yard is preparing for Bethlehem. Both groups draw from the same well, their buckets lined up beside it. The younger sister holds a basket out to you. "What if they take ours by mistake? I haven't put our names on them."
ev.cairo.caravan.choice.baskets: Help the sisters mark their baskets
ev.cairo.caravan.choice.bethlehem: Carry the baskets inside, then ask when the Bethlehem caravan leaves
ev.cairo.caravan.result.baskets:
You find a piece of charcoal. The younger sister draws a little star under each basket while the older writes their mother's name. Their mother comes out with the sewn waterskin and sees the marks at once. "Who taught you that?" The girl says she thought of it herself; even far from home, they will recognise their baskets.

The older sister puts the softest dates in her mother's small bag. They thank you, and the keeper of the yard remembers your help.
ev.cairo.caravan.result.bethlehem:
You carry the baskets to the door. Their mother is testing the waterskin seam and asks the girls to move the fruit into the shade. Outside, a driver bound for Bethlehem says his group leaves after dawn through the east gate and will wait for the rear wagons at the crossing.

The younger sister hears you asking directions and presses a date into your hand. "For the road. If you see a basket with a little star, that's ours."
ev.cairo.caravan.title: Date Baskets in the Caravan Yard
ev.calatu.a.body: Calatu is a great city within the Gulf of Calatu, lying six hundred miles north-west of Dufar upon the sea-shore. The people are Saracens and are subject to Hormos; the haven is very large and good, and ships from India crowd the anchorage with spices and other merchandise.
ev.calatu.a.choice.buy_pepper: Buy a sack of pepper from the Indian merchants
ev.calatu.a.choice.count_ships: Stand upon the mole and count the vessels at anchor
ev.calatu.a.choice.walk_walls: Walk the fort walls and look out upon the gulf
ev.calatu.a.title: The Gulf Fortress
ev.calatu.b.body: Whenever the Melic of Hormos is at war with some prince more potent than himself, he betakes himself to this city of Calatu, because it is very strong both from its position and its fortifications. They grow no corn here, but every merchant-vessel that comes brings some.
ev.calatu.b.choice.ask_inland: Ask the caravan masters which inland roads leave from here
ev.calatu.b.choice.buy_dates: Buy dates brought in with the grain ships
ev.calatu.b.choice.hear_refuge: Hear how the Melic of Hormos uses this city as a refuge
ev.calatu.b.title: The Melic's Retreat
ev.calatu.entry.body: Calatu is a great city, within a gulf which bears the name of the Gulf of Calatu. It is a noble city, and lies 600 miles from Dufar towards the north-west, upon the sea-shore. The people are Saracens, and are subject to Hormos. And whenever the Melic of Hormos is at war with some prince more potent than himself, he betakes himself to this city of Calatu, because it is very strong, both from its position and its fortifications. They grow no corn here, but get it from abroad; for every merchant-vessel that comes brings some. The haven is very large and good, and is frequented by numerous ships with goods from India, and from this city the spices and other merchandize are distributed among the cities and towns of the interior. They also export many good Arab horses from this to India. For, as I have told you before, the number of horses exported from this and the other cities to India yearly is something astonishing.
ev.calatu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.calatu.entry.title: Concerning the Gulf of Calatu and the City So Called
ev.camadi.a.body:
Banu leads her grandson through a broken arch. ‘Your great-grandfather kept his dates over there,’ she says, pointing to a patch of wall. The boy asks why they moved. She tells him that the old quarter was damaged in fighting, and the family built again closer to the water.

There is still a path through the ruins toward the Kerman road. Banu will walk it with you, sell you a small bag of dates to eat on the journey, or introduce you to caravan people who know the way toward Cobinan.

The boy asks whether the old house had the same door as theirs now. Banu shows him two stone sockets where a wooden door once turned. ‘Your great-grandfather could hear a camel coming before he saw it,’ she says. You ask what he sold. ‘Mostly dates. If a neighbour had no fruit that week, he let her use the cool room to store hers.’ A caravan driver passing the arch calls Banu by name and asks whether the Kerman turn is still open. She offers to walk there with you and show you.
ev.camadi.a.choice.ask_raids: Ask the caravan people how they choose a safe road
ev.camadi.a.choice.buy_dates: Buy a small bag of dates for 1.2 silver
ev.camadi.a.choice.walk_ruins: Spend a day walking Banu’s old street
ev.camadi.a.title: Banu’s Old Street
ev.camadi.b.body:
A narrow channel feeds Banu’s date palms. Her neighbour covers a basket of fruit against the sun, while two travellers share water under the trees. Beside the fruit stall is a bale of cotton cloth packed for a merchant caravan. One traveller asks where the inland road reaches Hormuz, the port for ships toward Calatu.

Banu says she can name the road to Hormuz and its onward sea passage toward Calatu, as well as the road back to Kerman. You may rest with the travellers for the day or buy the full bale of cloth from the neighbour.

‘Do the boats leave every day?’ the traveller asks. Banu shakes her head. ‘Ask the sailors when you reach the port. I can tell you the road, not their departure.’ Her neighbour lifts the corner of the cotton bale and asks whether you want to see the weave before buying the whole lot. You ask if the cloth has travelled far already. ‘Only from the fields to my loom,’ she says. ‘Your caravan would take it farther than I have.’
ev.camadi.b.choice.ask_calatu: Ask Banu about Calatu and Kerman
ev.camadi.b.choice.buy_cotton: Buy the merchant bale of cotton cloth for 108 silver
ev.camadi.b.choice.rest_shade: Spend a day sharing the shade and water
ev.camadi.b.title: A Hot Afternoon by the Canal
ev.camadi.entry.body:
Camadi stands on a hot plain at the foot of the hills. Old walls stand beside lived-in houses, and date palms shade a row of stalls. A fruit seller named Banu sorts dates while her grandson searches the basket for a pistachio he dropped. Nearby, a merchant asks whether she has any of the fruit travellers call ‘apples of paradise.’

‘Leave that nut,’ Banu tells her grandson. ‘The birds will find it before you do.’ She gives him another, then shows the merchant what remains of the fruit. She tells you where to refill water before crossing the plain. She remembers when more families lived beyond the old walls, and she still knows the names of the lanes there.

A mule driver asks Banu whether her old lane still has a roofed place to rest. ‘The roof is gone,’ she says, ‘but my cousin’s house is beside it. Tell him I sent you.’ Her grandson asks why everyone comes to her for directions. Banu hands him a date and says, ‘Because I have sent them all to your cousin at least once.’ You ask how far the next dependable water is. She sets down the basket to point it out rather than guessing while she works.
ev.camadi.entry.choice.market: Spend a day at the fruit stalls
ev.camadi.entry.title: Camadi at the Edge of the Plain
ev.camadi.oldwell.body:
Behind a row of date palms, two siblings are clearing stones from a well mouth. Their mother remembers drawing water there as a child. The younger one has already hauled out three baskets of gravel and wants to stop; the elder thinks they can finish before the next caravan arrives.

Their mother asks what help you can give. You can spend the day clearing the last stones with them, or walk to the caravan yard and bring the water carriers back to help finish the work.

The younger sibling asks how much more stone they must move. His sister lowers a rope and lets him hear it touch water. ‘Only the top is blocked,’ she says. Their mother laughs at how seriously they have taken a well she once thought abandoned. You ask whether other people may use it when they finish. ‘Of course,’ she answers. ‘That is why the water carriers should know about it.’ The brother looks toward the caravan yard and wonders whether anyone there will lend them a stronger basket.
ev.camadi.oldwell.choice.clear: Spend a day clearing the well
ev.camadi.oldwell.choice.tell: Bring the water carriers to help finish the well
ev.camadi.oldwell.result.clear: You work with the family until the well can be used comfortably. Their mother draws the first bucket and shares the cool water with everyone. After a day’s labour and rest, you feel refreshed.
ev.camadi.oldwell.result.tell: At the caravan yard, the water carriers listen and follow you back to the palms. They help move the last heavy stones, and the family thanks you for bringing them. Word of your help spreads through Camadi.
ev.camadi.oldwell.title: The Well behind the Date Trees
ev.cambaet.entry.body: A dyer in Cambaet is hanging lengths of indigo cloth above the lane. Her apprentice holds one end too low, and a passing merchant nearly walks into it. “Lift it above his turban,” she says. The merchant ducks and asks whether his order has dried. “The dark bolts have. Your sister asked for the lighter shade, remember?” she replies. He admits that he has forgotten which of his family placed the order and pulls a creased note from his belt. She smooths it against a board and reads the mark she made beside the sister’s name. You ask why she uses two blue threads to mark the bundle. “One tells me how often it went into the vat. The other tells the porter whose doorstep to find.” The merchant laughs and helps the apprentice raise the line. Across the lane, cotton is being bundled for the next caravan. The dyer points you toward the through road, then offers to show you the stalls if you can spare a day.
ev.cambaet.entry.choice.look: Spend a day among the dyers and merchants
ev.cambaet.entry.choice.pass: Ask the way through town and continue
ev.cambaet.entry.title: The Blue Cloth Lane
ev.cambaet.site_gap.body: At the dye yard, an apprentice has laid two lengths of cloth side by side. One is a deep blue; the other has pale streaks near its folded edge. “The customer says they were meant to match,” he tells his aunt. She asks whether he unfolded the second length before dyeing it. He looks down at the fold and answers, “I thought the colour would reach through.” She does not scold him. Instead she fills a basin and asks him to rinse both edges so they can see how much dye remains. You ask how long the cloth must stay in the vat. “That depends on the cloth,” she says, lifting the wet end for you to see. “Watch the edge when it dries. If the colour sits only on the surface, another dip won't help until we wash it.” The apprentice fetches clean water. His aunt puts a marker by the road leading toward Semenat so the customer can find them when he returns.
ev.cambaet.site_gap.choice.interact: Help check the two cloth edges
ev.cambaet.site_gap.choice.route: Ask her about the Semenat road
ev.cambaet.site_gap.title: A Colour Returned to the Vat
ev.cambaet.tidemark.body: A boatman's daughter is standing beside a row of stakes at the muddy landing. One has come loose and rolled against a cargo basket. “Father will blame the tide,” she says, “but I tied this one yesterday.” Her father comes up carrying a coil of rope and studies the knot. “You used the short end. Look how it slipped.” She asks whether they can put it back before the next boat arrives. He says yes, then notices that the stake's painted mark has worn away. Without it, the carriers cannot tell where the shallower boats should stop. The girl offers to fetch a pot of pigment from her mother's stall. “Tell her I need the red one,” he says. She gives him a look: “She has only one pot for the landing. You used the rest on the door.” He grins and hands her his rope. You can hold the stake while they reset it, or listen as he explains which waterside road the carriers take toward Tana.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.choice.help: Help reset and mark the stake
ev.cambaet.tidemark.choice.route: Ask where the porters take the goods
ev.cambaet.tidemark.result.help: You hold the stake upright while the boatman drives it into firmer ground. His daughter paints a fresh mark and makes him test her knot. It holds when the next shallow boat touches the landing. The carriers thank you for giving them a place to unload without sinking into the mud.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.result.route: The boatman points along the waterside road used by carriers travelling toward Tana. His daughter corrects him at one fork: the old bank washed out last season, and people now use the higher path. You follow her correction on the ground before moving on, better prepared for the next leg.
ev.cambaet.tidemark.title: The Missing Harbour Mark
ev.cambaluc.a.body: The palace of Cambaluc is the largest roofed building in the world. The great hall, where the Kaan holds his feasts and receives ambassadors, can hold six thousand men seated at table. The roof is painted vermilion, blue, green, and gold — dragons coil around the beams, and phoenixes spread their wings across the ceiling. The floors are of polished marble so clear that a man can see his reflection. The walls are hung with silk embroidered with scenes of hunts on horseback, battles between elephants and tigers, and the celestial palace where the gods feast. The Kaan sits on a raised dais at the northern end of the hall, on a throne of carved jade, so that his gaze falls on every guest.
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.admire: Stand before the great hall and marvel at its size
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.audience: Present yourself at the Kaan's court with gifts
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.talk_guards: Talk to the Kaan's guards about the empire
ev.cambaluc.a.title: The Palace of the Great Khan
ev.cambaluc.b.body: Cambaluc has twelve gates, and beyond each lies a suburb larger than many cities of Christendom or Islam. Merchants from across the empire—Cathay, Manzi, Tangut, Tibet, the Golden Horde, Persia and India—keep warehouses and counting houses there. A thousand carts of silk enter the city each day; forty more carts of pepper, spices and rare goods are consumed. The Great Khan keeps public granaries where those who ask receive rice and millet. Beyond every gate an inn receives travellers who reach the city after curfew. An innkeeper hangs a lantern outside while the staff sing of a bed and grain for the weary traveller, silk from Cathay and scent from Persia, and trading again in the morning. “After the gates shut, we still take people in,” he says. “The granary distributes food by its rules. First let them rest; business can wait until dawn.”
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.count: Count the cart-loads of silk entering the city in a day
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.granary: Visit the public granaries — no one goes hungry here
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.silk: Buy silk at the Cambaluc price
ev.cambaluc.b.title: The Twelve Suburbs
ev.cambaluc.c.body: In the great park behind the palace, the Kaan has caused a mountain to be raised — a hill of green jade, of jasper, and of lapis lazuli, brought block by block from the quarries of Badakhshan and Cotan. It is covered with evergreens: cedars, pines, and cypresses, each one dug up by the roots in distant forests, wrapped in silk and wet earth, and carried here on the backs of elephants. The trees do not know they have been moved; they grow as green as in their native soil. A thousand gardeners water them daily by hand, climbing the artificial mountain with buckets hung from shoulder-poles. The Kaan comes here in the evenings, when the shadows are long, and walks alone among the transplanted trees. No one may disturb him.
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.evening: Climb the hill at sunset and see the whole city
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.gardener: Talk to the gardeners who water the trees by hand
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.walk: Walk among the transplanted trees on the green hill
ev.cambaluc.c.title: The Mountain of Green Jade
