ev.cambaluc.entry.body: You must know that the city of Cambaluc hath such a multitude of houses, and such a vast population inside the walls and outside, that it seems quite past all possibility. There is a suburb outside each of the gates, which are twelve in number; and these suburbs are so great that they contain more people than the city itself [for the suburb of one gate spreads in width till it meets the suburb of the next, whilst they extend in length some three or four miles]. In those suburbs lodge the foreign merchants and travellers, of whom there are always great numbers who have come to bring presents to the Emperor, or to sell articles at Court, or because the city affords so good a mart to attract traders. [There are in each of the suburbs, to a distance of a mile from the city, numerous fine hostelries for the lodgment of merchants from different parts of the world, and a special hostelry is assigned to each description of people, as if we should say there is one for the Lombards, another for the Germans, and a third for the Frenchmen.] And thus there are as many good houses outside of the city as inside, without counting those that belong to the great lords and barons, which are very numerous. You must know that it is forbidden to bury any dead body inside the city. If the body be that of an Idolater it is carried out beyond the city and suburbs to a remote place assigned for the purpose, to be burnt. And if it be of one belonging to a religion the custom of which is to bury, such as the Christian, the Saracen, or what not, it is also carried out beyond the suburbs to a distant place assigned for the purpose. And thus the city is preserved in a better and more healthy state. Moreover, no public woman resides inside the city, but all such abide outside in the suburbs. And ’tis wonderful what a vast number of these there are for the foreigners; it is a certain fact that there are more than 20,000 of them living by prostitution.
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the shìbó sī (市舶司)
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.cambaluc.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cambaluc, and Its Great Traffic and Population
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.body: A chronologer of the Astronomical Bureau will sit with you fourteen days and teach the casting of hexagrams for the road. He does not ask after fortune. He asks after time and position — which season a road is open, and where a man stands when he chooses it.
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.ask: Hear how hexagrams speak of roads
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.learn: Pay the fee and learn I Ching
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.title: I Ching at Khanbaliq
ev.campichu.a.body: You stand in the capital of the whole province of Tangut, where the governor's clerks weigh out salt certificates and tally the tribute of the western marches. Caravans from the sandy desert to the north unload camels in the outer wards, and the market runs from dawn until the third watch without ceasing.
ev.campichu.a.choice.caravan: Bargain with desert caravans for tea
ev.campichu.a.choice.clerks: Watch the governor's clerks at their tally
ev.campichu.a.choice.pass: Pass through the government quarter without delay
ev.campichu.a.title: The Seat of Tangut
ev.campichu.b.body: In Campichu you find three very fine Christian churches standing near many idol abbeys after the local fashion. Within the latter lie enormous gilded figures, some ten paces in length, with lesser images adoring before them. Saracens also keep their mosques here, so that four faiths share one street without quarrel.
ev.campichu.b.choice.abbey: Walk the idol abbeys and note their gilded figures
ev.campichu.b.choice.churches: Enter one of the three Christian churches
ev.campichu.b.choice.offering: Leave a small offering at an abbey gate
ev.campichu.b.title: Churches and Abbeys
ev.campichu.entry.body: Campichu is also a city of Tangut, and a very great and noble one. Indeed it is the capital and place of government of the whole province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, Saracens, and Christians, and the latter have three very fine churches in the city, whilst the Idolaters have many minsters and abbeys after their fashion. In these they have an enormous number of idols, both small and great, certain of the latter being a good ten paces in stature; some of them being of wood, others of clay, and others yet of stone. They are all highly polished, and then covered with gold. The great idols of which I speak lie at length. And round about them there are other figures of considerable size, as if adoring and paying homage before them. Now, as I have not yet given you particulars about the customs of these Idolaters, I will proceed to tell you about them. You must know that there are among them certain religious recluses who lead a more virtuous life than the rest.
ev.campichu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.campichu.entry.title: Of the City of Campichu
ev.camul.a.body:
At the melon market, the seller Nuri is tying a reed tag to a basket. Her brother has been tending the water gate and says the next family has asked to open it early. Their melon vines are wilting. Nuri checks the wooden turn board: her own garden still has an hour of water left. ‘If they take it now, the end of our row stays dry,’ she says.

A child from the neighbouring garden arrives carrying a cut melon. She asks whether Nuri will trade the hour for this one. Nuri smiles but tells her the board belongs to everyone, so the adults must agree. You ask how they keep track. Her brother shows you the marks for each garden and the small channels leading from the well.

The child sits beside the baskets to wait for her mother. Nuri cuts a slice and holds it up for you to see while they talk. You can spend the day walking the beds and learn their watering routine, buy a small piece for 0.6 silver and eat it, or ask the drivers which roads lead to Lop and Suzhou.
ev.camul.a.choice.ask-traders: Ask the drivers about Lop and Suzhou
ev.camul.a.choice.buy-melons: Buy a small piece of melon for 0.6 silver
ev.camul.a.choice.walk: Spend the day among the melon beds
ev.camul.a.title: The Melon Seller’s Water Turn
ev.camul.b.body:
An older keeper is sweeping sand from the courtyard of a local shrine. His nephew has laid out mats for travellers, but one has a torn edge and catches on everyone’s shoes. The keeper asks him to take it back inside. ‘The visitors can use the good ones while I mend this,’ he says.

A woman arrives with her father, who needs shade after the road. She asks whether they may sit for a moment. The keeper pours tea and tells his nephew to bring the low stool. The boy asks about an old local tale of how their families once welcomed passing strangers. ‘I heard it from my uncle,’ the keeper answers. ‘First find this gentleman somewhere comfortable to sit. We can tell the story while he rests.’

You help move the stool and ask whether the old man would like more water. He says he would rather hear where the next well lies. You can stay a day to hear the keeper’s account, quietly observe the courtyard gathering, or ask him about the eastern road toward Etzina.
ev.camul.b.choice.ask-east: Wait a day for a returning driver and ask about Etzina
ev.camul.b.choice.listen: Stay a day and hear the keeper’s story
ev.camul.b.title: The Courtyard Keeper’s Guest
ev.camul.entry.body:
At the Hami oasis, a cart driver is counting the water skins beside a melon stall. His daughter has marked each one with a strip of cloth so the family will not confuse drinking water with water for washing the animals. She finds two with the same colour and asks him which he filled at the well. ‘The heavy one,’ he says, then lifts both and admits he cannot tell.

The melon seller calls them over. She calls the morning water carrier over. He recognises the patched strap on the skin he filled at the sweet well, and the seller gives the girl a fresh strip of cloth. You ask where a traveller can sleep. The seller points to a lodging yard; the driver says its owner keeps the animals under shade, though the courtyard fills quickly when caravans arrive.

The girl ties the new strip and asks whether you have room for a melon. Her father laughs: ‘First make sure your own water is marked.’ You can mark Hami and go on, spend a day among the market stalls, or visit the local place of worship and meet the people who care for it.
ev.camul.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the market stalls
ev.camul.entry.choice.shrine: Visit the local place of worship
ev.camul.entry.title: At the Hami Oasis
ev.camul.waterboard.body:
At a narrow channel beyond the market, two children are looking for the board that shows whose garden receives water next. Their grandfather set it beside the sluice, but the wind has carried it into the reeds. One child wants to guess from yesterday’s order; the other says their neighbours swapped turns this morning.

You ask the grandfather whether the board can be replaced. ‘We can make another,’ he says, ‘but the old marks will tell us what everyone agreed.’ A woman from the next garden arrives with a jar of drinking water and asks if they have found it. The younger child spots a corner of wood by the bank. All three lean down, and the grandfather warns them to hold the gate before anyone pulls the board free.

You can spend a day helping them recover and repaint the turn marks with the neighbours, or listen as the grandfather explains each mark and write down how the oasis shares the channel.
ev.camul.waterboard.choice.learn: Ask how the turn marks work
ev.camul.waterboard.choice.restore: Spend a day restoring the water board
ev.camul.waterboard.result.learn: The grandfather explains the marks while the children put the board back. You write down the watering order and the way they record changes, then leave them to open the gate for the next garden.
ev.camul.waterboard.result.restore: You help repaint the marks and wait while each neighbour checks their agreed turn. At dusk the children hang the board under shelter. Their grandfather thanks you, and the families along the channel know your name.
ev.camul.waterboard.title: The Missing Water Board
ev.caracoron.entry.body: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there. And beside it there is a great citadel wherein is a fine palace in which the Governor resides.] ’Tis the first city that the Tartars possessed after they issued from their own country. And now I will tell you all about how they first acquired dominion and spread over the world. Originally the Tartars dwelt in the north on the borders of CHORCHA.
ev.caracoron.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.caracoron.entry.title: Of the City of Caracoron
ev.caracoron.site_gap.body: Outside a tent, a groom twists horsehair into a thin cord and draws it taut around a wooden peg. It can stitch a saddlebag or tie down tent cloth, he says. Horsehair tightens when wet, so leave some slack in a knot. A young horse noses at your sleeve. The groom washes grease from the hair before twisting it, so the strands grip rather than slip.
ev.caracoron.site_gap.choice.interact: Try twisting a length of rope
ev.caracoron.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Camul
ev.caracoron.site_gap.title: Horsehair Rope Outside the Camp
ev.cascar.a.body:
In an orchard outside the market, grower Rima is checking a narrow channel with her daughter. Their neighbour’s branch takes water first today, but a loose stone has let some spill into the path. ‘Should I block it?’ the girl asks. Rima shakes her head. ‘Call him over. It is his turn, and he should see what we mend.’ The neighbour comes with a small spade and thanks them for waiting.

You ask whether the fruit has suffered. Rima points to one vine whose leaves are still cool, then to a younger row that needs the afternoon flow. The neighbour offers to lift the stone while you hold the channel gate. Her daughter has picked a melon for sale at 0.5 silver and packed a parcel of dried grapes for 1 silver. She asks which will travel better, and Rima lets her answer after she has carried both across the yard.

The water begins to run where it should. Rima invites you to stay a day and see the orchard after its turn; her daughter keeps the two parcels in the shade until you decide.
ev.cascar.a.choice.orchard: Stay a day to see the orchard water turn
ev.cascar.a.title: The Orchard Water Turn
ev.cascar.b.body:
At a weaving bench, Saliha is finishing a carpet while her aunt stirs a dye vat outside. Her younger brother has copied the border pattern onto scrap cloth, but he has left out the small turn at one corner. ‘It will still lie flat,’ he says. Saliha shows him the finished edge. ‘Yes, but your grandmother will know which hand made it.’ He tries again, this time watching her fingers.

You ask whether the pattern belongs to their family. The aunt says they learned it from her mother and have changed it for different buyers. She sets out a packet of dye samples for 1.5 silver; Saliha has one finished trading carpet priced at 116 silver. Her brother asks whether buyers care about the small turn. One waiting customer says he did not notice until Saliha pointed it out, but now he wants to see the whole border.

Saliha invites you to sit for a day if you wish to learn the work. The aunt checks the vat, and the customer bends down to follow the pattern around the corner.
ev.cascar.b.choice.carpet: Buy the finished carpet for 116 silver
ev.cascar.b.choice.dyes: Buy the dye samples for 1.5 silver
ev.cascar.b.choice.learn_weave: Stay a day and learn the border pattern
ev.cascar.b.title: The Weaver’s Narrow Border
ev.cascar.c.body:
At a cave outside Kashgar, keeper Mariam is sweeping the space where visitors sit. An older Muslim neighbour brings a lamp; a Christian traveller arrives with a small candle. Both ask where they may set them. Mariam points to separate shelves, then asks them to leave the walking path clear. Her son carries away a basket of spent wicks and asks whether the two visitors tell the same story about the sleepers.

‘We remember it in our prayers,’ the neighbour says. The traveller adds, ‘I learned different names from my father.’ Mariam tells her son to listen to each guest before repeating either version. You ask whether the cave itself has always been called by that story. ‘The people who come here know it by that name,’ she says. ‘My family looks after the place they actually use.’ The child checks the shelves and makes room for one more light.

The visitors invite you to sit with them. Mariam can give you a sheltered place for the night if you want to stay and help tidy the cave in the morning.
ev.cascar.c.choice.both: Stay the night and hear both visitors
ev.cascar.c.choice.christian: Hear the Christian traveller’s family version
ev.cascar.c.choice.muslim: Hear the neighbour’s version of the sleepers
ev.cascar.c.title: Two Visitors at the Cave
ev.cascar.entry.body:
At a relay yard in Kashgar, a weaver’s son named Tariq is repairing a cord that records the handover of pack animals. His father has sent him a roll of cloth, but one knot has slipped beneath the seal. ‘If I count it as an animal, they will charge us for a horse we never had,’ Tariq says. The yard clerk makes him loosen the cord and show the older mark.

You ask where to find water before the next stage. Tariq points to a channel running by the market, then asks the clerk whether it is flowing today. ‘It is,’ she says, ‘but the far orchard gets its turn after noon.’ A fruit seller behind her has a sealed lot of jade for 135 silver, though he is more interested in whether his melons have reached the stall without bruising. Tariq asks him to move the crate out of the animal path.

The clerk invites you to stay two days and learn the relay’s records. Tariq can introduce you to his family’s garden tomorrow. The merchant pulls a sample from the jade pack while the repaired cord dries on the fence.
ev.cascar.entry.choice.customs: Stay two days to learn the relay records
ev.cascar.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day with Tariq’s family in the gardens
ev.cascar.entry.choice.market: Buy the sealed jade lot for 135 silver
ev.cascar.entry.title: The Relay Cord at Kashgar
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.body:
Guide Habib is mending a harness at the relay bench when a young carrier asks how much water to take over the next pass. Habib does not answer until the carrier shows him the weight of his load. ‘Your uncle travelled light last week,’ he says. ‘You have two more bundles.’ The carrier looks at his pack and admits he copied his uncle’s plan without checking.

You ask how Habib learns when a path changes. He keeps notes from returning drivers and walks the first stage when he can. Tariq comes through the yard with his repaired cord and adds that one trough has been fixed since yesterday. Habib asks him to show the carrier the new mark. The carrier says he can wait while they check the next station’s water.

Habib invites you to listen at his bench if you have a day. He has a map cloth and several old accounts, and he wants to know what you noticed on your own way into Kashgar.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Habib about the next pass
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: Habib asks about your load, then has Tariq show you the repaired trough on the cord. The young carrier copies the same mark. You leave knowing the guide and the first question he asks every traveller.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay a day with Habib and check the route accounts
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day at Habib’s bench. He compares the cloth map with accounts from three drivers, and the young carrier writes his own load beside the water stops. Habib asks you to come back if you want to see how he checks the remaining stage.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank Habib and continue. He is still adjusting the harness for the young carrier, who has finally added a second water skin. Tariq calls out the next station’s name as you leave the yard.
ev.cascar.mentor_closure.title: The Relay Guide’s Bench
ev.cascar.redthread.body:
Near the weaving quarter, a girl named Nura is trying to match a short red thread to a much older one sewn into her grandmother’s shawl. Her mother has asked her to repair the loose edge before Grandmother’s visit. The new thread looks right in the sun, but indoors it turns brighter than the old dye. ‘She will see it at once,’ Nura says. Her younger brother answers that Grandmother mostly notices whether they come to sit with her.

You ask where the old thread came from. Nura’s mother says her own mother dyed it many years ago and has mended the shawl several times since. She does not mind a visible seam; she would rather the cloth hold through the next cold season. Nura tests a stitch on the inner edge, then asks whether the thread should run all the way around or only across the worn part.

Their mother can teach you the repair as she works. If you stay for the day, Nura will also tell her grandmother who helped finish it. The younger brother has already pulled up an extra stool.
ev.cascar.redthread.choice.learn: Ask the mother to show the stitch
ev.cascar.redthread.choice.sew: Stay a day and finish the shawl edge
ev.cascar.redthread.result.learn: Nura’s mother shows you how to catch the old edge without pulling it tight. You try a stitch on a scrap, and Nura compares it with her own. She keeps working on the shawl after you go; you record the small repair in your travel notes.
ev.cascar.redthread.result.sew: You spend the day sewing the worn edge with Nura and her mother. Grandmother arrives in the evening, feels the strong new seam, and asks Nura who sat with her through the work. The family thanks you, and the repaired shawl is ready for cold weather.
ev.cascar.redthread.title: The Red Thread for Grandmother
ev.chamba.a.body: The King of Chamba pays a yearly tribute to the Great Kaan, which consists of elephants and nothing but elephants. It was settled in the year 1278, when the Kaan sent Baron Sagatu against this kingdom and the aged King sought peace by offering this tribute alone.
ev.chamba.a.choice.buy_sandalwood: Buy sandalwood from the tribute quarter
ev.chamba.a.choice.hear_tribute: Hear the full tale of how the elephant tribute was settled
ev.chamba.a.choice.watch_harbour: Watch a day upon the harbour while tribute goods are tallied
ev.chamba.a.title: The Elephant Tribute
ev.chamba.b.body: Chamba is a very rich region lying west-south-west of Zayton, having a king of its own. The people are Idolaters, and the kingdom is wealthy with aloewood, spices, and the traffic of the southern seas.
ev.chamba.b.choice.ask_sea_road: Ask the mariners how many days' sail lie to Zayton and Fuzhou
ev.chamba.b.choice.buy_pepper: Buy pepper from the spice merchants
ev.chamba.b.choice.visit_court: Wait two days upon the harbour to hear word of the King's court
ev.chamba.b.title: The Idolater Kingdom
ev.chamba.entry.body: You must know that on leaving the port of Zayton you sail west-south-west for 1500 miles, and then you come to a country called CHAMBA, a very rich region, having a king of its own. The people are Idolaters and pay a yearly tribute to the Great Kaan, which consists of elephants and nothing but elephants. And I will tell you how they came to pay this tribute. It happened in the year of Christ 1278 that the Great Kaan sent a Baron of his called Sagatu with a great force of horse and foot against this King of Chamba, and this Baron opened the war on a great scale against the King and his country. Now the King was a very aged man, nor had he such a force as the Baron had. And when he saw what havoc the Baron was making with his kingdom he was grieved to the heart. So he bade messengers get ready and despatched them to the Great Kaan.
ev.chamba.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.chamba.entry.title: Of the Great Country Called Chamba
ev.chandu.a.body: The Great Kaan has a summer palace at Chandu built entirely of gilded cane — the columns, the walls, the roof-beams, everything. The cane is harvested from a forest in the south of Manzi, split, lacquered, and gilded with gold leaf before being lashed together with silken cords. The palace can be taken down and moved when the Kaan travels, for it is held together only by the silk bindings. Dragons in green, blue, vermilion, and gold coil up every pillar. Inside, the floors are laid with marble slabs so polished that they reflect the gilded ceiling. No other building in the world is so light and yet so splendid.
ev.chandu.a.choice.admire: Admire the palace from the meadow outside
ev.chandu.a.choice.enter: Bribe the guards and step inside the gilded cane palace
ev.chandu.a.choice.sketch: Spend a day sketching the palace in detail
ev.chandu.a.title: The Cane Palace
ev.chandu.b.body: Behind the palace, enclosed by a wall that runs for sixteen miles, is the Kaan's game park — a forest so dense and so large that a man on horseback cannot cross it in a single day. It is stocked with deer, boar, wild ass, bear, and leopard for the Kaan's sport. At the center is a lake fed by a stream, and on the lake every species of waterfowl known to man. The Kaan rides here with his falconers, his huntsmen, and his cheetah-keepers. In one corner of the park, a herd of a thousand white mares is kept — their milk is reserved for the imperial family alone, and the mares are so sacred that no one of lower rank may ride them, touch them, or even walk in their pasture.
ev.chandu.b.choice.falcon: Hire a falconer and hunt with the Kaan's own birds
ev.chandu.b.choice.horses: Find a gap in the wall and watch the sacred white mares
ev.chandu.b.choice.walk: Walk the edge of the sixteen-mile wall
ev.chandu.b.title: The Game Park
ev.chandu.c.body: In the meadow, a groom brushes a white horse. You ask about Mongol rites. He first makes sure you are not mocking them, then tells you that people have offered milk to Eternal Heaven and prayed for abundant pasture. At the mention of white mares, he lowers his voice. “Outsiders do not often hear that part.”
ev.chandu.c.choice.listen: Ask a monk what the ceremony means
ev.chandu.c.choice.offering: Pour an offering to the Eternal Blue Sky
ev.chandu.c.choice.watch_mares: Watch the monks milk the white mares at dawn
ev.chandu.c.title: The Meadow of the Milky Kine
ev.chandu.entry.body: And when you have ridden three days from the city last mentioned, between north-east and north, you come to a city called CHANDU, which was built by the Kaan now reigning. There is at this place a very fine marble Palace, the rooms of which are all gilt and painted with figures of men and beasts and birds, and with a variety of trees and flowers, all executed with such exquisite art that you regard them with delight and astonishment. Round this Palace a wall is built, inclosing a compass of 16 miles, and inside the Park there are fountains and rivers and brooks, and beautiful meadows, with all kinds of wild animals (excluding such as are of ferocious nature), which the Emperor has procured and placed there to supply food for his gerfalcons and hawks, which he keeps there in mew. Of these there are more than 200 gerfalcons alone, without reckoning the other hawks. The Kaan himself goes every week to see his birds sitting in mew, and sometimes he rides through the park with a leopard behind him on his horse’s croup; and then if he sees any animal that takes his fancy, he slips his leopard at it, and the game when taken is made over to feed the hawks in mew. This he does for diversion. Moreover [at a spot in the Park where there is a charming wood] he has another Palace built of cane, of which I must give you a description. It is gilt all over, and most elaborately finished inside. [It is stayed on gilt and lackered columns, on each of which is a dragon all gilt, the tail of which is attached to the column whilst the head supports the architrave, and the claws likewise are stretched out right and left to support the architrave.] The roof, like the rest, is formed of canes, covered with a varnish so strong and excellent that no amount of rain will rot them. These canes are a good 3 palms in girth, and from 10 to 15 paces in length.
ev.chandu.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods to the darughachi (overseer)
ev.chandu.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.chandu.entry.title: Of the City of Chandu, and the Kaan’s Palace There
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.body: Beside the meadow, a horse trainer asks which mount you like. He glances at your baggage. “First decide how far you must travel, then choose a horse that can carry you there.”
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask what the road will demand
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: The court horse-master answers without evasion: reading the land, and the wind, will be asked of you. His lesson is offered, and what you make of it lies with you.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay for a day and listen to the whole account
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day at the meadow with the horse-master, and he gives you the whole of the Kaan's keeping at leisure. What he lays before you at parting is a promise the northern meadow will honour.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank the guide and keep moving
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank the court horse-master and take the road. He lets you go with a blessing, and the lesson of Chandu remains unwritten.
ev.chandu.mentor_closure.title: The Horse Trainer by the Meadow
ev.charchan.entry.body:
By a stream outside Charchan, a boy is washing sand from a handful of river stones. His aunt, who buys stones for a trader, asks him to put the cracked pieces back. He holds one up to the light. ‘This one looks sound.’ She turns it in her fingers and shows him a thin line along the edge.

You ask whether every stream here has good drinking water. ‘No,’ the aunt says, and points to two water carriers walking in from different directions. One fills at a sweet well; the other brings water for washing from a bitter source. The boy asks how you can tell the difference. ‘You ask the person who filled the skin,’ she replies. The carrier agrees, then tells him to stop setting the clean stones in the wet sand.

The boy spreads his sleeve and starts again. His aunt says merchants take sound jasper and chalcedony east, though finding a piece worth keeping takes patience. You can mark Charchan and continue, or spend a day asking which wells travellers use and learning how she sorts the stones.
ev.charchan.entry.choice.look: Stay a day by the stream and ask about the wells
ev.charchan.entry.title: A River Stone at Charchan
ev.charchan.site_gap.body:
At the oasis well, a water carrier named Aysa is changing a worn rope. Her younger brother has tied the replacement to the bucket, but the knot catches on the stone rim each time he lowers it. Aysa asks him to pull it up and try again. He worries the people waiting with their jars will complain.

‘They have seen us fix worse,’ she says. A woman in the queue sets down her jar and asks whether Aysa can still fill it before the cooking fire goes out. Aysa tells her yes and asks you to hold the loose end of the rope. You do, while her brother unwinds the knot and tries a flatter one.

You ask which road reaches Pein. Aysa says she can show you after the bucket comes up smoothly; she knows the drinking wells on that road. Her brother gives the rope a cautious pull. This time the knot clears the rim, and the waiting woman leans forward to see whether the bucket has stayed upright. You can ask Aysa to trace the road, or stay at the well and learn the knot yourself.
ev.charchan.site_gap.choice.interact: Learn to tie the new rope
ev.charchan.site_gap.choice.route: Ask Aysa to trace the road to Pein
ev.charchan.site_gap.title: The Rope at the Oasis Well
ev.charchan.stonebag.body:
A girl at the river crossing is searching the sand for a small cloth pouch. She had gathered three stones for her grandfather, who teaches her to polish them, but one strap broke while she helped a traveller lift his basket. Her grandfather sits nearby with his polishing wheel and calls her back for a drink. She shakes her head: she remembers leaving the pouch above the wet bank.

You ask what the stones look like. ‘One dark, two pale,’ she says. ‘The dark one has a white line.’ A boatman points out that the water has already fallen since morning; anything dropped near the bank may still be between the reeds. Her grandfather calls again, asking whether she wants him to come. She finally tells him what happened. ‘We can look together,’ he says, leaving the wheel covered against the dust.

You can spend the day searching the reeds with them, or help the boatman finish sorting his cargo and earn a little money before the next crossing. The girl says she will keep looking either way, and her grandfather brings her water first.
ev.charchan.stonebag.choice.search: Search the reeds for a day
ev.charchan.stonebag.result.cargo: You sort the sacks by crossing and the boatman pays you 0.8 silver. As you finish, the grandfather and girl find the pouch at the edge of the reeds. She holds it up for you to see before they go home.
ev.charchan.stonebag.result.search: You find the torn strap caught beneath a reed root. The three stones are still in the pouch. The girl shows her grandfather the one with the white line; he says she may polish it tomorrow. You spend the day there, and the family thanks you.
ev.charchan.stonebag.title: The Missing Stone Pouch
ev.chinangli.a.body: A great and wide river runs through Chinangli, and upon it you see silk goods, spices, and other costly merchandize passing up and down without pause. The quays are stacked with bales, and boatmen shout the names of towns far south and north while they warp their vessels to the bank.
ev.chinangli.a.choice.quay: Walk the quay and count the upstream boats
ev.chinangli.a.choice.silk: Buy a bolt of river-traded silk
ev.chinangli.a.choice.spice: Ask which spices the downstream boats carry
ev.chinangli.a.title: The Great River Traffic
ev.chinangli.b.body: The people of Chinangli are idolaters subject to the Great Kaan, and they trade with stamped paper-money in every shop and stall. You watch clerks exchange worn notes for fresh ones, and merchants weigh out goods against the Khan's seal without once touching silver.
ev.chinangli.b.choice.clerks: Ask the exchange clerks how the notes are renewed
ev.chinangli.b.choice.exchange: Watch the paper-money exchange at a stall
ev.chinangli.b.choice.porcelain: Buy a small porcelain bowl with paper-money
ev.chinangli.b.title: Paper-Money of Cathay
ev.chinangli.entry.body: Chinangli is a city of Cathay as you go south, and it belongs to the Great Kaan; the people are Idolaters, and have paper-money. There runs through the city a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices and other costly merchandize passes up and down. When you travel south from Chinangli for five days, you meet everywhere with fine towns and villages, the people of which are all Idolaters, and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts, and have all the necessaries of life in great abundance. But there is nothing particular to mention on the way till you come, at the end of those five days, to TADINFU. This, you must know, is a very great city, and in old times was the seat of a great kingdom; but the Great Kaan conquered it by force of arms. Nevertheless it is still the noblest city in all those provinces. There are very great merchants here, who trade on a great scale, and the abundance of silk is something marvellous.
ev.chinangli.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.chinangli.entry.title: Arriving at CHINANGLI
ev.chinghianfu.entry.body: Chinghianfu is a city of Manzi. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by handicrafts and trade. They have plenty of silk, from which they make sundry kinds of stuffs of silk and gold. There are great and wealthy merchants in the place; plenty of game is to be had, and of all kinds of victual. There are in this city two churches of Nestorian Christians which were established in the year of our Lord 1278; and I will tell you how that happened.
ev.chinghianfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.chinghianfu.entry.title: Of the City of Chinghianfu
ev.chinginju.entry.body: Leaving the city of Chinghianfu and travelling three days south-east through a constant succession of busy and thriving towns and villages, you arrive at the great and noble city of CHINGINJU. The people are Idolaters, use paper-money, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They live by trade and handicrafts, and they have plenty of silk. They have also abundance of game, and of all manner of victuals, for it is a most productive territory. Now I must tell you of an evil deed that was done, once upon a time, by the people of this city, and how dearly they paid for it.
ev.chinginju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.chinginju.entry.title: Of the City of Chinginju and the Slaughter of Certain Alans There
ev.cobinan.entry.body:
At a Cobinan metalworker’s shop, an apprentice holds a polished steel mirror so her father can inspect the surface. His reflection wavers where she has not finished working, and he sends her back to the bench with a smile.

Across the lane, another workshop tends a furnace for mineral work. The workers keep the pale deposit caught above the furnace separate from the residue below; traders call the first tutiya and the second spodium. The apprentice points you toward a place to rest and asks whether you have seen a polished steel mirror before.

The apprentice asks her father whether she should start again on the uneven patch. ‘Just that patch,’ he says. ‘Turn it toward the doorway and look at the line of light.’ She does, and the uneven patch is easier to see in the shifting light. You ask what the workers across the lane sell from their furnace. The father names the two materials they keep apart and adds that traders come looking for them as well as for mirrors. His daughter asks you to come back when she has finished polishing; she wants another pair of eyes on her work.
ev.cobinan.entry.choice.look: Spend a day visiting the workshops
ev.cobinan.entry.title: At the Mirror Workshop
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.body:
At the metalworker’s shop, the apprentice’s father has finished a small mirror for his sister. She is opening a stall and wants it to hang beside the door. He has made a wooden case to protect it on the journey across town, but he cannot leave the forge before dusk.

He offers to pay you for taking it over and helping her hang it, a job that will take the day. If you are short of time, he can instead show you how the mirror’s face was finished while the case is still open.

His apprentice asks whether the case needs more padding. ‘Enough to keep the mirror from knocking against the lid,’ he says, pressing the cloth down around it. You ask why his sister wants a mirror beside a market door. ‘She sells ribbons,’ he replies. ‘People like to see how they look before buying.’ The apprentice suggests carrying it herself, but her father reminds her of the unfinished work at the bench. She asks you to tell her aunt who polished the mirror if you take it over.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.choice.deliver: Spend a day delivering and hanging the mirror
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.choice.learn: Ask how he finished the mirror’s face
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.result.deliver: You carry the case to his sister’s new stall and help hang the mirror. She checks its angle, then sends a note of thanks to her brother. When you return, he pays you 0.5 silver for the day.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.result.learn: He tilts the mirror in the light and shows you the faint marks left before the final polish. You write down what he tells you about Cobinan’s metalwork and leave him to his forge.
ev.cobinan.mirrorcase.title: The Mirror for His Sister
ev.codex_legend_seed.body: Among a scholar's papers you find wonder-tales and Chinese road chronicles — Prester John beside Wang Dayuan, paradise beside Zhenla. Will you copy them into your own book?
ev.codex_legend_seed.choice_1_result: You copy Prester John, the Earthly Paradise, and the Chinese road leaves into your codex.
ev.codex_legend_seed.choice_2_result: You leave the stack undisturbed. The wonder can wait.
ev.codex_legend_seed.title: Leaves of Wonder and Chronicle
ev.coigangiu.entry.body: Huaiyin — a boat-town on the Grand Canal. Every family keeps a sampan; the children learn to row before they learn to walk. The grain fleet passes through here in autumn on its way to Cambaluc; the inns are full of boatmen, and the smell of river-fish frying drifts across the water from dawn till midnight.
ev.coigangiu.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.coigangiu.entry.title: Arriving at Coigangiu
ev.coiganju.entry.body: Coiganju is, as I have told you already, a very large city standing at the entrance to Manzi. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They have a vast amount of shipping, as I mentioned before in speaking of the River Caramoran. And an immense quantity of merchandize comes hither, for the city is the seat of government for this part of the country. Owing to its being on the river, many cities send their produce thither to be again thence distributed in every direction.
ev.coiganju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.coiganju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Coiganju
ev.coilum.entry.body: When you quit Maabar and go 500 miles towards the south-west you come to the kingdom of COILUM. The people are Idolaters, but there are also some Christians and some Jews. The natives have a language of their own, and a King of their own, and are tributary to no one. A great deal of brazil is got here which is called _brazil Coilumin_ from the country which produces it; ’tis of very fine quality. Good ginger also grows here, and it is known by the same name of _Coilumin_ after the country. Pepper too grows in great abundance throughout this country, and I will tell you how.
ev.coilum.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.coilum.entry.title: Of the Kingdom of Coilum
ev.coilum.site_gap.body: Pepper sacks rise shoulder-high against the open warehouse door. A weighman sets a weight on the scale. Two sacks may look equal, he says, while dampness changes their weight. Weigh the empty sack first, then the goods. A dry leaf lies beside the scale: when it softens, he checks the sacks for moisture.
ev.coilum.site_gap.choice.interact: Help weigh a sack of pepper again
ev.coilum.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the coastal road to Maabar
ev.coilum.site_gap.title: The Pepper Scale at the Harbour
ev.constantinopolis.entry.body:
At the Golden Horn, a water carrier named Anna finds that one of her jars is empty. Her brother has taken the full jar to a household above the harbour and left her the empty one by mistake. She laughs, then counts her customers aloud so she can decide whom to visit first.

A channel brings water into the city, and covered cisterns hold supplies for its many households. Anna has spent years carrying water up these streets. She points out the dome of Hagia Sophia between the roofs, then asks whether you have a place to stay; she can show you the quay or the lodging lane once she gets her jar back.

A baker by the quay asks, ‘Have you forgotten my water again?’ Anna lifts the empty jar for him to see. ‘My brother has yours. I’ll bring it as soon as he comes down.’ He offers her a piece of bread while she waits. You ask whether the cistern is far. ‘The small covered one is around that corner,’ she says. ‘If you go up the hill, take the lane with the stone steps. My brother always chooses the flatter way and arrives late.’
ev.constantinopolis.entry.choice.look: Spend a day following Anna’s directions
ev.constantinopolis.entry.title: Water at the Golden Horn
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.body:
Anna’s brother returns carrying the empty jar and an apology. The household on the hill has asked for more water for a neighbour who is ill. Anna still has two regular deliveries to make before dark.

‘Come with me up the hill and I’ll manage the rest,’ she says. Her brother offers to carry your pack if you would rather pay for a filled cup and rest by the cistern. He is determined to deliver the next jar correctly.

Her brother says the sick neighbour is the baker’s mother. ‘I told her I’d come back,’ he says, taking the heavy end of the pole. Anna asks why he left an empty jar at the quay. ‘I thought you would want one ready to fill.’ She taps his shoulder with her free hand. You ask whether there is time for the hill before dark. Anna looks at the light on the roofs: ‘If we leave now, yes. Otherwise I can still sell you a cup from the cistern.’
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.choice.drin: Buy a cup of water for 0.4 silver
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.result.carr: You walk uphill with Anna and leave the jar at the neighbour’s door. She thanks you, and the people on her route learn your name before you return to the harbour.
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.result.drin: You pay 0.4 silver for water and rest beside the covered cistern. Anna’s brother sets down your pack, fills the cup once more, and returns to his deliveries. You feel ready to walk on.
ev.constantinopolis.waterjar.title: Anna’s Brother and the Empty Jar
ev.cotan.a.body:
At a shallow bend near Khotan, river washer Yusuf tips a tray of pebbles into the sun. His daughter Amina is sorting them by the marks she can see, but she has put a cracked stone with the smooth ones. ‘Turn it once more,’ he says. She finds the fine line only when water runs across it. A merchant waiting by the bank asks whether they have another full jade lot to sell; Yusuf says one sealed package is ready at 135 silver.

You ask how they decide where to search. Yusuf points to the changing current, then asks Amina where she found today’s stones. She remembers the gravel bar but not the exact place. He takes her to the bank to look at the water from above before either of them steps in. An older washer calls that he can show you what his hands learned here if you stay until the light changes.

Amina returns with a small dry cloth. Her father waits while the merchant checks the seal, and the older washer sets an empty tray beside you.
ev.cotan.a.choice.jade: Buy Yusuf’s sealed jade lot for 135 silver
ev.cotan.a.choice.wade: Spend a day learning the shallow river bend
ev.cotan.a.choice.watch: Listen to the older washer from the bank
ev.cotan.a.title: The River Washer’s Tray
ev.cotan.b.body:
In a Khotan weaving room, sisters Farah and Zuleika are finishing a length of silk for market. Farah reaches for a blue thread that should mark the edge and finds an empty bobbin. Zuleika says she wound another one after breakfast; their aunt has moved it to the shaded shelf so the colour would not fade. ‘I told you,’ the aunt says. Farah answers that she had heard, then forgot while counting the warp.

You ask how much cloth is ready to sell. The aunt points to a complete trading bolt priced at 100 silver, separate from the piece the sisters are still making. She also has a small packet of dye samples for 1.2 silver: indigo, madder, safflower and walnut, all labelled so travellers will not mix them. Zuleika asks whether the samples need extra wrapping. Her aunt says to keep them dry first, then worry about the sun.

Farah finds the blue bobbin and asks you to watch the edge for a day if you want to learn how the sisters divide the work. Zuleika shifts her seat to make room.
ev.cotan.b.choice.silk: Buy the finished silk bolt for 100 silver
ev.cotan.b.choice.weave: Stay a day to learn the sisters’ loom work
ev.cotan.b.title: The Missing Blue Thread
ev.cotan.c.body:
Beyond a watered field outside Khotan, farmer Rahman is clearing sand from the low wall that holds his channel in place. His mother brings him a painted pottery fragment she found after the last wind. ‘It came from our field,’ she says, ‘and I kept it so the children could see the colour.’ Rahman wants to set a support beside the wall before the next water turn. His mother warns him not to place a heavy stone over a patch of older brick that has begun to crumble.

You ask what stood here before the fields. She has heard neighbours talk of older religious buildings in this part of the oasis, but she knows only the pieces found by their family. The younger child asks whether the painted curve is a hand. She says it might be; the piece is too small to tell. Rahman asks you to help measure the firm ground where a support can stand.

Rahman sets his measuring cord against the firm ground. His mother gives the children a clay cup to carry water and asks them to stay clear of the wet wall.
ev.cotan.c.choice.explore: Spend three days repairing and studying the old wall
ev.cotan.c.choice.fragment: Accept the painted fragment from the family’s basket
ev.cotan.c.choice.listen_elder: Listen to Rahman’s mother speak of the field
ev.cotan.c.title: The Wall Beneath the Field
ev.cotan.entry.body:
At Khotan’s entry yard, clerk Samira is trying to keep a wet cargo register from curling. Her younger brother brings it inside, but a river washer follows him with two pebbles in his palm. ‘You have written my name beside the merchant’s pack,’ he tells her. Samira checks the marks. The merchant owns the sealed jade lot; the washer merely helped carry it from the riverbank. She asks both men to sign the corrected line.

You ask where travellers rest. Samira points to houses near a water channel and says the river washer can show you the safest place to fill a jar today. The merchant opens a corner of his pack and offers a full trading lot of jade for 135 silver. Her brother asks if the stone is all from this river. ‘Different hands have gathered it,’ the merchant answers, ‘and that is why we keep names.’

Samira invites you to stay two days and learn the register. Her brother wants to show you their mother’s collection of old river stones tomorrow. The washer holds out a jar of clear water; Samira’s brother takes a sip, then asks for the path to the channel.
ev.cotan.entry.choice.customs: Stay two days to learn the river register
ev.cotan.entry.choice.lore: Spend a day seeing the family’s river stones
ev.cotan.entry.choice.market: Buy the sealed jade lot for 135 silver
ev.cotan.entry.title: The River Register at Khotan
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.body:
At a well beside the river road, keeper Mahmud has laid out three clay cups. His daughter says travellers keep confusing the cup for rinsing hands with the ones for drinking. ‘Then I should mark the handles,’ he says. She points out that the cups have no handles. He laughs and asks her to find a piece of coloured cord instead. A river washer arrives to fill a jar and waits until they finish.

You ask how much water is left after the washing families draw their share. Mahmud shows you the depth mark inside the well wall and explains who checks it each morning. His daughter says yesterday’s mark was hard to see in the shade, so she has placed a small lamp nearby. Mahmud asks her to move it farther from the rope before someone knocks it in. The washer offers a stone to keep the lamp steady.

Mahmud invites you to stay a day and watch how the well is shared. The daughter has already tied a blue cord around the drinking cup and wants you to tell her whether it is easy to see.
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask Mahmud how to plan the next water stop
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: Mahmud asks how many people and animals travel with you, then points out where you should refill before the next dry stretch. His daughter offers the blue-marked cup while you listen. You know whom to ask if you return to this well.
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.choice_2: Spend a day recording the well’s turns
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day and write down when the washer, the nearby families, and the passing caravans use the well. Mahmud’s daughter checks the depth mark at dusk and finds it easy to see beside the moved lamp. Mahmud asks you to come back for the morning reading if you wish.
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank Mahmud and continue. His daughter hands the washer the cup with the blue cord, then catches herself and swaps it for the washing cup. ‘Good thing I can see the mark,’ she says, and her father smiles.
ev.cotan.mentor_closure.title: The Well Keeper’s Table
ev.cotan.twoscripts.body:
In a courtyard near the market, an older woman named Dilara is teaching her grandson to copy the names on a crate of cotton cloth. The seller wrote one name in the family’s hand and another in the script the next carrier can read. Her grandson thinks they name two different owners. ‘Look at the pack number,’ Dilara says. He finds the same mark beneath both lines and asks why the names still look so different.

You ask who taught her the second script. Dilara says a former neighbour carried letters east and showed her how to write addresses clearly. The boy wants to send his own note to an aunt who moved away, but he is embarrassed by his uneven letters. Dilara gives him a spare label and tells him to begin with her name. A carrier arrives to collect the cloth and says he can wait while the boy practises one line.

Dilara offers to pay 0.8 silver if you spend the day helping her check other cargo labels. Her grandson also invites you to sit for a short lesson and see how he writes his aunt’s name.
ev.cotan.twoscripts.choice.learn: Sit with Dilara and the boy to compare the two scripts
ev.cotan.twoscripts.choice.work: Stay a day checking the cargo labels
ev.cotan.twoscripts.result.learn: Dilara shows you how the pack number holds the two versions of the name together. The boy copies his aunt’s name again and asks you which line is easier to read. You note their method; the carrier accepts the corrected crate when he is done.
ev.cotan.twoscripts.result.work: You spend the day comparing names and pack marks with Dilara. The carrier takes each crate only after her grandson reads the label aloud. She pays you 0.8 silver, and the boy slips his carefully written note for his aunt into the right bundle.
ev.cotan.twoscripts.title: The Two Names on the Crate
ev.ctesiphon.entry.body:
The old brick arch rises above low walls and open ground. A family has set a shade cloth beside the ruins. A girl sits beneath it with a bowl of mortar, helping her father patch their small shelter.

She says her grandmother used to walk farther than anyone in the family and always stopped here to drink before taking the road to Baghdad. The girl has never made that whole journey. She asks you how far a traveller can go with a full skin of water, then laughs when her father reminds her that everyone drinks at a different pace.

She asks her father where the family will put the second water jar once the shelter wall is finished. ‘Inside the shade, where the clay stays cool,’ he says. You ask whether they sell water to travellers. The girl shakes her head: neighbours share the well, and her father offers a cup when someone stops. He tells her to rinse the cup first; she runs to the jar and returns with it dripping. From the road, a cart driver calls a greeting. She recognises him and asks whether his mother has recovered from her cough. He promises to tell her after he has watered the animals.
ev.ctesiphon.entry.choice.rest: Rest for a day under the shade cloth
ev.ctesiphon.entry.title: At the Great Arch
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.body:
Farid’s daughter has found a brick with her grandmother’s old mark on it. She wants it at the new doorway, where everyone can see it, but the stone step has to be levelled first. Farid can do that after his work tomorrow.

‘She used to stand there and make us wash our feet before coming in,’ the girl says. Farid brings out a length of cord to measure the step. His daughter keeps the marked brick beside her and asks whether he remembers which room Grandmother carried it from.

‘From the little room behind the oven,’ Farid says. ‘She said the mark would help us find it again.’ The girl asks whether the oven still stands. It does, but the room around it has been repaired more than once. You ask how the brick survived. Farid says his mother kept useful pieces under the shade cloth until she had a place for them. The girl rubs dust from the old mark and asks him to leave that side facing the doorway. A neighbour calls from the lane that the mat is ready; Farid tells her to bring it tomorrow, once the mortar has had a night to set.
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.choice.fit: Spend a day helping fit the step
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.choice.listen: Sit and listen to her stories
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.result.fit: You spend the day levelling the step with Farid. His daughter places the marked brick at the edge and walks through the doorway twice to test it. The family thanks you warmly, and your name becomes familiar here.
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.result.listen: She tells you how her grandmother once arrived home with a soaked loaf hidden under her coat, after giving her dry bread to another traveller. Farid laughs and brings out tea. You rest in the shade and recover some strength.
ev.ctesiphon.shelter.title: Grandmother’s Door Brick
ev.damascus.dyework.body:
Two lengths of blue cloth hang at the dyer's door. His apprentice, Layla, begins to roll one up, but a woman stops her. “Wait. My mother stitched a little red thread into the edge.”

Layla searches and cannot find it. Rain sent both customers' cloth indoors last night. In the morning the marks were hidden under the new blue dye. The woman, Samiya, brought a length her mother had kept. She plans to make a new coat for her younger brother when he returns from his travels. As a boy, he wore a robe their mother had sewn, and Samiya wants to keep that little stitch in his new coat.

The master comes over from the dye vat and feels the corner. “The thread is still there. When the cloth dries a little, we'll all look.” Samiya puts her sewing box on a stool and helps Layla work along the hem. Layla looks up at you. “You have good eyes. Will you check the other side? I'd hate to send her home empty handed.”
ev.damascus.dyework.choice.help: Help Layla look for the red thread
ev.damascus.dyework.choice.route: Ask how Samiya's brother travels back from Tyre
ev.damascus.dyework.result.help:
You spread the hem beside the window. In the light you see a red thread tucked into a small repair. Samiya lifts the loose end with her nail and recognizes her mother's stitch.

Layla brings her some water and asks her to return once the cloth is fully dry. The master thanks you for helping. On her way out, Samiya laughs that her brother will probably complain that the sleeves are too long. You leave knowing a few more people in Damascus.
ev.damascus.dyework.result.route:
As she searches the cloth, Samiya tells you her brother travels with a caravan from Tyre. She knows the stretch along the coast and the turn inland toward Damascus. She even describes the green-painted cart he rides beside.

Layla finds the red thread and calls her over. Samiya holds the corner up to the light. “When he comes home, I'll make him try the coat on first.” You thank her and mark Tyre and the road on your map.
ev.damascus.dyework.title: A Piece of Blue Cloth
ev.damascus.entry.body:
As you enter Damascus, Nura is wrapping a narrow-necked bottle in soft cloth. Her nephew stands beside her stall, holding half of a broken stopper and stamping his foot.

“What will we do with the bottle for Mother?” he asks. “She leaves with the caravan tomorrow.”

Nura dries the neck and finds a new stopper. “Hold it for me. Your mother wants a little of home to take to Tripoli. Once I change the stopper, she can carry it.”

Her nephew says his mother lived in Mizza as a child. Every summer she ran to the rosewater workshops to smell the petals. Nura laughs. “She used to put her nose against the door. The maker called her back so she wouldn't burn herself.”

Nura presses in the new stopper and turns the bottle upside down. The cloth stays dry. She sees you beside the stall and asks whether you would like to rest. Her nephew has already picked up the basket to take the bottle to his mother.
ev.damascus.entry.choice.look: Help Nura's nephew deliver the rosewater and ask about the Tripoli road
ev.damascus.entry.choice.pass: Ask Nura which gate to take and continue your journey
ev.damascus.entry.title: Damascus
ev.delli.battuta_a.body:
At a grain courtyard in Delhi, Shirin has laid a damp register beneath a cloth weight. Rain blurred several household marks before the morning distribution. Her daughter Safiya brings an empty sack and asks, ‘Did Uncle Rahim get his share?’ Shirin holds the page toward the light. ‘I can see his name. I cannot tell whether I wrote one measure or two.’ The old clerk at the next table says he still has the wooden tally from yesterday, but his hands are busy weighing the next family’s grain.

You ask why everyone is waiting in the yard. ‘If I guess at a number, somebody will go home short,’ Shirin says. Safiya offers to carry the register to her uncle; her mother stops her because the wet ink may smear again. A trader waiting with the other families says his pack animals leave for Cambay after noon. He has used these grain yards on the westward road and can name the places where travellers find water.

Shirin asks you to hold down the page while she brings the tally over. Safiya points to the mark beside her uncle’s name, and the clerk squints at it before he answers.
ev.delli.battuta_a.choice.ask: Help Shirin explain the corrected shares to the families
ev.delli.battuta_a.choice.court: Spend a day asking the trader about the road to Cambay
ev.delli.battuta_a.choice.pyre: Help compare the tally and the register for a day
ev.delli.battuta_a.title: The Courtyard Register
ev.delli.battuta_b.body:
At a travellers’ house in Delhi, keeper Bibi Hina is sorting two bundles of letters before their carriers leave. Her nephew marked one bundle for the westward caravan and the other for the long eastern road, then set both beneath a leaking roof tile. ‘I know which cloth I used,’ he says, ‘but the ink on the tags has run.’ Hina has him open the outer wraps and read the names aloud before anyone takes a letter away.

You ask who will carry the westward bundle. A driver bound toward Cambay raises his hand from the doorway; his sister lives near a stopping place on that road. The eastern carrier says the route toward Khotan takes many changes of hands, so each address must be clear. Hina asks whether he has enough dry cloth to rewrap it. He shows her a single piece and admits he had saved the rest for his own bedding. She sends her nephew to fetch another piece from the storeroom.

A family has arrived looking for a room, and Hina must settle them before dark. She asks you to hold the letters in order while her nephew brings back the dry wrapping.
ev.delli.battuta_b.choice.embassy: Spend a day preparing the eastern letters and road list
ev.delli.battuta_b.choice.gwalior: Spend a day with the westward driver and learn the Cambay road
ev.delli.battuta_b.choice.house: Stay a day helping Hina settle the guests
ev.delli.battuta_b.title: The Two Road Bundles
ev.delli.entry.body:
At a Delhi water yard, a carrier is marking household jars with a bit of chalk. His younger sister has just returned from a lane where two neighbours share the same doorway. She put the full jar at the wrong threshold and wants to fetch it back before either household starts supper. ‘Read the mark to me,’ her brother says, holding out the empty jar. She does, then notices that rain has blurred the chalk.

You ask whether the two families will mind. ‘They know us,’ she says, ‘but one has a sick child and needs the water first.’ Her brother takes a fresh piece of chalk and draws a wider sign. A caravan scribe waiting nearby asks if they can fill his skin as well. He is copying a long route list toward Khotan, with many stops between Delhi and that far-off city, and needs water before the drivers leave.

The sister carries the corrected jar to the sick child’s home and returns for the other. Her brother asks the scribe to hold the chalk while he fills the skin. The scribe looks at you and says he can show you his route list after the water is delivered.
ev.delli.entry.choice.look: Stay a day and read the long Khotan route list
ev.delli.entry.title: The Water Carrier’s Chalk Mark
ev.delli.jarbands.body:
In the water yard, a young potter is tying a blue thread around a household jar. Her aunt ordered two of the same size, one for drinking water and one for washing, and wants the family to tell them apart at a glance. The potter has only enough thread for one full loop. Her little cousin suggests painting a mark on the other; the potter worries the paint will rub off when the jar is carried.

You ask why the aunt did not choose different shapes. ‘They have to fit the same shelf,’ the girl says. Her cousin fetches a scrap of red cloth and asks whether it will last longer than paint. The aunt arrives with a carrying pole, sets the jars side by side, and has both children lift them. One handle catches on the pole. She asks the potter to smooth it before she takes either home.

The potter can pay you 0.6 silver if you stay the day to help finish and test the jars. If you are leaving soon, she will show you how she tests the handles and marks vessels for the family.
ev.delli.jarbands.choice.finish: Stay a day and help finish the jars
ev.delli.jarbands.choice.learn: Watch how the family marks and tests jars
ev.delli.jarbands.result.finish: You spend the day helping smooth the handle and testing both jars on the pole. The aunt chooses blue thread for drinking water and red cloth for washing. The potter pays you 0.6 silver before they carry the jars home.
ev.delli.jarbands.result.learn: The potter lets you feel the rough spot beneath the handle before she smooths it. Her aunt shows why the pole catches there, and the cousin ties on the red cloth. You record the small craft of keeping the two jars distinct.
ev.delli.jarbands.title: The Blue Thread on the Jar
ev.dongola.entry.body: Dongola — a Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile, Christian since the sixth century. The cathedral of painted saints overlooks the river; the king still mints coins with the cross. Caravans bring gold and ivory from the interior and slaves from the pagan south. The desert on either side is waterless for ten days' journey.
ev.dongola.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.dongola.entry.title: Arriving at Dongola
ev.dongola.site_gap.body: At the ferry, the boatman winds a bundle of reed rope round a post, checking each strand for cracks. A chain would pull the boat too hard as the river rises; the rope gives a little. He asks travellers to move their cargo to the middle before crossing. Marks on his pole show familiar water levels, which he checks before every departure.
ev.dongola.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Mecha
ev.dongola.site_gap.title: Reed Rope at the Ferry
ev.dufar.entry.body: Dufar is a great and noble and fine city, and lies 500 miles to the north-west of Esher. The people are Saracens, and have a Count for their chief, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden; for this city still belongs to the Province of Aden. It stands upon the sea and has a very good haven, so that there is a great traffic of shipping between this and India; and the merchants take hence great numbers of Arab horses to that market, making great profits thereby. This city has under it many other towns and villages. Much white incense is produced here, and I will tell you how it grows.
ev.dufar.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.dufar.entry.title: Concerning the City of Dufar
ev.dufar.site_gap.body: A frankincense seller picks bark from a few grains of resin and wraps them in thick paper. Sunlight weakens the scent; he advises storing it in a clay jar sealed with wax, well away from dried fish. He lets you smell two different packets. A thin cord around each wrapper keeps out dust and allows it to hang when the room is damp.
ev.dufar.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Esher
ev.dufar.site_gap.title: How the Frankincense Merchant Seals His Goods
ev.edessa.clayletter.body:
At a potter's yard, Safa holds a letter flat against a board with a lump of clay. Her father sent it from Tarsus, where he took a load of bowls to sell. A corner got wet on the journey home. She can still read the part where he asks if her little brother has stopped hiding his shoes, but the directions for his return are fading.

Her brother says he hid the shoes because their father always set them beside the door as though the boy were about to leave too. Safa reads that line aloud again, and both of them laugh. Their father promises to bring back a pair that fits.

Several bowls must also be moved into the shade before they dry too quickly. Safa has put off that work to save the letter. She asks you to help copy the remaining directions, or stay and move the bowls while she writes. She has money set aside for a day's help.

‘Does Father know you hide my shoes?’ Safa asks her brother. ‘He found them last time,’ he says, ‘and put them back by the door.’ She smooths the damp corner of the letter without rubbing the ink. You ask whether another carrier might remember the road their father named. Safa says the pottery buyer knows the same route and will come for the bowls before sunset. Her brother takes the wooden board at the dry end so she can lift the letter carefully. ‘Ask him about the shoes too,’ he says. Safa laughs, then notices the shade moving across the clay pieces and calls him to help shift them.
ev.edessa.clayletter.choice.copy: Copy the surviving route in the letter
ev.edessa.clayletter.choice.work: Stay a day and move the bowls into shade
ev.edessa.clayletter.result.copy: You hold the board steady while Safa copies the legible names and turns onto a clean sheet. Her brother reads them back, slowly enough for her to catch a missed stop. She adds a line of her own, asking their father to bring shoes with room to grow. You copy the road toward Tarsus into your map as she speaks, and mark the city at its far end.
ev.edessa.clayletter.result.work: You spend the day carrying unfired bowls beneath the awning. Safa finishes copying the letter while her brother counts the bowls, losing his place whenever he finds a pair that matches. When the light fades, she pays you the agreed wage. Her brother shows you where he has hidden his shoes this time; he intends to leave them there until their father comes home. You leave the next morning.
ev.edessa.clayletter.title: A Letter at the Potter's Yard
ev.edessa.entry.body:
The road into Edessa passes a water trough. Miran is filling a leather bag from a jar, while his niece Derya sits nearby with a pile of flat stones. She has arranged them into a winding line and says it is the road her uncle took when he went away to buy wool.

“That road had more turns than this,” Miran says. Derya adds two stones. He went away long enough for her to outgrow the shoes she was wearing when he left, and she has made him tell the story of his return three times.

Miran asks where you are headed and shifts his bag so you can fill yours. Derya wants to know if your road has a river. When you show her the map, she finds Edessa before Miran does. He tells you where travellers stop for water beyond the town; she puts another stone beside the trough to mark the place where you met.
ev.edessa.entry.choice.pass: Thank Miran and continue through Edessa
ev.edessa.entry.choice.rest: Stay with Miran's family for a day
ev.edessa.entry.title: Arriving at Edessa
ev.egrigaia.entry.body: Starting again from Erguiul you ride eastward for eight days, and then come to a province called EGRIGAIA, containing numerous cities and villages, and belonging to Tangut. The capital city is called CALACHAN. The people are chiefly Idolaters, but there are fine churches belonging to the Nestorian Christians. They are all subjects of the Great Kaan. They make in this city great quantities of camlets of camel’s wool, the finest in the world; and some of the camlets that they make are white, for they have white camels, and these are the best of all. Merchants purchase these stuffs here, and carry them over the world for sale.
ev.egrigaia.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.egrigaia.entry.title: Of the Kingdom of Egrigaia
ev.egrigaia.site_gap.body: A host shows you the adjustable opening at the roof of his felt tent. In a light wind he narrows it; in a strong one he opens it to keep smoke from blowing back inside. He lifts the door flap slightly: cool air enters low and smoke leaves high. He points to patches sewn around the opening, which keep out wind and snow.
ev.egrigaia.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Tenduc
ev.egrigaia.site_gap.title: The Smoke Hole of a Felt Tent
ev.ephesus.entry.body:
The road climbs toward the houses on Ayasuluk Hill. Below, the older stones of Ephesus spread across the ground where streets once led to the sea. Leyla and her daughter Nisa are gathering fallen twigs beside the path. Nisa has found a smooth piece of marble and is trying to carry it with the firewood.

“That one will not burn,” Leyla says. Nisa knows. She wants to show it to her grandfather, who tells stories about the old town whenever he sees a stone with a carved edge. Leyla agrees to take the marble if Nisa carries the smaller bundle of wood.

They ask where you have travelled from. Leyla points out the path to the houses and the place where travellers can draw water. Nisa asks whether the stones in your own town are as white as this one. She holds it up beside your map, leaving a pale dust mark on her thumb.
ev.ephesus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Leyla and continue past the old stones
ev.ephesus.entry.choice.rest: Stay a day with Leyla's family
ev.ephesus.entry.title: The Houses Above Old Ephesus
ev.ephesus.olivejar.body:
At the foot of the hill, Marika and her son Petros are sealing jars of olive oil. Petros's older sister has gone to Smyrna to learn a trade. Her last letter said she missed the oil their mother pours on warm bread. Marika has saved a small jar for her, wrapped in cloth so the stopper will stay firm.

Petros wants to carry it himself. Marika points to the larger jars ready for sale and reminds him he has promised to help finish them first. He says he can do both, then gets oil on his sleeve while testing a lid. Marika hands him a rag and asks him to slow down.

One sealed jar is available for travellers to buy. Marika also asks if you will accompany Petros to the caravan stop the next day. He knows the stops toward Smyrna from his sister's letters and would be glad of company on the first stretch.

You ask whether the sister knows a parcel is coming. ‘She asked for a taste, not a whole jar,’ Marika says. Petros answers, ‘Then she can share it with the family who lets her work there.’ His mother checks the stopper and tells him to write her name on the cloth before the oil goes into anyone else’s load. He reaches for charcoal, then remembers his sleeve is still oily and asks you to hold the jar steady. Outside, a driver calls that he can wait until morning if the road is wet. Petros looks to his mother; she says to finish the labels tonight and decide about departure after they hear the weather.
ev.ephesus.olivejar.choice.buy: Buy a sealed jar of olive oil for 120 silver
ev.ephesus.olivejar.choice.walk: Walk with Petros to the caravan stop
ev.ephesus.olivejar.result.buy: You pay Marika and take a sealed jar of olive oil. She checks the stopper once more before handing it over. Petros wraps his sister's smaller jar in fresh cloth and tells you she will put the oil on bread before reading the rest of his letter. You carry your purchase onward.
ev.ephesus.olivejar.result.walk: You spend the next day walking with Petros. He tells you about the sister who taught him to read and the stopping places she named on the road toward Smyrna. At the caravan stop he finds a traveller going that way and gives her the small jar and his letter. You add Ephesus, Smyrna, and the route between them to your map. Petros heads home to help his mother with the larger jars.
ev.ephesus.olivejar.title: The Oil Jar for Smyrna
ev.esher.a.body: Esher is a great city lying four hundred miles north-west of the Port of Aden. It has a king who is subject to the Soldan of Aden, and a very good haven where many ships from India come with various cargoes; from hence they export many good chargers to India.
ev.esher.a.choice.buy_horse: Buy an Arabian horse from the export pens
ev.esher.a.choice.walk_harbour: Walk the haven and note how the Soldan's customs are kept
ev.esher.a.choice.watch_ships: Stand upon the mole and watch the Indian ships unload
ev.esher.a.title: The Haven of the Soldan
ev.esher.b.body: A great deal of white incense grows in this country, and brings in a great revenue to the Prince; for no one dares sell it to any one else. The Prince takes it from the people at ten livres of gold for the hundredweight, and sells it to the merchants at sixty. Dates also grow very abundantly here.
ev.esher.b.choice.ask_axuma: Ask the Saracen merchants where the coast trade runs southward
ev.esher.b.choice.buy_dates: Buy dates from the coastal orchards
ev.esher.b.choice.buy_frankincense: Buy frankincense at the Prince's price in the harbour market
ev.esher.b.title: The Frankincense Coast
ev.esher.entry.body: Esher is a great city lying in a north-westerly direction from the last, and 400 miles distant from the Port of Aden. It has a king, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden. He has a number of towns and villages under him, and administers his territory well and justly. The people are Saracens. The place has a very good haven, wherefore many ships from India come thither with various cargoes; and they export many good chargers thence to India. A great deal of white incense grows in this country, and brings in a great revenue to the Prince; for no one dares sell it to any one else; and whilst he takes it from the people at 10 livres of gold for the hundredweight, he sells it to the merchants at 60 livres, so his profit is immense. Dates also grow very abundantly here. The people have no corn but rice, and very little of that; but plenty is brought from abroad, for it sells here at a good profit.
ev.esher.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.esher.entry.title: Concerning the City of Esher
ev.etzina.entry.body: When you leave the city of Campichu you ride for twelve days, and then reach a city called ETZINA, which is towards the north on the verge of the Sandy Desert; it belongs to the Province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, and possess plenty of camels and cattle, and the country produces a number of good falcons, both Sakers and Lanners. The inhabitants live by their cultivation and their cattle, for they have no trade.
ev.etzina.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.etzina.entry.title: Of the City of Etzina
ev.ev_accon_battuta_a.choice_1_result:
You spend a day with Hamid at the resting places along the shore, helping him find a companion who knows the hill roads. At Kark Nuh, he says, travellers can drink at the lodge, and someone will show them where the tomb stands. It lies inland, and he hopes to go with someone who knows the way.

Back beneath the shade cloth, Safa has cut open the pomegranate. She offers Hamid a piece. He tastes it and laughs that she chose a good one. Adil gives you a piece too and thanks you for helping Hamid find a companion. The travellers who rest at Acre come to know you.
ev.ev_accon_battuta_a.choice_2_result:
You walk with Hamid along the old harbour steps. He points north along the coast and describes the road towards Tyre. He once watched people mending boat nets there and borrowed a small knife from one of them.

You spend the day asking people along the shore. At dusk a netmender lends you a small knife. When Safa hears, she brings out the pomegranate at once. You mark the direction of Tyre on your map.
ev.ev_accon_battuta_a.choice_3_result:
Hamid sets the mat aside. Travellers, he says, tell another story about Abu Yaakub Yusuf: that he once turned the copper vessels of a young woman's dowry into gold. Safa stares and asks whether Hamid saw it himself.

“I saw the lodge and his tomb,” Hamid says. He tells you how he lost the road inland until a man with a donkey led him to the door. You listen through the day and record the marvel as a story alongside the road Hamid actually travelled. At dusk, Adil borrows a knife and Safa cuts the pomegranate for everyone. Then he invites you to tell the story to newly arrived travellers, who are glad to listen.
ev.ev_accon_entry.choice_1_result: You ask Safa where the main road begins. She sets down the water jug and points to an earthen track beside the old harbour steps. “Follow it to the fork and ask whoever is travelling there.” Yusuf has already run off with the basket. You follow her directions and mark Acre on your map.
ev.ev_accon_entry.choice_2_result:
