You walk along the road with Safa and Yusuf. The driver is still loading a sack of beans. Their uncle is crouched beside him, holding a rope taut. Yusuf hands him the basket and lifts the bread. The letter is still underneath. Their uncle tucks it into his clothes and asks Yusuf to tell his grandmother that he'll have someone write back from Jerusalem.

You spend the night at a resting place by the shore. The next morning their uncle meets you beside the road and points out the direction his party will take to Jerusalem. You add the city and road to your map.
ev.ev_aden_a.choice_1_result: You walk the sheds and watch the lighters load. It costs you 1 day on the road. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_aden_a.choice_2_result: You buy a sack of Malabar pepper for the onward road. You pay 900 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. You set what you saw into your travel book.
ev.ev_aden_a.choice_3_result: You ask the camel-masters which roads leave the harbour. The road to Dufar opens on your map. The road to Cambaet opens on your map. Fortune bends a little your way.
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.body: On the quay where India's ships discharge into lighters, a camel master who has walked the thirty-day road to the river of Alexandria lays his ledger beside the pepper sheds. He says Aden is the gate of Egypt's spice — and that Dufar and Cambaet are written in the margin if you mean to leave the harbour with more than a sack.
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_1: Buy Malabar pepper at the camel master's price
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_1_result: He sells you pepper sealed for the camel road. The sack will keep through the thirty days.
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_2: Ask him to mark the roads that leave the harbour
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_2_result: Dufar and Cambaet are marked on your map. The harbour exits are clear.
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_3: Walk the sheds a day and watch the lighters load
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.choice_3_result: You spend a day among the bales. The camel road to Alexandria is noted, and fortune bends a little your way.
ev.ev_aden_a_followup.title: Aden: The Camel Masters' Ledger
ev.ev_aden_b.choice_1_result: You stand aside and observe the customs at the mole. You spend 1 day before the way is clear again. You set what you saw into your travel book. Your name carries a little more weight here now.
ev.ev_aden_b.choice_2_result: You pay the harbour fee and buy frankincense from a Somali trader. You pay 350 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. The road to Esher opens on your map.
ev.ev_aden_b.choice_3_result: You listen at the mosque door as the Soldan's men pray. You set what you saw into your travel book. A small turn of fortune favours you.
ev.ev_aden_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through the darvāzā without delay. The road to Aden opens on your map.
ev.ev_aden_entry.choice_2_result: You walk through the bāzār. You spend 1 day before the way is clear again. You set what you saw into your travel book. You set the way to Aden on your map.
ev.ev_aden_entry.choice_3_result: You stand a while in the mandir's shade. The worshippers mark your face and call down a blessing that goes with you out the door. The way to Aden lies drawn on your map.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_a.choice_1_resu: You stand by the gate while the keeper cries in irony: Enter, Mr Judge. The poor scholar answers: Yes, judge, if that be God's will. The evening passes in waiting, and the tale of the gate stays with you; your name is spoken well of in Alexandria.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_a.choice_2_resu: The scholar tells you he will not enter until he has seen a favourable omen; he has come from the Hejaz, poor. You learn how he took up reading in a college until his name reached the king of Egypt, and the road he travelled from the Hejaz settles on your map.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_a.choice_3_resu: You answer as he does — judge, if that be God's will — and pass through the gate behind him. In the months to come you will hear how the office of judge of Alexandria came to the poor scholar who expected nothing, and your name is spoken well of in the city.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_b.choice_1_resu: You swear it. The saint's words run before you like a thread to the east — India, Sind, China, and in each a brother to be greeted. The oath is written in your journal, and Alexandria speaks well of the promise you carry.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_b.choice_2_resu: He tells them off one by one: Farīd Oddīn in India, Rokn Oddīn Ibn Zakaryā in Sind, Borhān Oddīn in China. The far countries take names and bearings, and the first road east settles on your map.
ev.ev_alexandria_battuta_b.choice_3_resu: You take your leave, the prophecy folded in your mind. In the years to come you will meet all three brothers and present the saint's compliments, as he said you would; Alexandria speaks well of the promise you keep.
ev.ev_alexandria_entry.choice_1_result: You ask the porter how to leave the city. He shifts the crate to his other shoulder. "Follow the wall to the water seller's shelter. He watches the caravans pass every day; ask him there." He steadies the swaying crate and heads back towards the quay.
ev.ev_alexandria_entry.choice_2_result:
Hasan arrives at last. He scolds his escort for leaving the tally behind, then apologises to the clerk. The clerk checks tally against ledger and finally lowers the sack onto the scale.

The porter points towards the merchants waiting under the arcade. "If you carry someone else's goods, bring the tally. Otherwise the pepper may hang there until dark." You spend a day at the quay and talk with merchants about the roads out of town. One is leaving for Bethlehem in the morning. He draws the caravan's gate on a sheet of paper and tells you where to find them.
ev.ev_alexandria_mentor_geomancy.choice_: You pay and learn geomancy. You pay 8000 coins. You spend 10 days learning the art. You can now read it on any road. A mark is set on this affair.
You ask what Populus means for a voyage. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_antiochia_entry.choice_1_result: The keeper pins the board with his foot until the last mule crosses. He points towards the city gate. "Eastwards? Go out that way. More carts are coming; don't stand on the bridge looking for signs." You cross with the queue while the river moves beneath your feet.
ev.ev_antiochia_entry.choice_2_result:
A carpenter arrives with his tools and prises up the loose board. A nail has broken underneath it; each wheel has pushed the end a little higher. The driver who had shouted the loudest now holds the new board steady for him.

By the time the carpenter drives in the last nail, it is growing dark. You stay in town that night and return to the bridge in the morning. The keeper recognises you and points east. "For Edessa, go out that way. There are guarded roads in the hills. Follow the one the other travellers use." Carts are crossing the bridge again.
ev.ev_axuma_entry.choice_1_result: The priest walks with you as far as the fig tree and points to the road onward. His daughter calls after him to remember the empty jar he promised to return. He goes back for it, waving you on. You know where the station lies when you need water again.
ev.ev_axuma_entry.choice_2_result: You stay for a day and help move the jars under the roof. The daughter brings bread and a bowl of lentils when the work is done. “You saved me two trips in the sun,” she says. After a full night's rest you leave with your strength restored and with the station's turn fixed in mind.
ev.ev_axuma_site_gap.choice_1_result: The niece takes you to the fork and points out the stones that mark the Dongola road. “The spring path ends among the trees; this one keeps going,” she says. You trace the turn for yourself before returning her tile.
ev.ev_axuma_site_gap.choice_2_result: You hold the jar while she presses clay into the crack and winds a strip of cloth around the rim. Her uncle waits until the patch has dried before pouring in a little water. It holds. He explains how he checks a jar before trusting it with a day's supply.
ev.ev_babylonia_cairus_entry.choice_1_re:
The carrier entrusts the basket to the boatman and takes up his jars for the next house. He shows you the way to the city gate. "Follow the stalls with awnings. Don't turn into the grain yard."

The girl waves from the boat. It has not left yet, but she is already checking whether the bread in the basket has been crushed.
ev.ev_babylonia_cairus_entry.choice_2_re:
You help the carrier deliver his water and stay by the river that night. The boatman carries the first basket across for the girl. In the morning she prepares another basket of bread, and her father takes her to the island. Her uncle eats the bread she brought and shows you the marked column inside the measuring well. He records where the water reaches each day. People who tend the canals and fields come to ask him.

On the way back, the carrier points out the yard where caravans for Petra gather. He says his daughter has won this time: she will set the hour for future lunch deliveries.
ev.ev_badashan_a.choice_1_result: You spend the day beside their felt rug. Farid’s sister shows you how she checks each wrapping; their mother corrects the porter’s tally. You record the stone trade and are invited to return when the next ledger is opened.
ev.ev_badashan_a.choice_2_result: You pay 135 silver for the full lapis lot. Farid and his sister count the parcels with you; their mother names the way carriers travel toward Balkh. You mark that city on your map and keep the receipt with the goods.
ev.ev_badashan_a.choice_3_result: Farid’s mother explains which approaches lead toward Taican and Kashmir and which valleys become difficult after rain. You mark both places and remember to ask about local conditions before travelling.
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.body:
Farid opens a second ledger when the porter returns from the lower road. His sister notices one parcel has been marked twice: once for the buyer who changed his mind and once for the new offer. ‘If we leave both names, someone will come back for a stone we no longer have,’ she says. Farid crosses out the old entry and asks his mother to check the carrier’s route.

She finds a water stop omitted from the margin. You ask whether that matters to the price. ‘It matters to the people carrying it,’ she replies. The porter points to Balkh on a rough map and explains where he pays for animal feed. Farid has a second merchant lot available for 135 silver if you want the whole shipment.

His sister dries the corrected ink while you decide. You can buy the lot, ask them to trace the road toward Balkh, or stay the day until the broker’s report is complete and study how the family settles a disputed entry.
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_1: Buy the lapis lot for 135 silver
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_1_resul: You pay 135 silver for the full lapis lot after Farid corrects the entry. His sister checks the count a final time, and you record both the purchase and what their ledger taught you.
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_2: Ask them to draw the road toward Balkh
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_2_resul: The porter describes the lower road toward Balkh, including a stop where he feeds his animals. Farid’s mother checks his directions, and you mark Balkh on your map with notes on the tolls.
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_3: Stay a day for the completed report
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.choice_3_resul: You stay the day while the family matches parcels to names. Farid shows you the completed report, with old offers crossed out and the carrier’s costs added. You leave better able to judge another stone bargain.
ev.ev_badashan_a_followup.title: Farid’s Second Ledger
ev.ev_badashan_b.choice_1_result: You spend the day listening to the clerk compare names in the old books. His niece repeats the parts she can remember, and you record the family’s claim as a claim, alongside the valley names. They ask you to return if another traveller brings a new spelling.
ev.ev_badashan_b.choice_2_result: You pay 2 silver. The clerk teaches you greetings and a question about a stone’s origin; his niece makes you say each phrase to the messenger before he leaves. People at the market answer you more warmly afterward.
ev.ev_badashan_b.choice_3_result: You pay 135 silver for the uncut balas ruby. The broker and clerk check the broker’s receipt together, then wrap the stone for travel. You record where they came from and keep the receipt.
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.body:
The clerk’s niece brings you a note with three words she heard from stone carriers. She has written each as it sounded to her, then left room for the clerk’s correction. A messenger from the next valley is waiting; he can speak the words aloud before he takes his letter.

The first word names a pass. The clerk asks the messenger whether it is the approach toward Taican or the one travellers use for Kashmir. The messenger draws two lines on a scrap and says the roads divide after the pasture. You repeat his words, and he grins at your careful accent. The niece asks him to say them more slowly for both of you.

The clerk can give you a short lesson for 2 silver, with a chance to practise among the local traders. You can instead ask the messenger to show the two mountain directions, or buy one uncut balas ruby for 135 silver while the broker is still in the yard.
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_1: Pay 2 silver for a short lesson
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_1_resul: You pay 2 silver and practise with the clerk and messenger. At the market you manage a short exchange with a stone carrier; he remembers your effort and introduces you to another trader.
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_2: Ask the messenger to draw the two mountain approaches
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_2_resul: The messenger draws the routes toward Taican and Kashmir and names the pasture where they divide. You mark both places on your map and note the local names beside them.
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_3: Buy the uncut balas ruby for 135 silver
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.choice_3_resul: You pay 135 silver for the uncut balas ruby. The broker and clerk check the licence and receipt together; the niece writes you a clean copy. You record the trade and keep the stone wrapped for travel.
ev.ev_badashan_b_followup.title: The Clerk’s Mountain Words
ev.ev_badashan_entry.choice_1_result: The boy waves his ledger at you as you leave. You mark Badakhshan on your map and follow the road beyond the market.
ev.ev_badashan_entry.choice_2_result: You spend a day hearing the traders compare stones, origins, and transport costs. By evening the boy can read the corrected figures without help. You record what you learned and mark Badakhshan on your map.
ev.ev_badashan_entry.choice_3_result: You visit the caretakers and listen to the people who gather there. They guide you back toward the market, remember your courtesy, and give you a small token of the visit. You mark Badakhshan on your map.
ev.ev_balc_a.choice_1_result: You help Farid measure and set the doorway over two days. The caravan woman comes back with details of the road to Samarkand, which you add to your map. Mina insists on keeping one carved flower visible from the street; the neighbour agrees when she sees it in the afternoon light.
ev.ev_balc_a.choice_2_result: Farid gives you the thin carved fragment once the sound stones are set aside. Mina wraps it in a scrap of cloth and tells you which flower on the wall resembles it. You keep the fragment and make a note about the repaired lane.
ev.ev_balc_a.choice_3_result: Farid tells you how his father showed him the first stones he was allowed to set. Mina interrupts to ask whether he dropped one. ‘Two,’ he says, making her laugh. You record the family’s account of the old wall. A little later Mina comes to ask about another piece she found.
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.body:
Mina returns to the doorway with another carved piece. Her uncle Farid turns it over and finds a line of old lettering under the dust. ‘That is why we measure before we build,’ he tells her. ‘If the writing goes into the wall, no one can read it again.’ She asks him to set it where neighbours can see it. He agrees to ask the owner of the house.

You ask where the stone came from. Mina shows you a heap beside the lane; it had been saved after earlier repairs, but nobody had recorded who moved it. A trader from Badakhshan stops to look and says he knows a stone worker in his home valley who reads old marks. Farid does not know whether that will help, though he will let Mina draw the letters.

The householder comes out and approves a place above the doorway for the larger piece. Farid sets a small loose fragment aside for you. Mina brings a bit of charcoal. The trader steadies the paper while she tests the first letter, and Farid calls her back before the mortar sets.
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.choice_1_result: Farid gives you the loose fragment after Mina has copied its pattern. She folds the drawing into her uncle’s tool bag, and you put the stone into yours. You add the doorway and the family’s account to your notes.
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.choice_2: Ask the Badakhshan trader where to find the stone worker
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.choice_2_result: The trader tells you the name of his valley in Badakhshan and how caravans reach it. Mina writes the place beside her drawing in case the family sends a message. You add Badakhshan and the old stone to your travel notes.
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.choice_3: Help Mina draw the letters for the neighbours
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.choice_3_result: You hold the paper while Mina rubs charcoal across the letters. The householder carries the drawing indoors for her children to see, then thanks you for staying with the work. Farid points out the flower that will face the street once the mortar dries.
ev.ev_balc_a_followup.title: Mina’s Second Stone
ev.ev_balc_b.choice_1_result: After the woman signs the corrected ledger, you pay 135 silver for the full lot of lapis. Yunus writes your pack number carefully this time, and his mother checks the seal before the chest is closed. You take the stone cargo with you.
ev.ev_balc_b.choice_2_result: You inspect the single uncut balas ruby in the innkeeper’s daylight and pay 135 silver. The trader wraps it separately, and Yunus writes only one stone against your name. The woman with the cloth reminds him to dry the new page before closing the book.
ev.ev_balc_b.choice_3_result: The lapis trader names Badakhshan’s mountain markets, and the cloth trader traces the Samarkand road past the wells she trusts. You mark both destinations. Yunus asks whether you can come back after supper to check a newer entry in the ledger.
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.body:
After supper at the inn, Yunus brings the ledger you were asked to check. A newly arrived driver has written the number of his lapis packs in the column for nights of lodging. ‘My mother will charge him for twenty beds,’ Yunus says, embarrassed. The driver, who is standing nearby, laughs and points out the mark he meant to make. Yunus asks him to wait until his mother can witness the correction.

You ask whether the driver is bound for Samarkand. He says his sister lives on that road and wants a letter carried before he turns back to Badakhshan. He can describe the stops, but first he needs Yunus to copy her address without losing a character. The lapis trader from earlier has another sealed lot for 135 silver and sets it on the table while he waits for his own account.

Yunus’s mother arrives, sees the wrong column and hands him a fresh pen. He looks at you for help with the letter. The driver sits down, ready to repeat the address as many times as needed.
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_1: Buy the other lapis lot for 135 silver
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_1_result: You check the separate sealed lot and pay 135 silver. Yunus’s mother records the sale in the right column while her son corrects the driver’s lodging. The second lapis cargo leaves the inn with you.
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_2: Copy the Samarkand address and learn the road
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_2_result: You copy the sister’s address and ask the driver to trace each stop toward Samarkand. He checks the spelling twice before taking the letter. You note the city and the family’s route; Yunus’s mother thanks you for keeping the ledgers apart.
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_3: Stay a day to help Yunus sort the records
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.choice_3_result: You stay through the next day, helping Yunus move each pack mark to its proper column. By evening he can explain the book without asking his mother at every line. She sets aside a dry shelf for his papers and sends you out with a bowl of supper.
ev.ev_balc_b_followup.title: Yunus Checks the Night Ledger
ev.ev_balc_c.choice_1_result: You contribute 2 silver for oil and incense. The visiting woman adds it to the keeper’s small box, and the grandson promises to bring the right wick next time. You spend a while hearing the family’s account of the shrine before returning to the road.
ev.ev_balc_c.choice_2_result: You sleep behind the shrine wall and rise after a full night. In the morning the grandson is waiting to tell you about the dream he had, though his grandfather first makes him eat breakfast. You record the family’s stories and remember this night on the hill.
ev.ev_balc_c.choice_3_result: At dawn the keeper recites a short verse his mother taught him, then tells his grandson what its old words mean to him. You listen beside the newly lit lamp and add the hill shrine to your notes before the day’s visitors arrive.
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.body:
After the night at the hill shrine, the keeper’s grandson tells you he dreamed that the oil jar rolled downhill. His grandfather asks whether he checked the shelf before telling everyone. The boy runs inside and returns with the jar steady in both arms. ‘It was only a dream,’ he says. ‘Still, I should move it farther from the edge.’ The visiting woman from yesterday helps him clear a space.

You ask the keeper how he remembers the stories his mother taught him. He points to a little carved scrap kept in a niche. It came from a piece of wall his family once repaired; he uses it to remind the boy which parts he knows from his mother and which he heard from other travellers. The boy asks whether you will take the spare piece they kept beside it. The keeper says the family has made a copy and you may have the loose original.

The woman stays to refill the lamp. The keeper offers to spend the day talking with you, while the boy waits to see whether you will tell him about a place you have visited.
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.choice_1_result: The keeper gives you the small carved fragment after showing you the family’s rubbing. The boy wraps it, then moves the oil jar to the new shelf. You carry a piece of the shrine’s history with you.
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.choice_2: Stay a day and exchange stories with the keeper
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.choice_2_result: You spend the day at the shrine. The keeper tells you what he remembers of his mother, and you answer the boy’s questions about another road. The woman tends the lamp while you write down what the family told you.
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.choice_3: Hear the boy’s account and go on
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.choice_3_result: The boy tells his dream again, this time including the jar he checked in the morning. His grandfather laughs and sends him to fetch breakfast. You remember their lamp and shelter as you take the road down from the hill.
ev.ev_balc_c_followup.title: The Grandson’s Morning Dream
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.body:
The clerk’s son Umar finds you at the inn with the damp register folded under his arm. ‘Father wants me to check a name before the western caravan leaves,’ he says. His sister Laila copied it from a driver’s wooden tally, but the driver’s mark looks like another family’s. Umar knows both households and does not want either charged for the other’s pack.

You ask whether he can ask the driver directly. ‘He is loading at the next yard,’ Umar says, ‘and will be gone before I fetch Father.’ The innkeeper offers to send her boy across the lane. Laila arrives a moment later with the old list you used at the toll station. She says the second family’s pack was a jar, while this one is a chest; the shapes beside the names differ.

Umar writes the correction, then asks whether you would carry a note to the next record keeper if your roads meet. Laila reminds him to put the family name on the outside so nobody opens the note merely to learn who it is for.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.choice_1: Carry Umar’s note and ask who will receive it
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.choice_1_result: Umar names the keeper at the next station and Laila copies the name onto the outside of the note. You keep it dry beneath your own papers. The family asks you to come back before you leave so they can check the final wording together.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.choice_2: Leave the correction with the clerk’s family
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.choice_2_result: You thank Umar and leave the delivery to his family. Laila folds the corrected list into a fresh cloth, and the innkeeper’s boy returns with news that the driver is still loading. They have time to speak to him before he goes.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a.title: The Clerk’s Second List
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a_resolution.body:
Before you leave Balkh, Umar and Laila bring the finished note. Their father has signed beneath the corrected pack number. ‘I thought he would tell us to begin again,’ Umar says, ‘but he only asked why we had left so much space around the name.’ Laila says the space makes the mark easier to read. The clerk, standing behind them, admits that she is right.

You ask whether the next keeper will recognise the family. The father says yes, but he wants the letter delivered by hand so the correction is entered once, in the proper book. Umar shows you where the fold is sealed. Laila has written the recipient’s name large enough to read without unfolding it.

The inn’s breakfast is being cleared away. Umar turns the signed note so the name faces you. Laila lifts the breakfast bowls before the ink can touch them.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_a_resolution.choi: Carry the signed note to the next keeper
You take the sealed note with its clear name. Umar watches you slip it beneath your dry papers; Laila nods when she sees it will stay flat. The family’s correction is now in your care.
Spend a day copying the corrected record

You spend the day copying the pack number and both family names. Umar compares each line with the signed note, and Laila corrects one letter before you close the book. You keep the record even if the next road never takes you past that station.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.body:
Laila’s younger brother Karim catches up with you near the market. He is carrying a chipped bowl from the family’s shelf of old objects. ‘Laila said you would look at it before I ask the potter,’ he says. A former owner scratched two names beneath the rim, and Karim cannot tell whether the second is a person or a place. His sister arrives to warn him that the bowl still holds water; it should not be carried by its thin handle.

You ask why the names matter to him. Karim says their grandfather used to set the bowl at supper and tell a different story each time. ‘Did he ever say who scratched it?’ Laila asks. Karim shakes his head. A potter at the next stall calls over that he can repair the chip, but the writing may become harder to see if the glaze runs across it.

Karim wants to make a copy of the letters first. He has brought paper and charcoal, though the bowl is slippery in his hands. Laila steadies it and asks whether you want to see the marks with them.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.choice_1: Help Karim copy the letters and keep his account
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.choice_1_result: You hold the bowl while Karim rubs charcoal across the paper. Laila adds the story their grandfather told most often. Karim asks the potter to leave the names visible, then promises to bring you the finished copy before you travel on.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.choice_2: Leave the drawing with Karim and Laila
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.choice_2_result: You tell Karim the drawing belongs with the bowl. He folds it carefully, and Laila finds a clean cloth to wrap both pieces before they go to the potter. The siblings thank you and continue their search together.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b.title: Laila’s Brother Brings the Bowl
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b_resolution.body:
Karim finds you again after the potter has repaired the bowl. The chip is smooth, and the two scratched names are still legible. He has copied them twice: one sheet for home, one for you. Laila reads the second name aloud, then says she has heard it used for a settlement on the road toward the mountains. ‘Grandfather may have known someone there,’ she says. Karim wishes he had asked him when he could.

You ask whether the family wants the spare copy back. Karim says they made it for you, though he would like to know if another traveller recognises the name. Laila tells him to write his own address on the back so a reply can find them. He does, taking a moment to spell the street properly.

The potter calls them to collect a small cup he repaired as well. Karim hands you the paper, then runs back when the potter calls his name again.
ev.ev_balc_consequence_b_resolution.choi: You fold Karim’s copy into your travel book and promise to look out for the name. Laila sees that the paper will stay dry. Karim runs to collect the cup, leaving you with a way to write back.
Spend a day asking around about the name

You spend the day showing the copied name to traders and potters. Two remember hearing it, though they disagree about the exact turning. Karim writes their answers beside his own copy and thanks you for taking the question seriously.
ev.ev_balc_entry.choice_1_result: You spend two days checking names and marks with the clerk. Laila discovers that the third caravan’s record was filed beneath a different driver’s name. You note Balkh on your map and in your travel book. The clerk’s son later comes looking for you with a question about the list.
ev.ev_balc_entry.choice_2_result: Laila takes you to a shelf of stones her family has kept from old buildings. She tells you which ones her grandfather found and which came from travellers. You spend the day with her and record what you learned of Balkh. Before you leave, her younger brother asks whether you can look at another object.
ev.ev_balc_entry.choice_3_result: The merchant opens the sealed package and lets you check the jade against his tally. You pay 135 silver for the whole trading lot, spend the day settling the purchase, and load it with your goods. Laila makes sure the merchant’s name is legible in the register before she ties it shut.
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.body:
When you return, Nadir has set aside the page he promised. The driver’s sister has added a note: a well on the Badakhshan road has a broken lip, so a loaded animal needs help at the edge. Her brother says he would have called it a small matter. She asks him to imagine lifting their heaviest pack there alone. He takes the pen and adds a mark beside the warning.

You ask whether Nadir pays people for such details. ‘I return their pages with the names spelled correctly,’ he says. The sister answers that this is payment enough when a letter must find her. She shows you the route as far as she knows it and lets Nadir fill the gaps from drivers who came through yesterday.

The copyist offers you a clean copy of their account. He also has a spare seat if you want to spend the day copying the places for yourself. The sister checks the ink before either of you touches the page.
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.choice_1_resu: Nadir hands you the clean page, and the sister points out her note about the damaged well. You fold it only after she shows you where the ink will not smear. Their road account travels with you.
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.choice_2: Ask the sister to trace the Badakhshan road
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.choice_2_resu: The sister traces the Badakhshan road to the point she knows, and Nadir adds the stops he checked with other drivers. You mark Badakhshan on your map. Her brother asks her to say the well warning once more so he will remember it too.
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.choice_3: Spend a day copying the account yourself
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.choice_3_resu: You spend the day copying the road account. Nadir has you read each place back to the sister; she catches one mistaken letter and tells you why a carrier might take it to the wrong village. You leave with the pages in your own hand.
ev.ev_balc_mentor_followup.title: A Second Page from Nadir
ev.ev_baldacum_a.choice_1_result: You spend two days walking the channels and listening to Yusuf and the river workers. His granddaughter draws the last bend for you; you mark Basra downstream on your map and record how water reaches the courtyard. Yusuf asks you to come back when he opens an old service passage.
ev.ev_baldacum_a.choice_2_result: You pay 146 silver for the full Damascus steel bundle. The merchant opens the wrapping and checks every piece with you on the dry stones; Yusuf’s granddaughter carries the old tile safely away from the loading path. You record the purchase.
ev.ev_baldacum_a.choice_3_result: You stay a day while Yusuf clears the channel. He shows you which walls were rebuilt and where older work remains; his granddaughter finds a tile with a familiar mark. You write down their account and keep a reminder of the courtyard.
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.body:
Yusuf has cleared the old service door beside the water channel. His granddaughter insists on sweeping the step before anyone enters; loose grit made her slip there yesterday. Behind the door is a narrow storeroom where workers once kept spare tiles and tools. A neighbour who collects old coins is waiting with one he says came from this quarter. He offers it for 3 silver.

‘Did it really come from here?’ the girl asks. The collector says he bought it from a river porter and cannot prove the exact room. Yusuf tells her to write down what the man knows and leave the rest blank. You ask whether the channel continues beyond the wall. Yusuf takes a stick and traces its way to the river, then farther south toward Basra where the cargo boats go.

His granddaughter has put the blue tile safely on a shelf. She wants to walk the rooms once more before dark, and Yusuf invites you to come. The coin collector waits at the door, holding the piece flat in his palm.
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_1: Buy the old coin for 3 silver
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_1_resul: You pay 3 silver and take the coin. Yusuf’s granddaughter writes down the collector’s account of where he bought it, leaving its earlier history open. You keep the coin with that note.
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_2: Ask Yusuf how the river reaches Basra
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_2_resul: Yusuf traces the water from the yard into the Tigris, then names the downstream stops toward Basra. His granddaughter adds the landing where she watched the boats load; you mark Basra on your map and record their directions.
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_3: Spend a day walking the old rooms with them
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.choice_3_resul: You spend the day with Yusuf and his granddaughter, checking which doors still open and where the water enters. She puts the blue tile back in its place; you leave with a lasting reminder of the old courtyard.
ev.ev_baldacum_a_followup.title: Yusuf’s Service Door
ev.ev_baldacum_b.choice_1_result: You pay 135 silver for Mariam’s full brocade length. She and her apprentice fold it with the repaired edge inside, and she asks you to return when the next piece is finished. You keep a reminder of her workshop.
ev.ev_baldacum_b.choice_2_result: The pepper seller names Hormuz, and the river porter names Basra. The money changer adds what each route costs him; you record their account and mark both places on your map.
ev.ev_baldacum_b.choice_3_result: You spend the day talking with the money changer and Mariam over fruit syrup. The apprentice finishes his repair before the cup warms; by closing time the stallholders know your name and you have pages of notes on their trade.
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.body:
Mariam’s apprentice has finished mending the first brocade length. Today he is setting up the next one, counting the warp threads aloud. Mariam stops him at the fourth group: he has counted a strand twice. He looks embarrassed, but she makes him find the mistake himself before the loom begins to move.

A pearl seller waits outside with news of ships from Hormuz. He asks whether Mariam can make a border like the one on a cloth a buyer showed him. ‘Bring the cloth tomorrow,’ she says. ‘I will not guess from your fingers in the air.’ You ask the seller where the pearls came from. He points toward the Gulf, then admits he bought them from a broker and knows the port better than the diver.

Mariam has a full new length of brocade for 135 silver. The apprentice finishes his count and asks her to check it. She offers to let you watch the loom through a full day, and the pearl seller waits to show you his route.
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_1: Buy the new brocade length for 135 silver
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_1_resul: You pay 135 silver for Mariam’s new length. Her apprentice folds it and checks the repaired edge on the other cloth before you leave; she gives him a nod that makes him grin.
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_2: Ask the pearl seller about Hormuz
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_2_resul: The pearl seller tells you which river landing he uses before travelling toward Hormuz and where he meets sea traders. You mark the port on your map and record what he knows of the pearl trade.
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_3: Stay a day to watch Mariam weave
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.choice_3_resul: You stay the day beside the loom. Mariam lets the apprentice make the first full row while she watches; by evening you can recognise the border she planned. You keep a reminder of the visit.
ev.ev_baldacum_b_followup.title: The Next Length on Mariam’s Loom
ev.ev_baldacum_c.choice_1_result: You listen as the daughter reads each family’s account, including where the tellers disagree. The storyteller lets you keep a copy for your notes and invites you back when another relative speaks.
ev.ev_baldacum_c.choice_2_result: You pay 2 silver for the old coin. The dealer lets you examine both sides before wrapping it; the storyteller tells you which part of its history he can actually trace. You keep the coin and write down its known origin.
ev.ev_baldacum_c.choice_3_result: Over two days you speak with three families and copy their names beside their memories. One points to the riverbank, another to a gate, and the third remembers only carrying her brother through smoke. You write each account clearly and leave the storyteller a copy.
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.body:
The storyteller’s daughter has brought back a page from a family near the river gate. It names an aunt who kept an old coin in her sewing box, though no one remembers who first gave it to her. The storyteller places a similar coin beside the page and asks you to look at its worn edge. ‘I can give you this one,’ he says. ‘Just keep the name with it.’

His daughter asks a visiting boatman whether his family ever used that gate. The boatman says his uncle took the river route south, toward Basra, after the siege, but the family does not agree on which night. You ask whether they have written down the uncle’s name. The daughter finds it on the back of the page and smiles; they have at least that much right.

The storyteller asks you to stay a day if you want to help copy the remaining account. He leaves the coin beside the page while the boatman reaches for his tea.
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_1: Accept the old coin with its note
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_1_resul: You accept the old coin and the daughter’s note. She writes down what the family knows and leaves the unknown owner blank; you keep both pieces together as a reminder of their story.
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_2: Ask the boatman about the route toward Basra
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_2_resul: The boatman names the southbound landings his family used and tells you where a traveller can change boats. You mark Basra on your map and add his account to your notes.
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_3: Stay a day and help copy the family account
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.choice_3_resul: You spend the day copying names and letting each visitor check the line about their family. By evening the daughter has a clean page to keep; the people at the tea house thank you for the care you took.
ev.ev_baldacum_c_followup.title: The Coin and the Family Name
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.body:
The customs clerk catches up with you near the river gate, carrying the second paper he promised to show you. It lists two crates under the same boatman’s mark. He has checked the crates, and only one belongs to that family. ‘If I copy this as it stands, his sister will be asked to pay for a stranger’s goods,’ he says.

The boatman arrives with his sister. She takes one look at the mark and points to a small stroke that should not be there. ‘That is the other driver’s sign,’ she tells the clerk. He asks her to name someone at the gate who can confirm it. She knows two guards, but neither is on this shift. You ask whether the paper can wait. The clerk says he must finish the register before dusk.

He writes down the two guards’ names on a scrap for you and says they may help if you want to take it over. His pen hovers above the list while the sister checks the last crate herself.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.choice_1: Take the guards’ names and ask who can confirm the mark
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.choice_1_re: You take the scrap and ask at the river gate. A porter knows the two guards and tells you when one will return. The clerk keeps the disputed crate off the family’s bill until you can check.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.choice_2: Thank the clerk and leave the matter with the family
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.choice_2_re: You thank the clerk and leave the paper with the boatman’s sister. She says she will bring the right driver back before the register closes. The clerk nods and returns to his desk.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_a.title: The Clerk’s Second List
One of the river gate guards comes off duty with the porter you met. He knows the other driver’s mark because he helped unload the same crates that morning. The clerk asks him to point to the stroke that distinguishes it from the boatman’s mark. The guard does, then asks the sister whether she has eaten since the first boat arrived.

‘Not yet,’ she says, keeping a hand on the disputed crate. Her brother offers to bring bread while the clerk corrects the list. You ask whether the guard is willing to put his name beneath the correction. ‘I am,’ he replies, ‘after I see both crates once more.’ They walk together down the line, and the clerk carries the wet original beside a clean sheet.

The boatman returns with bread. His sister takes it, finally letting go of the crate. The guard is ready to confirm the mark before dusk; if you stay another day, the clerk can introduce you to the other people who use this landing.
Ask the guard to confirm the mark now

You walk the line with the guard. He confirms the mark, the clerk corrects the bill, and the boatman’s sister thanks you with her mouth full of bread. You carry the corrected note as proof of what was settled.
Stay a day and meet the landing workers

You stay a day while the clerk introduces you to the porters and boatmen. By evening the list is corrected, the crates have gone to their owners, and you know whom to ask if another cargo mark puzzles you.
The Guard Who Knew the Crate
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.body:
Near sunset, the boatman who brought you news draws a line in the dust with the end of his oar. His younger brother was due to come upriver today, but the boat has not arrived. ‘It may be waiting where the channel shallows,’ he says. His wife brings a lamp and asks whether he has heard any word from the next landing.

You ask how far south the river carries cargo. He names the places he knows, including Basra, then marks the bend where heavy boats sometimes wait for water. His wife leans over the drawing. ‘You have put the old sandbar back,’ she says. ‘The last flood moved it.’ He rubs out the line and asks her where she saw the new one.

A boy from the landing comes with a message: the missing boat stopped to mend a rope, and everyone aboard is safe. The boatman laughs at himself, then offers to draw the route clearly for you before the lamp burns low.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.choice_1: Ask him to draw the river route
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.choice_1_re: The boatman draws the main channel and his wife adds the new sandbar. You copy their marks before the lamp burns out; the boy carries the message on to the next family.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.choice_2: Thank them and decide on the river later
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.choice_2_re: You thank the family and leave them to welcome the younger brother when his boat arrives. The boatman folds his rough drawing; he says to ask again when you have a sailing date, because the water will keep changing.
ev.ev_baldacum_consequence_b.title: The Boatman’s Water Line
While you are finishing the sketch, the boatman’s younger brother reaches the landing with the rope he stopped to mend. His sister-in-law asks him whether the new sandbar is where she drew it. ‘Closer to the southern bank,’ he says, and lays the damp rope beside their sketch. He wants to sleep before unloading but agrees to check your copy first.

You show him the route. He points out a place where light boats can stop and heavy ones should keep moving. His older brother asks whether this is the same advice he gave last year. ‘Last year there was more water,’ the younger man says. His wife offers him breakfast and reminds both brothers that travellers need the date of the observation, not just the shape of the river.

You write the date beside the bend. One brother will let you carry a copy for the next boatman; the other will stay a day to compare the older notes with today’s water.
Carry the updated river note onward
You carry the dated note to the next boatman. He compares it with the level at his landing and keeps the changed sandbar in mind. Back at the family’s boat, the brothers finally sit down to eat.
Stay a day and compare the older notes
You spend a day comparing the old drawings with the brothers’ fresh observations. Their sister-in-law adds dates to the pages; you leave knowing which marks belong to this season’s water.
ev.ev_baldacum_entry.choice_1_result: You spend two days at the desk while the clerk checks the cargo marks and copies your name. The boatman’s sister helps you identify the river landings, and you mark Baghdad on your map. Before you leave, the clerk asks you to look at a second paper.
ev.ev_baldacum_entry.choice_2_result: You spend a day with the river workers and the old keeper, writing down what each remembers of the channels and former palace wing. The keeper shows you a surviving tile; you keep the visit in your travel notes. Near evening a boatman comes with fresh news of the water.
ev.ev_baldacum_entry.choice_3_result: You spend the day checking the merchant bundle, then pay 146 silver for the Damascus steel. The merchant and clerk count it together; the boatman’s sister shows you where to record the lot in your travel book.
ev.ev_baldacum_geomancy_court.choice_1_r: You lay out the figures with the sand-reader at the courtyard gate. His daughter watches your hand, then asks what question you had in mind. You finish the reading together.
ev.ev_baldacum_geomancy_court.choice_2_r: You thank the reader and continue along the lane. His daughter smooths the sand for the next visitor while he answers her question about a crooked line.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_bazi.choice_1_resu: You pay 100 silver and study with the traveller for twenty-one days. His niece makes you copy the four pillars yourself; the boatman sometimes comes by with fresh river news for your practice. When the course ends, the teacher promises to show you his own calendar before you leave.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_bazi.choice_2_resu: You pay 80 silver and spend ten days learning the sand figures from his colleague. The teacher of calendars introduces you to the other table; when you can set out the figures yourself, the sand-reader asks you to return for one more exercise.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_bazi.choice_3_resu: The traveller shows you how he writes the boat’s possible departure days beside the four pillars, then points to the latest message from the pilot. You record his explanation and leave the niece to correct the calendar.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.body:
The calendar teacher is preparing to move his books to another room before the river air dampens them. His niece has laid the pages in sunlight and asks which one he promised to show you. He finds a sheet covered with notes from boatmen, including the pilot who changed his loading time during your lessons.

‘This mark is not a prediction,’ the niece says, pointing to a stain. ‘That is where you spilled tea.’ Her uncle laughs and gives you a cleaner page with the four pillars drawn in the margin. You ask when boats normally travel south toward Basra. He asks the returning boatman instead of guessing; the man names the landings he used last season and where he stopped for fresh water.

The teacher offers you a copy of the calendar page. His niece is also sorting a stack of older notes and would welcome help for a day. The boatman waits by the door in case you need the southern route explained again.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.choice_1: Accept a copy of the calendar page
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.choice_1_: The niece makes you a clean copy. The teacher checks the four pillars in the margin and hands it over; you keep the page with your notes from the course.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.choice_2_: The boatman names the downstream landings toward Basra while the teacher’s niece marks them beside the dates. You add Basra to your map and write down both the route and what you learned at the table.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.choice_3: Spend a day helping sort the older notes
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.choice_3_: You spend the day sorting river notes by date. The niece finally finds the boatman’s missing sheet, and the teacher thanks you before the books are carried indoors. The family speaks well of your help.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_followup.title: A Date in the Traveller’s Calendar
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_geomancy.choice_1_: You pay 80 silver and study the sand figures for ten days. The reader has you practise while his daughter checks that you have copied each figure correctly. On the last day he asks you to bring one question of your own.
ev.ev_baldacum_mentor_geomancy.choice_2_: The sand-reader makes one set of marks and asks you to count before he names the figure. His daughter points out where you missed a line. You record the example in your notes.
The sand-reader’s daughter is carrying a covered tray to the courtyard gate. The wind lifted yesterday’s marks before her father could copy them, so she has asked him to work under a cloth today. He raises one corner and shows you four carefully drawn lines. ‘They are easier to check when the dust stays put,’ she says.

You ask what question he set for your last exercise. He points toward the river and asks how one would plan a journey south toward Basra when the water level changes. His daughter says the boatmen know that part; she went to ask one before you arrived. The man is coming back after unloading, and her father leaves an empty space beside the figures for his answer.

He can give you a copy of the finished figures. You may also wait for the boatman’s route, or stay the day and help his daughter protect and copy each new pattern before the wind reaches the tray.
Take a copy of the finished figures
The reader copies the figures onto a small sheet while his daughter holds the cloth against the wind. You keep the page with your lessons and note what question he used.
Wait for the boatman and ask about Basra

The boatman names the river landings toward Basra and explains where the current is strongest. You mark Basra on your map; the reader’s daughter adds the boatman’s observations beside the sand figures.
Stay a day to copy the covered figures

You spend the day copying figures as the reader draws them. His daughter checks each sheet before lifting the cloth; when the wind rises again, the pages are already safely inside. They thank you for keeping pace.
ev.ev_basora_entry.choice_1_result: Nura’s son points out the path between the warehouses. You thank him, mark Basra on your map, and follow it into town.
ev.ev_basora_entry.choice_2_result: You spend the day in the shade while boats come and go. By evening your strength has returned. Nura’s son draws the canal bend in the dust for you, and you add Basra to your map.
ev.ev_berrhoea_entry.choice_1_result: You thank Safiya and continue through the streets. Her father calls after her to make sure she has written the new price on every sheet. You mark Aleppo on your map as you leave.
ev.ev_berrhoea_entry.choice_2_result: You spend the day with Safiya. She takes you past the water place, the bread ovens, and the sellers whose letters go farthest. One of them has a brother near Trebizond; Safiya asks him to repeat the stopping places on the northward road. By evening you have marked Aleppo, Trebizond, and the route between them on your map. Safiya goes back to her stall with the revised price list, and you depart the next morning.
ev.ev_bethleem_entry.choice_1_result: You ask Yona to show you the road. He sets down the peel and walks you to the edge of the path so you can see the next fork. Lina calls him back to taste a loaf, and he answers her. You continue on your way and mark Bethlehem on your map.
ev.ev_bethleem_entry.choice_2_result:
You spend the day by the oven. That afternoon Lina remembers to turn the tray. Every loaf comes out evenly coloured. She offers one to her father. Yona breaks it open and tastes it. “Done right through. These are ready for the travellers.”

At dusk they invite you and a few passersby to share warm bread, olives, and soup. Lina breaks her burnt loaf from the morning and finishes it with the soup. You sleep on one of the pallets they lend to travellers and leave the next morning with your strength restored. You mark Bethlehem on your map.
ev.ev_bochara_battuta_a.choice_1_result: The seller takes you along the surviving wall and shows you which rooms people remember as part of the school. You spend the day listening to her family and neighbours; they remember that you took an interest in their quarter.
ev.ev_bochara_battuta_a.choice_2_result: The neighbour tells the blacksmith story as a tale he cannot verify. He then spends the day describing the caravan stops toward Samarkand, where he once sent melons. You mark that city and its road on your map.
ev.ev_bochara_battuta_a.choice_3_result: You pay 0.4 silver for a fresh piece of melon and eat it beneath the shade. The seller fixes the last corner of the cloth while her father cuts another slice for himself. You leave with more strength for the road.
ev.ev_bochara_entry.choice_1_result: The dyer’s daughter steps aside to let you pass and calls after you to check your water before the next stretch. You mark Bukhara on your map and carry on.
ev.ev_bochara_entry.choice_2_result: You spend the day resting near the yard. By supper, the daughter has retied all six rolls, and the neighbour’s son has brought his family’s bundle. You regain your strength and mark Bukhara on your map.
ev.ev_cabul_entry.choice_1_result: The cobbler’s daughter shows you the road out of the yard before returning to her stitching. You mark Kabul on your map and continue.
ev.ev_cabul_entry.choice_2_result: You spend the day resting in the yard and regain your strength. At supper the driver is wearing his repaired boots and offers you a place beside the fire. You mark Kabul on your map.
ev.ev_cabul_site_gap.choice_1_result: She draws the branch she trusts and names its water stop. You mark the route toward Taican on your map while the driver checks the straps on his boots again.
ev.ev_cabul_site_gap.choice_2_result: You watch him roll damp wool and stitch it above the leather sole. His daughter tests the driver’s fit once more; you record the craft and understand why each layer has its place.
ev.ev_cacanfu_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through without stopping. You set the way to Cacanfu on your map.
ev.ev_cacanfu_entry.choice_2_result: You rest and ask what men say of this place. The road to Cacanfu opens on your map. The account is written down before the hour turns. It costs you 1 day on the road.
ev.ev_cachanfu_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through without stopping. You set the way to Cachanfu on your map.
ev.ev_cachanfu_entry.choice_2_result: You rest and ask what men say of this place. The road to Cachanfu opens on your map. The account is written down before the hour turns. It costs you 1 day on the road.
ev.ev_caffa_entry.choice_1_result: You thank Arslan and move on. Sada calls after you to say there are seven and a half apples now, because she has eaten her half. You mark Caffa and the shore road on your map.
ev.ev_caffa_entry.choice_2_result: You stay at Arslan's shelter for the day. He shows you where the carts gather, while Sada makes you count the apples twice to prove she has not hidden any. They share supper and give you a place to sleep. You leave the next morning stronger and mark Caffa on your map.
ev.ev_caffa_mentor_runes.choice_1_result: You pay and learn the runes. You pay 5000 coins. You spend 7 days learning the art. You can now read it on any road. A mark is set on this affair.
ev.ev_caffa_mentor_runes.choice_2_result: You ask what Raidho names on this quay. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_caiju_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through without stopping. The road to Caiju opens on your map.
ev.ev_caiju_entry.choice_2_result: You rest and ask what men say of this place. You set the way to Caiju on your map. You set what you saw into your travel book. You spend 1 day before the way is clear again.
ev.ev_cail_a.choice_1_result: You stand a day upon the quay and watch the horses come ashore. You spend 1 day before the way is clear again. You set what you saw into your travel book. You set the way to Melibar on your map.
ev.ev_cail_a.choice_2_result: You buy an Arabian charger from the Hormos merchants. You pay 18000 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_cail_a.choice_3_result: You ask the shipmasters where their vessels touch next. You set the way to Coilum on your map. You set the way to Samara on your map. You set what you saw into your travel book.
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.body: On the quay where western ships land horses, a charger broker who serves King Ashar's harbour draws you into the shade of the landing sheds. He says Cail is where Hormos horses meet Maabar cotton — and that Melibar, Coilum, and Samara are written in his landing book if you mean to ride or sail onward.
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_1: Buy a charger at the harbour's measured price
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_1_result: He sells you a charger fit for the Maabar road. The price is steep, and the horse is sound.
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_2: Ask which sea road leads toward Melibar and Coilum
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_2_result: Melibar and Coilum are marked on your map. The pepper coast is clear.
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_3: Watch the landing a day and hear the brother-kings named
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.choice_3_result: You spend a day at the landing. Samara is named in the talk, and fortune bends a little your way.
ev.ev_cail_a_followup.title: Cail: The Horse Quay's Second Page
ev.ev_cail_b.choice_1_result: You wait two days upon the concourse in hope of seeing the King pass. It costs you 2 days on the road. Your patient waiting is spoken of at the gate. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_cail_b.choice_2_result: You listen while the brokers speak of the five brother-kings. You set the way to Melibar on your map. You set the way to Coilum on your map. You set what you saw into your travel book.
ev.ev_cail_b.choice_3_result: You buy cotton cloth in the harbour market. You pay 400 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. After the bargain, the cloth merchants call your name across the wharf.
ev.ev_cail_battuta_a.choice_1_result: You take the rough way of Baba, holding to the iron pins and the ten chains fixed in the rock. At the last chain, the chain of witness, you look down, and the frightful notion seizes you that you shall fall. Beyond it lies the cave of Khizr, and above that, two miles higher, the hollow in the stone where the foot of Adam rests, eleven spans long; you touch the blessed foot-mark and make your pilgrimage.
ev.ev_cail_battuta_a.choice_2_result: The Jogees, who walk to the foot-mark every year, show you the nine excavations cut in the rock about the impression, where pilgrims press gold, rubies, and jewels, and race to be first at the hollows. They tell you the Chinese once cut out the place of the great toe with the stone about it and carried it to a temple in El Zaitun, where pilgrimages are made to it from the most distant parts of China.
ev.ev_cail_battuta_a.choice_3_result: The rubies of Serendib are found all over the island and sold by the inhabitants as property. You buy a stone cut from the white fissured rock in which the rubies lie, and pay the islander his price; the merchants of Malabar and the Maabar carry away the wood of the coast for a few articles of clothing, but the ruby keeps its worth.
ev.ev_cail_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through the darvāzā without delay. You set the way to Cail on your map.
ev.ev_cail_entry.choice_2_result: You walk through the bāzār. It costs you 1 day on the road. The account is written down before the hour turns. The road to Cail opens on your map.
ev.ev_cail_entry.choice_3_result: You visit the mandir (temple). Your name carries a little more weight here now. You carry away a small sign of the place. You set the way to Cail on your map.
ev.ev_cail_entry.choice_4_result: A traveller who came this way tells of the mountain of Serendib, of chains and iron pins and the eleven-span foot-mark; his tale sets you on the pilgrims' road, and he promises the rest at the harbour.
ev.ev_calatu_a.choice_1_result: You walk the fort walls and look out upon the gulf. It costs you 1 day on the road. The road to Ormus opens on your map. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_calatu_a.choice_2_result: You buy a sack of pepper from the Indian merchants. You pay 12000 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. You set what you saw into your travel book.
ev.ev_calatu_a.choice_3_result: You stand upon the mole and count the vessels at anchor. The road to Dufar opens on your map. The account is written down before the hour turns. Fortune bends a little your way.
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.body: On the walls of the gulf fortress a watch captain who has counted ships for the Melic of Hormos draws you along the parapet. He says Calatu is six hundred miles from the open sea and yet every pepper ship from Dufar and every inland caravan from Camadi must answer to this mole — if you mean to leave with more than a glance at the gulf.
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_1: Buy pepper at the fortress mole price
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_1_result: He sells you pepper sealed for the gulf. The price includes the mole fee.
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_2: Ask which inland road leads toward Camadi
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_2_result: Camadi is marked on your map with the inland days. The plain road is clear.
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_3: Count the ships a day and hear Ormus named
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.choice_3_result: You spend a day counting masts. Ormus and Dufar are named, and fortune bends a little your way.
ev.ev_calatu_a_followup.title: Calatu: The Gulf Fortress Wall-Walk
ev.ev_calatu_b.choice_1_result: You hear how the Melic of Hormos uses this city as a refuge. You set what you saw into your travel book. You set the way to Ormus on your map. A small turn of fortune favours you.
ev.ev_calatu_b.choice_2_result: You buy dates brought in with the grain ships. You pay 180 coins. You add 1 item to your stores. The account is written down before the hour turns.
ev.ev_calatu_b.choice_3_result: You ask the caravan masters which inland roads leave from here. You set the way to Camadi on your map. You set the way to Dufar on your map. You set what you saw into your travel book.
ev.ev_calatu_entry.choice_1_result: You pass through the darvāzā without delay. The road to Calatu opens on your map.
ev.ev_calatu_entry.choice_2_result: You walk through the bāzār. You spend 1 day before the way is clear again. You set what you saw into your travel book. You set the way to Calatu on your map.
ev.ev_calatu_entry.choice_3_result: You sit a while among the lamps of the mandir. The keeper knows your name by the time you leave, and a pinch of incense is pressed into your hand. The sea road to Calatu is marked on your map.
ev.ev_camadi_a.choice_1_result: You spend the day with Banu among the old walls. She names the families who once lived there and points toward Kerman beyond the plain. You mark it on your map and write her account in your travel book. She asks you to return if you want to hear more.
ev.ev_camadi_a.choice_2_result: You pay 1.2 silver for a small bag of dates. Banu’s grandson ties it shut while she tells you which grove produced the fruit. You eat some on the road and feel refreshed. You note the grove in your travel book, and Banu invites you back to hear more about the old street.
ev.ev_camadi_a.choice_3_result: The caravan people show you where the road reaches Cobinan. You mark the town on your map and write down how the old conflicts changed their stopping places. Their practical advice makes you more confident about the next journey.
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.body:
Banu spreads a worn cloth under her palm and draws the old quarter as she remembers it. Her grandson adds the well and the house they live in now. ‘That part is your map,’ she tells him.

She has a caravan lot of dates ready to sell to traders at a fixed price. You can buy the lot, ask her how travellers reach Hormuz and take ship toward Calatu, or stay a day and help the boy put the family’s names in the right places on the cloth.

The boy puts his finger on a blank space in the cloth. ‘Who lived here?’ Banu names a baker and then remembers his daughter has a stall by the present market. You ask whether she will show the daughter this drawing. ‘When it is finished,’ she says. ‘She may remember where her father kept the oven.’ Another trader arrives to ask about the date lot but has not agreed to buy it. Banu looks up at you and asks whether you want to discuss the price first.
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_1: Buy the caravan lot of dates for 108 silver
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_1_result: You pay 108 silver for the caravan lot of dates. Banu’s grandson checks the bundles in front of you and ties them firmly. You record the exchange and her family’s story in your travel book.
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_2: Ask Banu about the road to Calatu
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_2_result: Banu names the wells on the inland road to Hormuz and says sailors there can take you onward to Calatu. You mark the town on your map and write down what she remembers of the route.
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_3: Stay a day to finish the family map
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.choice_3_result: You spend the day listening and writing names beside the boy’s drawing. Banu’s family thanks you for helping preserve it, and people in Camadi come to know you through them.
ev.ev_camadi_a_followup.title: A Map under Banu’s Palm
ev.ev_camadi_b.choice_1_result: You spend the day in the shade, sharing water and stories with the travellers. You write down what you learned about the heat of this plain. They remember you kindly when the party moves on.
ev.ev_camadi_b.choice_2_result: Banu shows you the inland road toward Hormuz, where ships continue across the gulf toward Calatu, and the road back to Kerman. You mark both towns on your map and record her directions in your travel book.
ev.ev_camadi_b.choice_3_result: You pay 108 silver for the merchant bale of cotton cloth. Banu’s neighbour wraps it against the dust, and the other stallholders greet you as a familiar trader.
ev.ev_camadi_entry.choice_1_result: Banu’s grandson points you toward the road out. You mark Camadi on your map and continue.
ev.ev_camadi_entry.choice_2_result: You spend the day tasting fruit and talking with the stallholders. You write down what you learned in your travel book and mark Camadi on your map.
ev.ev_camadi_entry.choice_3_result: You visit the mosque courtyard and speak with people resting there. One offers you a small keepsake from the town. They greet you warmly when you leave, and you mark Camadi on your map.
ev.ev_cambaet_entry.choice_1_result: The apprentice steps aside so you can pass beneath the cloth. At the far end of the lane he points out the road beyond the market. “Come back when the cloth is dry,” he says, returning to his line. You continue with the town's turns clear in mind.
ev.ev_cambaet_entry.choice_2_result: You spend a day walking the stalls with the dyer. She introduces the cotton seller who buys her offcuts and the porter who carries finished cloth to the water. When the merchant returns, he recognizes his sister's two blue threads on the bundle. You leave with the neighbourhood's trades and paths in mind.
ev.ev_cambaet_site_gap.choice_1_result: The dyer takes you to the corner where carts leave for Semenat and points out the road marker she uses for deliveries. “Ask at the next water stop before taking a side track,” she says. You trace the turn on your map while the apprentice carries his basin back to the yard.
ev.ev_cambaet_site_gap.choice_2_result: You help rinse and spread the cloth. The streaks remain near the old fold, so the apprentice opens the whole length before his aunt returns it to the vat. She shows you how to judge the dried edge and gives him the task of checking the next batch himself.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a.choice_1_result: You present yourself at the Kaan's court with your gifts, and the chamberlain receives them with practiced courtesy. He measures you as he speaks, and when the audience ends he makes you a small sign to stay.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a.choice_2_result: You stand before the great hall and measure its size with your eyes until it overwhelms you. The palace of the Kaan is now marked in your book.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a.choice_3_result: The Kaan's guards speak of the empire's breadth: a road runs from this gate to the city of Kinsay, where the Kaan's granaries never empty. Its name is now on your map.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.body: A chamberlain of the Kaan's household finds you as you leave the shadow of the great hall. He has served at three feasts beneath those painted beams and can read a guest's worth by the way he stands. He does not ask what you saw; he asks what you mean to carry away from the hall. The court, he says, keeps tokens for travellers it intends to remember.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_1: Take the cord of the hall's own silk the chamberlain offers
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_1_resul: The chamberlain knots a cord of vermilion silk about your wrist, the same silk that hangs in the great hall. In Cambaluc the knot is known; those who see it will know you stood where the Kaan holds his feasts.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_2: Ask which road the envoys take when they leave for the south
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_2_resul: The chamberlain draws the road the envoys ride southward, past Kinsay, marking the post-stations where horses are changed. The way to Kinsay is now clear on your map, and you know how the Kaan's word travels.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_3: Promise to speak well of the great hall in the cities ahead
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.choice_3_resul: The chamberlain accepts your promise and asks nothing else. In Cambaluc your word now carries weight among those who heard you give it.
ev.ev_cambaluc_a_followup.title: Cambaluc: The Chamberlain's Token
ev.ev_cambaluc_b.choice_1_result: You buy silk in the suburb at the Cambaluc price, and the counting-house keeper watches the transaction with sharp eyes. When the bolt is wrapped, he motions you inside to a quieter chamber.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b.choice_2_result: You spend a day counting the cart-loads of silk that enter the city. By evening the tally is beyond counting, and the city's hunger for silk is in your book.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b.choice_3_result: You visit the public granaries and find them full in a year when no one goes hungry. The men who keep them remember your interest.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.body: The keeper of a counting-house in the suburbs calls you over from his abacus, where the day's carts are being tallied. He has seen your face among the thousand cart-loads of silk, and he knows which travellers understand the city's measure. He does not sell you his silence; he offers what the suburbs sell to those who ask the right questions.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_1: Buy a bolt of silk at the price written in his ledger
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_1_resul: The keeper sells you a bolt of silk at his own list price, no bargaining and no tricks. The cloth is real, the price fair, and the suburb lets you leave with it.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_2: Ask him to draw the road the northern carts come by
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_2_resul: The keeper draws the road the northern carts take to the twelve suburbs, marking the watering places and the toll-houses. The way to Chandu is now on your map, and you know what the north sends south.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_3: Stay a day and count cart-loads with the tally-men
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.choice_3_resul: You spend a day at the counting-house, learning how the suburbs are numbered in silk and pepper and grain. It costs you time, but the measure of Cambaluc stays with you when you go.
ev.ev_cambaluc_b_followup.title: Cambaluc: The Counting-House Keeper
ev.ev_cambaluc_c.choice_1_result: You walk among the transplanted trees of the green hill, where cedars brought from the south shade the jade terraces. A gardener tending the roots looks up at your footsteps and sets down his spade.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c.choice_2_result: You climb the hill at sunset and see the whole city at once — the palace, the market, the relay stations, all below one roof of light. The sight settles in you.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c.choice_3_result: The gardeners who water the trees by hand speak of the summer palace at Chandu, a day's ride north. Its name is now on your map, and their craft is in your book.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.body: On the lower slope of the mountain of green jade, the oldest of the thousand gardeners sets down his buckets and waves you over. He watered these trees when they were carried in on the backs of elephants, and he has climbed this hill every day since. He does not forbid you the mountain; he asks only that you understand what it cost to raise it.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_1: Ask him how a tree can be moved without knowing it
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_1_resul: The gardener shows you the wet earth bound in silk about the roots, and the way the diggers take a tree whole in winter. The art of the green hill is now written in your travel book.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_2: Ask him to draw the road the trees came by from the north
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_2_resul: The gardener draws the road the trees came by from the forests of the north, past Chandu, marking the passes and the places where the elephants rested. The way to Chandu is now on your map, and you know what a mountain is made of.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_3: Take up a bucket and help water the trees for a day
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.choice_3_resul: You climb the hill with a shoulder-pole and buckets, learning the gardeners' pace and their water. The gardeners of Cambaluc remember that you helped, and the hill keeps a part of you.
ev.ev_cambaluc_c_followup.title: Cambaluc: The Gardener of the Green Hill
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.body: The first answer does not end at the gate. A clerk of the relay stations draws you aside and asks what you intend to carry away from Cambaluc. Beyond the question lies the palace gate and the relay stations; he offers to set a name to your name, the name of a courier who reads the roads of the empire. Choose what you will make of the sign.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.choice_1: Take the name and ask the relay clerk who can vouch for it
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.choice_1_re: You take the name the clerk offers and ask who can vouch for it. He names two relay masters, and the matter opens again.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.choice_2: Thank the relay clerk and keep your own counsel
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.choice_2_re: You thank the clerk and keep your own counsel. The matter closes at the relay station, and nothing more is asked of you in Cambaluc.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_a.title: Cambaluc: The Mark at the Gate
You have agreed to carry the relay's seal with you — the name of a courier who reads the roads of the empire. It will not decide the whole journey, but at the next relay station his name may win you a fresh horse.
Send the seal on before nightfall
You send the seal on before nightfall. The courier's word now travels with your name, and the relay stations have a reason to receive you.
Keep the seal in your travel book
You keep the seal in your travel book and spend a day setting it down plainly. The record is made; the favour waits for a road that may never call on it.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_b.body: The answer sends a rumour along the road. Before the day is out, a guard of the granaries finds you at the gate with a second account of the palace gate and the relay stations — how the couriers count their days, and who reads the road ahead. It is less grand than a traveller's tale, and more useful.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_b.choice_1_re: You follow the guard's practical advice and ask him to set it down. He writes the account out for you, and the road's true measures come into your hand.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_b.choice_2: Leave the account with the guard
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_b.choice_2_re: You leave the account with the guard and keep your own counsel. It goes back to the granary gate, and Cambaluc asks nothing more of you.
ev.ev_cambaluc_consequence_b.title: Cambaluc: The Road Behind the Answer
You have chosen to carry the guard's account with you — how the couriers count their days, and who reads the road. It will not decide the whole journey, but it will keep you on the swift road among the slow ones.
Pass the couriers' count before nightfall
You pass the couriers' count to the next rider before nightfall. The road's measures now travel ahead of you, and where they land, your name follows.
Keep the couriers' schedule in your travel book
