You ask Pavel if his mother knows about the lining. ‘She does,’ he says. ‘She keeps asking when I’ll stop measuring it and start sewing.’ His apprentice calls from the shaded rack that the pelt is dry enough now. Pavel makes him bring it over and checks the back for stiff patches. ‘This part goes under the collar,’ he tells him. ‘She’ll notice if it scratches.’ He offers to show you where the Kyiv caravans gather after the fitting is cut.
ev.gap.moscovia.scene.choice.route: Ask about the road to Kyiv
ev.gap.moscovia.scene.result.route: Pavel tells you where the southbound caravans meet and which road reaches Kyiv. You mark the road and city while his apprentice folds the lining.
ev.gap.moscovia.scene.result.talk: You feel the pelt along its grain while Pavel checks the leather side. He folds it for his mother and points out his stall on your map of Moscow.
ev.gap.moscovia.scene.title: The Fur Lining
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.body:
A potter named Theodoros sets a cooled, plain glazed bowl in the shade. The glaze has gathered in one thick line near the rim. His daughter Maria holds it up to the light, looking for the place where she first touched the wet clay.

“I thought I spoiled it,” she says. Theodoros pours water into it and sets it on the table. “Your grandmother asked for a bowl that would hold soup. It does.” Maria asks if she can give it to her grandmother herself. He says she should, once they have dried it.

Theodoros asks Maria to show you where the glaze thickened. His brother has left a list of stops on the way to Constantinople; Maria puts it beside the dry bowl so neither is forgotten.

You ask whether Grandmother knows the bowl is ready. Maria says she promised to bring it after the afternoon meal. Theodoros wants her to carry it in a basket, with cloth around the rim so it will not knock against the other dishes. Maria asks if the thick glaze will show when soup is inside. ‘Only if she looks closely,’ he says. She turns the bowl in her hands and says Grandmother always looks closely at anything her family makes.
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.choice.route: Read the potter's list of stopping places
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.choice.talk: Stay while Maria prepares the bowl
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.result.route: Theodoros finds the travel list under a stack of bowl moulds. His brother went west toward the Marmara shore and continued to Constantinople; the list records the places where he changed carriers. You copy the names and mark Nicaea, Constantinople, and the route between them. Maria asks you to leave the list where her uncle will find it on his return.
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.result.talk: Maria tests the bowl with water once more, dries it, then wraps it in cloth for her grandmother. Theodoros takes you around the potter's yard and shows you where the lane reaches the lake. You add this part of Nicaea to your map. Maria leaves with the bowl held in both hands.
ev.gap.nicaea.scene.title: The Potter's Family Bowl
ev.gap.ninive.scene.body:
The grain sack has a hole near the seam. Laila’s niece, Mariam, is trying to cover it with her hand while her father finds a needle. Across the river, an older woman waves from beside the landing.

‘That’s her,’ Mariam says. ‘If she comes over to help, she’ll tell me the bowl was big enough without this whole sack.’ Her father stitches the seam while you steady the load. He knows the roads south; Mariam wants him to finish before the next boat leaves.

You ask whether the grain is for Laila alone. Mariam says her aunt usually saves a portion for the neighbour who helps her carry water. Her father says the bag is heavy because Mariam wanted to include enough for that household too. Across the water, Laila lifts the empty bowl for them to see. Mariam calls that they are coming; the boatman tells her to save her breath and keep hold of the sack. She grins at him, then asks her father to make the last stitch a tight one. He tests it with a short pull before he stands.
ev.gap.ninive.scene.choice.route: Ask him about the road to Baghdad
ev.gap.ninive.scene.choice.talk: Hold the sack while he sews
ev.gap.ninive.scene.result.route: He points south along the river and names the stopping places he uses on the way to Baghdad. You mark the road and the city. Mariam calls him back: the seam is done and the boat is leaving.
ev.gap.ninive.scene.result.talk: The last stitch holds. Mariam carries the sack to the boat with her father and waves to her aunt. On the opposite bank, Laila is already holding out the bowl. You mark the ferry and Mosul on your map.
ev.gap.ninive.scene.title: A Bowl for Laila
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.body:
The scales come back with one pan bent. Anfisa’s neighbour says it slipped from his cart, and he offers to repair it. Her father is ready to weigh the wax by hand, but Anfisa wants the pan straight before she sells any.

Her daughter asks you to hold the stand while the neighbour works. ‘He borrowed it to weigh flour for his sister,’ she explains. ‘She was making bread for the boatmen.’ Anfisa knows the southbound road toward Moscow and can tell you where it starts.

The neighbour tries the pan against the edge of his cart and asks Anfisa to look. ‘A little more,’ she says. Her father offers a wooden wedge, but the neighbour says he can straighten it without one. You ask why she is so particular about a small bend. Anfisa sets a piece of wax in the pan: ‘The buyer will put his own weight on the other side. If this pan hangs low, we argue all afternoon.’ Her daughter holds the stand steady as he makes one last adjustment.
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.choice.route: Ask Anfisa about the Moscow road
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.choice.talk: Hold the scales while they repair them
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.result.route: As Anfisa tells you which yard the southbound carts leave from, the neighbour straightens the pan. She tests it with a small wax bundle, then explains how the road reaches Moscow. You mark the route and city before the next boat unloads.
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.result.talk: You steady the stand while the neighbour bends the pan back into shape. Anfisa weighs one small bundle to test it. It balances, and you mark her trading yard in Novgorod on your map.
ev.gap.novogardia.scene.title: Anfisa’s Borrowed Scales
ev.gap.petra.scene.body:
Rashida's son Hassan sits beside the shelter mending a waterskin. He pulls out an old leather cord and hands it to his daughter Nadia. “This can still serve. Try tightening the mouth of the bag.”

Nadia does, but a small drop seeps from the side. She admits she patched that spot only yesterday. Hassan holds the skin up to the light. “Your new stitches are firm. It's the old seam beside them that's leaking. I used to check only the part I'd just sewn too.”

Nadia threads her needle and asks whether you will hold the bag for her. Hassan has drawn several routes towards Egypt in the sand and is showing another traveller where to carry extra water.

You ask Nadia whether she has repaired a water skin alone before. ‘Only the small one my grandmother carries,’ she says. Hasan shows her how to keep a little slack beside the seam so it does not tear when the skin is filled. Rashida comes over with a cup and asks whether they have tested the patch. Nadia fills the skin partway, holds it over the sand, and waits. No drop falls this time. Her father asks her to mark the repaired side with a bit of thread so they can check it again before the next journey.
ev.gap.petra.scene.choice.route: Listen to Hassan describe the Cairo road, then check on Nadia
ev.gap.petra.scene.choice.talk: Hold the waterskin while Nadia repairs the old seam
ev.gap.petra.scene.result.route: Hassan draws the road to Cairo in the sand and shows you where travellers may miss a water source. You copy his directions. Beside you, Nadia finishes her stitching, tests the skin with water, and hangs it in the shade again. Hassan sees that she has checked the old seam as well. You add Cairo and this road to your map.
ev.gap.petra.scene.result.talk: You hold the leather while Nadia sews along the loose stitches. Hassan pours in half a bowl of water and has her hang up the skin to test it. After a while, the seam is still dry. Nadia puts the needle back into the ball of thread. “I'll check my own bag tonight.” You remember where to find the shelter if you need a waterskin repaired on another journey through Petra.
ev.gap.petra.scene.title: The Waterskin's Seam
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.body:
At the shore, fisherwoman Dora is mending a net. Her younger brother Theo holds the line while she replaces a torn mesh. Their father has gone to sell today's catch, and the two of them want the net ready before he comes back.

Theo says he can mend it faster. Dora gives him a needle and watches him make one knot. It is tight enough, but he has tied two meshes together. He sighs and begins again. “Our father taught me when I was your age,” Dora says. “I did exactly that.”

Dora can show you where the fishing families work along the bay. Their father once carried fish north toward Constantinople, and Theo knows the stops from hearing the story so often.

You ask Theo who tied the knots in the older part of the net. ‘Father did, before he left this morning,’ he says. Dora points to a patch where she made the same knot last year and asks him to compare their size. Theo tries again with a shorter loop. ‘That is close,’ she says, ‘but pull it once before you call it finished.’ A gull lands beside the fish basket, and Theo waves it away with his free hand while keeping hold of the line. Dora tells him that is exactly why two people mend a net together.
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.choice.route: Hear Theo tell his father's northern journey
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.choice.talk: Watch Theo finish the torn mesh
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.result.route: Theo recounts his father's journey north, naming each place where the fish was sold or the boat stopped. Dora corrects him when he swaps two towns. You mark Smyrna, Constantinople, and the route between them on your map. Their father returns in time to hear Theo pronounce the last stop correctly.
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.result.talk: Theo unties the extra loop and makes a new mesh. Dora pulls it gently to test it, then lets him finish the next one himself. She walks you past the nearby sheds and points out where the fish sellers gather. You add this part of Smyrna to your map before their father returns.
ev.gap.smyrna.scene.title: The Net for Tomorrow's Catch
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.body:
At the landing, Murad's father Karim is packing salted fish into a barrel. Murad has written marks on the lid for each layer. He has added one mark too many and is waiting for his father to notice.

Karim sees it, counts the fish, and asks where the missing layer went. Murad says he marked a place for tomorrow's catch. “Then we shall need another barrel,” Karim replies. Zoya brings a dry cloth and helps them cover the fish while they decide how much room to leave.

Karim has carried barrels by water toward Caffa and can tell you how boats get out of the river. You can also stay and see how Murad finishes the barrel he started counting.

You ask Murad how he will tell tomorrow’s fish from today’s if both go into the same barrel. He says he will put the next catch on top. Karim shows him that the lid barely closes already, so a second barrel will keep the salt from spilling. Zoya asks whether the new barrel has been washed. Murad starts toward the shed to check. His father calls him back to finish the mark for the fish they have now; tomorrow’s count can wait. Murad scratches the correct number of lines and asks Zoya to read them back.
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.choice.route: Hear Karim describe the water route to Caffa
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.choice.talk: Stay until Murad finishes the barrel
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.result.route: Karim draws the Don, the Sea of Azov, and the passage out toward the Black Sea with a wet finger on a board. He names the places where his boat stopped on the way to Caffa. Murad adds a mark for each one. You record Tana, Caffa, and the route between them on your map.
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.result.talk: Murad counts each layer again, erases the extra mark, and helps Karim fit the lid. Zoya points out the dry ground where they store the barrels and the track from there to the landing. You add this part of Tana to your map. Murad says the next barrel will have its own marks, even if tomorrow's catch is small.
ev.gap.tana-azov.scene.title: Salt Fish at the Landing
ev.gap.tarsus.scene.body:
Meryem spins cotton thread in a small courtyard. Her nephew Cem has been asked to wind the finished thread into a ball. Every few turns he stops to straighten a tangle, then winds so quickly that another one forms.

“The cloth is for your mother,” Meryem reminds him. Cem says he knows; he wants her to have it before his father leaves with a caravan. He has never been to Antioch himself, though his father has carried bundles there and told him about the road.

Meryem passes you the spindle so she can free the thread caught beneath Cem's foot. She can show you the lanes around this courtyard. Cem offers to fetch his father's travel notes if you are going toward Antioch.

You ask Jem whether his mother knows about the new cloth. ‘She knows Aunt Meryem has wool,’ he says. ‘She does not know we chose the blue thread.’ Meryem tells him to leave the surprise alone until the weaving is done. He asks how many more bundles need winding. She holds up three fingers; he looks at the tangle by his shoe and admits it may take longer than he hoped. A neighbour knocks at the gate to collect a spindle, and Meryem asks Jem to show her where he put it before he starts another ball.
ev.gap.tarsus.scene.choice.route: Look at Cem's father's road notes
ev.gap.tarsus.scene.result.route: Cem finds his father's notes beneath a folded cloth. He reads out the stopping places on the way southeast toward Antioch, and Meryem corrects the name of one village from her own memory. You mark Tarsus, Antioch, and the road between them. Cem puts the notes back carefully; his father will want them when he leaves.
ev.gap.tarsus.scene.result.talk: You lift the spindle while Meryem frees the strand beneath Cem's foot. Cem starts winding again, more slowly this time. Meryem takes you around the nearby lanes as the thread dries, pointing out the courtyard where travellers can ask for clean water. You add this part of Tarsus to your map.
ev.gap.tarsus.scene.title: Meryem's Spindle
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.body:
At the waterfront, sailor Mikhail and his sister Iona are spreading a torn sail across clean stones. She has brought a square of cloth from home. He says the patch needs to reach farther beyond the tear, and she goes back to the bundle for a larger piece.

Their father taught both of them to sew before either was allowed near his boat. Iona says she was the better student. Mikhail says their father trusted her with the needle because she did not leave it in the sail. She finds a bigger patch and asks you to hold the corner while they sew.

They have both travelled by water toward Caffa. Iona keeps the list of stopping places because Mikhail remembers boats by the people he met rather than by where they docked.

You ask Iona whether their father ever checked the sails after teaching them to sew. ‘Every time,’ she says. ‘He pulled each patch until we thought he would rip it off himself.’ Mikhail tries the new cloth against the tear and admits the larger piece fits better. He asks his sister to hold the needle while he shifts the sail away from a puddle. She tells him to put it in the little wooden case first. The boatman waiting nearby calls that the wind may rise by evening, so a sound patch matters more than finishing at once.
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.choice.route: Ask Iona to show you her Caffa stops
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.choice.talk: Hold the sail while Iona sews
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.result.route: Iona reads the stops on the way to Caffa from a folded sheet. Mikhail adds the names of people he met at two of them; she confirms the places and laughs when he swaps their order. You mark Trebizond, Caffa, and the sea route between them on your map. Then you help fold the repaired sail.
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.result.talk: You keep the sail flat while Iona sews around the larger patch. Mikhail folds the finished edge and carries it back to the boat. Iona points out the waterfront sheds and the lane to the houses as you walk. You add this part of Trebizond to your map.
ev.gap.trapezus.scene.title: A Patch for the Boat Sail
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.body:
Samia packs olives into clay jars in a courtyard behind the harbour. Her ten-year-old son passes her washed stones to weigh down the fruit. A piece of red thread is tied around one jar.

"That one goes on a ship to my uncle," the boy says. "Last year he left a whole jar there and came home saying ship rats ate it."

Samia pours in brine and laughs. "This year we'll write his name on it. If the rats can read, I'll let them have it." The boy reaches for a piece of charcoal, then asks you whether a ship or the road through the mountains is faster.
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.choice.route: Ask where travellers leave for Antioch
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.choice.talk: Help the boy write the name and hear about his uncle
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.result.route:
Samia points beyond the courtyard. "Leave by the north gate for Antioch. Snow can close the mountain road in cold weather; go with a caravan that knows it."

The boy says he will tell his uncle the route next time the ship docks, so his uncle can come home by land for once. Samia tightens the red thread. "First let him bring this jar back."
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.result.talk:
The boy writes so large that his uncle's name wraps halfway around the jar. Samia says he will recognise it. Her brother works as a cook aboard ship. On his first voyage he took a full jar, worried he might feel sick, then shared it all with the crew before landfall. The boy laughs and adds one more stone under the lid.

Samia gives you an olive preserved last year. The boy takes one too and drinks water after tasting the salt.
ev.gap.tripolis.scene.title: Olive Jars in the Courtyard
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.body:
At a work space near the shore, Rana rinses a piece of dyed wool. Her daughter sets smooth pebbles on its corners so the wind will not lift it. A small sea shell lies in the basket of pebbles. The daughter says her grandfather picked it out of an old wall and told her that people here once made purple dye from such creatures.

“He told me the cloth was worth a house,” she says. Rana laughs. “He told you a good story. This piece is for your aunt, and she would rather have it before the cold weather.” The girl touches the wet edge, then withdraws her hand when Rana gives her a look.

Rana has been walking the shore to find people willing to carry finished cloth inland. She asks you to help her remember where you met the last caravan. She can also describe the coast road toward Acre; she has relatives who have travelled that way.
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.choice.route: Ask Rana about the road toward Acre
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.choice.talk: Tell Rana where you met the caravan
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.result.route: Rana traces the coast southward in the damp sand. She has family who have travelled toward Acre and tells you where they stopped for water. Her daughter adds a shell to the starting point so you cannot mistake Tyre for the next bend. You record Tyre, Acre, and the route between them on your map.
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.result.talk: You name the place and show Rana the mark in your notebook. She calls her daughter over so both of them can remember it. The girl adds a shell beside your mark; Rana promises to take the finished cloth to the next caravan herself. You add this part of Tyre to your map, including the place where travellers gather.
ev.gap.tyrus.scene.title: The Shell in the Cloth Worker's Basket
ev.hierusalem.entry.body:
As you enter Jerusalem, workers in a soap shop are cutting hardened soap into blocks. Nadia, the apprentice, counts them against a list of names. She needs six for an inn downhill. On the fifth, the master takes a block with a chipped corner away.

"It still washes," Nadia says. The master turns the chip towards her. "Last time the innkeeper said the children thought a chipped block had already been used. Give him a whole one."

The shop smells of olive oil. People with different accents pass the door, some going to worship, others looking for a room. Nadia shows you her list. "I have a delivery to make. Tell me which way you're leaving town. I know these lanes."
ev.hierusalem.entry.choice.look: Help Nadia deliver the soap and stay in town for a night
ev.hierusalem.entry.choice.pass: Ask Nadia for the gate and continue
ev.hierusalem.entry.title: The Soap Basket
ev.ispahan.clothnote.body:
Parvin has finished the blue cloth, but her sister’s letter to the bride has arrived too late for the first carrier. Her nephew suggests sewing it into the hem before the next caravan leaves. Parvin worries that the bride might never think to look there.

The boy finds a reel of red thread and asks whether one bright stitch will make the letter easy to find. Parvin takes the letter and reads the bride’s name aloud, checking it against the order before anyone sews.

You ask whether the first carrier has already left. ‘At dawn,’ Parvin says. ‘My sister’s letter came after he closed his pack.’ Her nephew says he could run to the caravan courtyard before supper, but Parvin asks who will watch the cloth while she finishes the wrapping. The neighbour who helped with the washing passes the door and offers to stay a moment. The boy looks at you, then at the letter: ‘If it goes separately, tell the carrier whose hands should receive it. My aunt writes neatly, but he has many families’ letters.’ Parvin folds the paper once and keeps the address facing out.
ev.ispahan.clothnote.choice.carry: Carry the letter to the Basra caravan
ev.ispahan.clothnote.choice.stitch: Help mark the hem with red thread
ev.ispahan.clothnote.result.carry: The caravan master places the letter in a separate pouch and tells you when his people will take the road toward Basra. You mark that route and destination. Parvin’s nephew runs back to tell her the letter is safe.
ev.ispahan.clothnote.result.stitch: You hold the hem while Parvin sews a red stitch beside the folded letter. Her nephew writes the bride’s name on the wrapping. Parvin thanks you; the family speaks of your care to their neighbours.
ev.ispahan.clothnote.title: A Note Sewn into the Hem
ev.ispahan.entry.body:
The lanes around Isfahan’s Friday Mosque are full of work. A dyer carries folded cloth into the shade, and a boy runs after her with the wooden clips she forgot. Beyond the houses, water from the Zayandeh River feeds gardens and workshops.

The dyer, Parvin, says the boy is her nephew. ‘He remembers every customer’s name and never remembers the clips,’ she says. The boy catches up and hands them over. ‘I remembered today,’ he protests. Parvin counts them, nods, and points out a place where you can rest or continue toward the market.

You ask whether the cloth is for a customer nearby. ‘My sister lives beyond the city,’ Parvin says. ‘She sent the measurements for a wedding cloth and then sent another message because the bride changed her mind about the blue.’ Her nephew asks whether they must dye it again. Parvin unfolds one corner and shows him that the darker border is already there. He leans close and admits he had only looked at the middle. A neighbour calls from the water channel to ask when her own linen can be rinsed. Parvin says after this length is hung, then asks the boy to keep the clips where she can reach them.
ev.ispahan.entry.title: The Street by the Friday Mosque
ev.java-major.battuta_a.body: The people of Tawalisi are handsome and strong; their land, named after its king, is so great that he will oppose the Emperor of China with his junks. Their women ride on horseback, excel in throwing the javelin, and fight like men in battle. In the port of Kailuka the governor is the king's daughter: she sits on the throne of government, her women before her with the papers of state, greets you in Turkish, and writes the Bismilla with her own hand. She wonders at the wealth of India and says she must conquer it for herself. She keeps a regiment of women in her army, and no suitor has dared to overcome her in the tournament.
ev.java-major.battuta_a.choice.aloes: Buy aloeswood as the merchants do
ev.java-major.battuta_a.title: The Warlike Queen of Tawalisi
ev.java-major.entry.body: Out from Zaitūn the junks of El Malik El Zāhir, King of the southern islands, take the monsoon for India and the archipelago. Ten days' fair wind, then storm and strange seas — and at last landfall where that Muslim king holds court, returning from victory with captives, marrying his heir with rites no traveller from the lands of the Franks has seen elsewhere. Pepper, nutmeg, and the woods of the islands fill the holds; the king's servants are of the Faith, and he supplies the stranger with all that is needful. You must know that men of China and of India both name this great island among the richest of the southern ocean, and that its harbours take junk and dhow alike.
ev.java-major.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.java-major.entry.title: Arriving at Java Major
ev.jerusalem.sandals.body:
At the inn, Maria the cobbler sets two pairs of sandals on the steps. Two travellers brought them in together yesterday; today each claims the pair on the left. One says its sole has red stitching. The other says a friend stitched that red line for him.

Maria turns both pairs over. "No need to grab. Which of you had a pebble caught in the heel? I kept it in a box while I worked." One man touches his heel and admits he walked with it half the day.

The other is travelling to Bethlehem and worries his companions will leave at noon. Maria asks you to hold the little box. "I remember what was wrong with the other pair too. Let me tell them."
ev.jerusalem.sandals.choice.road: Ask the traveller where the Bethlehem group leaves from
ev.jerusalem.sandals.choice.sort: Help Maria return both pairs to their owners
ev.jerusalem.sandals.result.road:
The traveller points south. "Leave by the south gate for Bethlehem. We're going soon; you can meet us there." He reaches for a pair and then stops to ask Maria which is his.

She shows the old tear in each shoe. He puts his pair on, runs to the corner and back, and says it no longer rubs his heel. Then he and his companion head for the southern gate.
ev.jerusalem.sandals.result.sort:
Maria turns back a strap on the second pair and shows you a fresh mend. "I caught it on a doorstep yesterday," the other traveller says. They put on their own shoes and walk a few steps along the street, laughing at the mix-up.

Maria tips the pebble into the dirt beside the steps. The innkeeper brings water and remembers that you helped her.
ev.jerusalem.sandals.title: Two Pairs of Sandals at the Inn
ev.kenjanfu.a.body: West of the city you walk fine plains planted with mulberries, the trees whose leaves feed the silkworms. Gardeners spread fresh trays in the shade, and the road from Cachanfu is lined with boroughs that sell cocoons by the basket before noon.
ev.kenjanfu.a.choice.gardens: Walk the mulberry gardens with a silkworm keeper
ev.kenjanfu.a.choice.silk: Buy raw silk from a cocoon market
ev.kenjanfu.a.choice.watch: Stand at the roadside and watch the cocoon carts pass
ev.kenjanfu.a.title: Mulberry Plains
ev.kenjanfu.b.body: When you leave Cachanfu and travel eight days westward you meet cities and boroughs abounding in trade and industry before ever you reach Kenjanfu. Here Prince Mangalai keeps his palace outside the walls, and the workshops weave cloths of silk and gold and forge harness for the Khan's host.
ev.kenjanfu.b.choice.lacquer: Buy lacquerware from an armourer's quarter
ev.kenjanfu.b.choice.palace: View Prince Mangalai's palace from the plain
ev.kenjanfu.b.title: Cities of Industry
ev.kenjanfu.entry.body: And when you leave the city of Cachanfu of which I have spoken, and travel eight days westward, you meet with cities and boroughs abounding in trade and industry, and quantities of beautiful trees, and gardens, and fine plains planted with mulberries, which are the trees on the leaves of which the silkworms do feed. The people are all Idolaters. There is also plenty of game of all sorts, both of beasts and birds. And when you have travelled those eight days’ journey, you come to that great city which I mentioned, called KENJANFU. A very great and fine city it is, and the capital of the kingdom of Kenjanfu, which in old times was a noble, rich, and powerful realm, and had many great and wealthy and puissant kings. But now the king thereof is a prince called MANGALAI, the son of the Great Kaan, who hath given him this realm, and crowned him king thereof. It is a city of great trade and industry.
ev.kenjanfu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.kenjanfu.entry.title: Concerning the City of Kenjanfu
ev.kerman.a.body:
The buckle Soraya’s brother brought back belongs to a smith named Rashid. He sets out two sizes for the boy to compare. Beside his shop, a trader has a merchant parcel of rough turquoise from the hills and keeps turning one sample stone in the light.

Rashid says he can show you how he tests a saddle fitting. The trader will sell you the parcel, and the caravan masters in the lane can name the roads toward Yazd and Hormuz.

Rashid hands the boy a strap and asks him to find the worn hole. The boy finds two. ‘That is why your new buckle was too short,’ Rashid says. The stone trader asks whether you have come to buy or only to look. You ask how he knows the stones belong together in a trade parcel. He opens the wrapping and shows the marks he made while sorting them. ‘The buyer may check every piece,’ he says. ‘I would rather he did it here, before we tie the parcel again.’
ev.kerman.a.choice.ask-roads: Ask the caravan masters about Yazd and Hormuz
ev.kerman.a.choice.buy-turquoise: Buy the merchant parcel of turquoise for 100 silver
ev.kerman.a.choice.watch-forge: Spend a day watching Rashid work
ev.kerman.a.title: The Smith and the Stone Seller
ev.kerman.b.body:
Soraya and her mother spread an embroidered cloth on their worktable. It has birds among branches, and the hem still needs finishing before a buyer arrives. A falconer comes in to collect a small cloth hood they have sewn for his bird.

He says you may visit the mews in the hills; he has a trained falcon for sale. Soraya shows you a full merchant bundle of embroidered silk if you wish to trade in cloth, or you can stay and watch how she finishes the hem.

Soraya’s mother asks the falconer if the hood sits properly over the bird’s eyes. ‘It does, but this tie is long,’ he says. Soraya folds the cord back and takes two quick stitches. You ask whether the silk bundle is all one pattern. ‘No,’ she says, opening a corner so you can see several colours. ‘A merchant can offer them in different towns. I would keep one length for someone I know.’ The falconer waits for his hood, listening to her explain the work.
ev.kerman.b.choice.browse: Spend a day watching Soraya finish the cloth
ev.kerman.b.choice.buy-silk: Buy the merchant bundle of silk for 100 silver
ev.kerman.b.choice.visit-mews: Buy a trained falcon for 135 silver
ev.kerman.b.title: Soraya’s Embroidery and the Falcon Mews
ev.kerman.entry.body:
At a Kerman workshop, a young embroiderer named Soraya holds a silk panel while her mother checks the stitches. Her brother arrives from the smiths’ lane with a new buckle for the pack saddle. He has bought the wrong size again.

‘Leave it by the door,’ their mother says. ‘The smith can exchange it after lunch.’ Soraya points out the market, the mosque, and the road to the hills. Turquoise traders, metalworkers, and needleworkers share the streets here; each family seems to know someone in the next shop.

Soraya’s brother asks if he should return the buckle himself. ‘Of course,’ his mother says. ‘Tell Rashid what you measured, not what you guessed.’ He looks at the saddle strap and admits he never measured it at all. You ask Soraya whether the embroiderers and smiths often work for the same caravans. ‘My mother sews covers for their packs,’ she says. ‘They repair our frames when the wood splits. If you stay, you’ll see half the street come through this door.’
ev.kerman.entry.choice.market: Spend a day in the market
ev.kerman.entry.title: The Kerman Workshop Street
ev.kerman.patternbook.body:
Soraya’s brother has found an old cloth with a small bird stitched in one corner. He wants to copy it for their mother’s birthday, but the cloth is too worn to leave on the table for long. Soraya promises to show him the first stitches after her current order is done.

He asks you to sit with him while he draws the shape. You can spend the afternoon helping him make a paper copy, or walk with him to the shop that sells fresh thread and hear about the road to Yazd from its owner.

‘The wing looks like a leaf,’ the boy says, holding up his drawing. Soraya looks over and turns the old cloth a little: ‘See the tail? Leave room for that, or your bird will be sitting on its own feathers.’ He rubs out one line and asks you to hold the cloth steady. His mother calls from the other room to ask whether a customer’s blue cloth has been cut yet. Soraya quickly covers the drawing with a plain sheet. You can help finish it quietly, or take the boy out for thread while she distracts their mother.
ev.kerman.patternbook.choice.copy: Help him copy the bird pattern
ev.kerman.patternbook.choice.thread: Walk to the thread shop and ask about Yazd
ev.kerman.patternbook.result.copy: You help him trace the bird’s outline. Soraya adds a few marks showing where to begin each colour, and her brother tucks the paper away for their mother’s birthday. The family thanks you warmly.
ev.kerman.patternbook.result.thread: At the thread shop, the owner names the caravan that goes toward Yazd and shows you where it leaves town. You mark the route and Yazd on your map while Soraya’s brother chooses his colours.
ev.kerman.patternbook.title: The Pattern for Soraya’s Brother
ev.keshimur.a.body:
At the old hill shrine, a caretaker is replacing a small oil lamp while the guide’s cousin asks about the image inside. ‘Did it ever speak?’ the boy asks. The caretaker says he has heard the tale from many travellers, each with a different sentence. He has heard the boy’s own family tell it differently too.

You ask which part he knows for himself. ‘That the lamp goes out when this window is open,’ he says, and lets the boy feel the draught. The cousin closes the shutter and the flame steadies. A wool carrier resting nearby asks the caretaker how to reach the road toward Badakhshan. He points to a lower path but tells her to check the day’s mist with a guide.

The cousin wants you to stay and hear the older versions of the tale. The caretaker is finishing the lamp and can show you the hill path; he also knows travellers heading toward Kabul. The boy waits by the shutter, ready to tell you his own version first.
ev.keshimur.a.choice.listen_tales: Stay a day and hear the family versions
ev.keshimur.a.choice.watch_shrine: Observe the shrine and ask about Badakhshan
ev.keshimur.a.title: The Story at the Hill Shrine
ev.keshimur.b.body:
The guide from the lodging yard has spread several weather notes beside the hearth. His cousin drew the bent pine on one page but put it on the wrong side of a stream. The guide asks him to walk through the route aloud. When the boy reaches the stream, he pauses and corrects his drawing.

You ask how the guide chooses a day to cross. He says the high path may be clear in the morning and hidden by afternoon cloud. His mother sets down food and asks whether the family can spend a week in the lower valley while the next party gathers. The guide says that would let the cousin learn the way properly. A stone merchant visiting the yard offers a merchant parcel of turquoise for 100 silver.

The guide can work with you for seven days for 6 silver and share the paths toward Delhi. His mother has room if you stay the same week to rest among the families. The cousin turns the page around and smiles: now the pine stands on the right bank.
ev.keshimur.b.choice.buy_turquoise: Buy the turquoise merchant parcel for 100 silver
ev.keshimur.b.choice.hire_guide: Pay 6 silver for seven days with the guide
ev.keshimur.b.choice.rest_valley: Rest with the valley families for seven days
ev.keshimur.b.title: The Guide’s Mist Notes
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.body:
Near the lower valley, two sisters are fitting a new plank to a narrow footbridge. Their father carries wool across it each market day; last week he caught his sandal in a split board. The younger sister wants to nail the replacement at once, but the older asks her to set a loaded basket on it first.

You hold the basket while they test the span. The board rocks at one end. ‘I cut it to the old length,’ the younger says. Her sister points to the worn ledge where the old plank used to rest. Their father arrives with wool on his back and asks whether he may cross. ‘Wait for one more cut,’ both daughters say together. He sets the wool down and shows them the mark he made on the stone years ago.

They offer you 0.7 silver if you stay the day to help fit and test the bridge. If you have to leave sooner, their father can show you how the boards are supported above the stream.
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.choice.fit: Stay a day and help fit the bridge plank
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.choice.learn: Ask how the boards rest on the stone ledge
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.result.fit: You spend the day testing the new board with baskets and then with the wool load. The sisters pay you 0.7 silver; their father crosses without catching his sandal and calls back to thank all three of you.
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.result.learn: Their father shows you the ledge and the old mark he made. You record the small bridge design while the sisters fit the final board and test it with the wool basket.
ev.keshimur.bridgeplank.title: A Plank for the Footbridge
ev.keshimur.entry.body:
At a Kashmir lodging yard, a guide is helping his mother set bowls of rice and milk for travellers. His younger cousin is late bringing firewood. When the boy finally appears, he says mist hid the path near the upper orchard. The guide asks him which tree he used to find the turn. ‘The bent pine,’ the boy says, then admits he walked past it twice.

You ask whether that same path leads toward the market. The mother points to the lower lane and says people carrying saffron and mountain wool come that way. She asks her son to take the boy’s damp cloak to the fire before it chills him. The guide sets out another bowl for you and asks where you mean to travel. He knows several mountain approaches, but wants to hear your destination before naming a pass.

The cousin eats quickly, then tells you a funny tale about an old image at a hill shrine that supposedly spoke to a traveller. His mother smiles and asks what the traveller had eaten before hearing it. The boy says he will find out tomorrow.
ev.keshimur.entry.choice.market: Spend a day among the market families
ev.keshimur.entry.title: A Guest at the Mountain Yard
ev.kinsay.a.body: Kinsay is a city built on water — it is said there are twelve thousand bridges of stone, and all of them are so tall that a ship with its mast raised can pass beneath without lowering the yard. Some have shops built on them. The streets are canals; the boats are the carriages. A man could spend his whole life in Kinsay and never walk more than a hundred paces on dry land. From the top of the drum-tower in the center of the city, a hundred canals radiate in every direction, each one lined with stone embankments as straight as a sword-cut. The city has no walls — the water is its wall, and the Kaan maintains a fleet of patrol boats to keep the peace.
ev.kinsay.a.choice.boat: Hire a boat and spend the day on the canals
ev.kinsay.a.choice.tower: Climb the drum-tower and see the hundred canals below
ev.kinsay.a.choice.walk: Walk the bridges and see if you can count them all
ev.kinsay.a.title: The Twelve Thousand Bridges
ev.kinsay.b.body: The markets of Kinsay are ten great squares, each one half a mile on a side, surrounded by double-storied warehouses with shops below and counting-houses above. Every fish of the sea and lake, every fruit of the earth, every fabric known to man, every spice and drug and perfume is sold in one of these ten squares. Forty cart-loads of pepper pass through the customs house every day. The main street that connects the markets is paved with stone and brick so finely joined that no water stands on it even in the heaviest rain. On either side are bathhouses and restaurants where a man can bathe in hot water perfumed with flowers and then dine on ten courses for a few copper coins.
ev.kinsay.b.choice.bath: Bathe in perfumed water and dine on ten courses
ev.kinsay.b.choice.count_pepper: Count the forty cart-loads of pepper passing the customs
ev.kinsay.b.choice.pepper: Buy two sacks of pepper from the customs house
ev.kinsay.b.title: The Ten Great Markets
ev.kinsay.battuta_a.body: You go down the river from El Khansa, past Kanjanfur, to El Zaitun, where you find junks bound for India, and take passage in a junk of El Malik El Zahir, the King of Sumatra, whose servants are Muslims. For ten days a good wind holds; then the sky grows dark, and a storm drives the junk into a sea unknown to the sailors. At daybreak a mountain stands twenty miles away, and the sailors take leave of one another, saying it is a Rokh, and if he sees us we are lost. You betake yourselves to prayer, and God gives a good wind; after two months you reach Java, and shortly after, Sumatra.
ev.kinsay.battuta_a.choice.passage: Take passage on the King of Sumatra's junk
ev.kinsay.battuta_a.choice.prayer: Pray with the merchants in the storm
ev.kinsay.battuta_a.choice.rokh: Ask the sailors about the mountain in the sea
ev.kinsay.battuta_a.title: The Homeward Voyage to the West
ev.kinsay.c.body: On the West Lake, just outside the city walls, the pleasure boats of Kinsay float day and night — painted in gold, blue, and vermilion, with silk awnings and cushioned seats. Each boat is a floating pavilion. Musicians play the pipa and the guqin on the open deck. Dancers perform in costumes embroidered with phoenixes. Wine flows from porcelain cups, and lanterns hang from the awning poles, their reflections dancing on the black water. The lake is so large that a circuit takes a whole day. The islands in the lake have pleasure-palaces where the wealthy hold banquets that last three days. A man who has not seen the West Lake by moonlight has not seen the most beautiful thing in the empire of the Kaan.
ev.kinsay.c.choice.boat: Hire a pleasure boat with musicians and wine
ev.kinsay.c.choice.moonlight: Wait for moonlight — the most beautiful thing in the empire
ev.kinsay.c.choice.watch: Stand on the shore and watch the floating palaces
ev.kinsay.c.title: The Pleasure Boats of the West Lake
ev.kinsay.entry.body: When you have left the city of Changan and have travelled for three days through a splendid country, passing a number of towns and villages, you arrive at the most noble city of KINSAY, a name which is as much as to say in our tongue “The City of Heaven,” as I told you before. And since we have got thither I will enter into particulars about its magnificence; and these are well worth the telling, for the city is beyond dispute the finest and the noblest in the world. In this we shall speak according to the written statement which the Queen of this Realm sent to Bayan the conqueror of the country for transmission to the Great Kaan, in order that he might be aware of the surpassing grandeur of the city and might be moved to save it from destruction or injury. I will tell you all the truth as it was set down in that document. For truth it was, as the said Messer Marco Polo at a later date was able to witness with his own eyes. And now we shall rehearse those particulars. First and foremost, then, the document stated the city of Kinsay to be so great that it hath an hundred miles of compass. And there are in it twelve thousand bridges of stone, for the most part so lofty that a great fleet could pass beneath them. And let no man marvel that there are so many bridges, for you see the whole city stands as it were in the water and surrounded by water, so that a great many bridges are required to give free passage about it. [And though the bridges be so high the approaches are so well contrived that carts and horses do cross them.] The document aforesaid also went on to state that there were in this city twelve guilds of the different crafts, and that each guild had 12,000 houses in the occupation of its workmen. Each of these houses contains at least 12 men, whilst some contain 20 and some 40,—not that these are all masters, but inclusive of the journeymen who work under the masters.
ev.kinsay.entry.choice.battuta: Ask of the traveller who sailed home from here
ev.kinsay.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the shìbó sī (市舶司)
ev.kinsay.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.kinsay.entry.title: The City of Heaven
ev.kinsay.mentor_jiaobei.body: A temple reader in Kinsay will teach the three answers of the cups — leave, refuse, or ask again. She says the laugh of the cups is not failure; it is the craft admitting it has no counsel yet.
ev.kinsay.mentor_jiaobei.choice.ask: Ask only how the cups are read
ev.kinsay.mentor_jiaobei.title: Cups at Kinsay
ev.kiovia.entry.body:
Boats are being loaded on the Dnieper below Kyiv’s hill. A woman named Olena wraps a wax candle in cloth so it will not bend against the other cargo. Her son has brought an extra bundle of honeycomb and is trying to find room for it.

‘Take it to your uncle first,’ she tells him. ‘He asked for it yesterday.’ The boy runs uphill with the bundle. Olena shows you where travellers gather for the northern road. The town has old walls and churches above the river; people still trade here, even as the streets carry traces of earlier wars.

You ask why the uncle needs honeycomb today. Olena says he melts some wax for household candles and shares the rest with a neighbour who keeps bees farther uphill. Her son calls back from the steps, asking whether he should bring the empty basket home. ‘Bring it if your uncle is finished with it,’ she says. A boatman asks which of her wrapped candles should travel in the shaded crate. Olena picks up the one she protected first and shows him how its wick lies straight. You ask when the northbound group meets. She points to a courtyard above the landing, where a driver is checking his wheel before setting out.
ev.kiovia.entry.choice.look: Spend a day talking with the river people
ev.kiovia.entry.title: The Dnieper Landing
ev.kiovia.mentor_runes.body:
A traveller from the northern road shows you rune marks cut into a birch stave. He says his sister taught him to draw one when he could not decide which ferry to take. He turns the stave so you can see each cut and offers to explain his method.

You ask whether his sister carved the marks herself. ‘Some of them,’ he says, turning the staff. ‘She learnt the older forms from a book and changed the handle so I could tell them apart by touch.’ A ferryman calls for passengers while the traveller is still showing you a worn line. He says he once drew that sign before choosing a boat, then stayed to ask the ferryman about the weather anyway. His sister laughed when he told her: the piece of wood had made him stop and think long enough to ask.

He lays the staff across his knees and demonstrates how he selects a marked piece without seeing it first. You ask what he charges for instruction. Fifty silver for seven days, he says; there is time to practise and to hear how his sister taught him. If you are only passing through, he will show you a single draw now, before the next ferry calls.
ev.kiovia.mentor_runes.choice.ask: Hear how a single rune is drawn
ev.kiovia.mentor_runes.title: The Northern Traveller’s Runes
ev.kiovia.runes_ford.body:
At the Kyiv ferry, a traveller from the northern road holds a carved rune token between his fingers. He says his sister gave it to him when he left home. Now he offers to draw one for you before the crossing.

The ferryman is still loading sacks. ‘Ask him if you like,’ she says, ‘but keep your bag in your hands when you board.’ The traveller laughs and puts his sister’s token safely away while you decide.
ev.kiovia.runes_ford.title: A Rune at the Kyiv Ferry
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.body:
Olena’s son returns from his uncle with a small wooden case. Inside is a candle mould he borrowed without asking. His uncle wants it back before evening prayers, and the boatman wants Olena’s wax on board now.

‘You could have told me,’ Olena says. The boy admits he wanted to make a candle to give his uncle. He asks you to take the mould uphill while he helps load the boat. Olena sets the mould on a flat board and checks whether the wick will stay centred. Her son puts down a small piece of wax, waiting to hear if there is still time to make the gift before the boat leaves.

You ask why he took the mould without asking. ‘Uncle always lets me watch, and I thought I could surprise him,’ the boy says. Olena answers that a surprise can wait until the owner knows where his tool is. The boatman calls again from the cargo ramp. The boy says he can load the wax crate while you carry the mould uphill. Olena checks the pot: it is warm enough to pour one small candle if they work steadily. Her son looks from the ramp to the mould, then asks whether his uncle will still be pleased if the gift arrives a little late.
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.choice.pour: Stay to make a candle with Olena
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.choice.return: Return the mould to his uncle now
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.result.pour: You hold the mould while Olena pours the warm wax. Her son waits until the candle is firm, then takes it uphill with the mould. He returns later to say his uncle lit it for the evening prayers. Olena thanks you, and the family remembers your help.
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.result.return: His uncle has already received the honeycomb. You return the mould and explain why the boy borrowed it. He smiles, then tells you where the northbound road leaves the landing and how travellers follow it toward Moscow. You mark the route and city on your map.
ev.kiovia.waxcandle.title: Olena’s Candle
ev.linju.entry.body: On leaving the city of Sinju-matu you travel for eight days towards the south, always coming to great and rich towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are all subjects of the Great Kaan, use paper-money, and burn their dead. At the end of those eight days you come to the city of LINJU, in the province of the same name of which it is the capital. It is a rich and noble city, and the men are good soldiers, natheless they carry on great trade and manufactures. There is great abundance of game in both beasts and birds, and all the necessaries of life are in profusion.
ev.linju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.linju.entry.title: Concerning the Cities of Linju and Piju
ev.lop.bazaar.body: The bazaar of Lop spills out of the town walls onto the gravel plain where the caravans assemble. Merchants from Khotan and Sachiu spread their goods on carpets laid on the ground: bolts of silk, sacks of dried melon, blocks of pressed tea, and — rarest of all — river jade from the streams above Cotan. The jade merchants sit apart, their stones displayed on black velvet to show the color. A piece of mutton-fat white jade the size of a man's fist costs more than a camel. The trader smiles and holds it up to the sun; the light passes through it like water.
ev.lop.bazaar.choice.ask_prices: Ask where the jade comes from
ev.lop.bazaar.title: The Jade Market
ev.lop.caravanserai.body: At the caravan inn, travellers newly out of the desert drink water while those preparing to leave gather round a guide. The keeper lays out sacks of grain, dried meat and waterskins. “Rest seven days first. The camels need to breathe too.” Names and prayers cover the wall, some worn almost away by sand.
ev.lop.caravanserai.choice.wait_caravan: Wait for a caravan (8 days, 120 coins)
ev.lop.caravanserai.title: The Caravanserai
ev.lop.entry.body: Sacks of grain fill the entrance to an inn in Lop. The keeper looks through your baggage. “Take a month's food for the desert crossing. Camels eat little for what they carry, which is why caravans use them; some take donkeys too. If provisions fail entirely, an animal may become the last food.” He circles water sources on a map. The travel account says sweet water can be found after a day and a night, enough for fifty to a hundred people and their animals. It does not mean there is water every day. Some wells serve only a smaller party; others taste bitter and salty. Rest seven days and inspect your skins, food and pack animals.
ev.lop.entry.choice.ask: Ask what men say of the desert crossing
ev.lop.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.lop.entry.title: The Town of Lop
ev.lop.mentor_closure.body: A man who reads the wind asks whether you fear the desert. You say you do. He nods. “Fear is no shame. If you hear a voice at night, do not leave the party to follow it.”
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask what the road will demand
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_1_result: The listener of the desert wind answers without evasion: water, and the reading of the sky, will be asked of you. His lesson is offered, and what you make of it lies with you.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay for a day and listen to the whole account
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_2_result: You stay a day with the listener who reads the desert wind, and he gives you his whole counsel at length. It is not a map, but it will read the sand for you.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank the guide and keep moving
ev.lop.mentor_closure.choice_3_result: You thank the listener of the desert wind and take the road. He lets you go with a blessing, and the lesson of the desert remains unwritten.
ev.lop.mentor_closure.title: The Guide of Lop
ev.lop.shrine.body: In the low cliffs east of the town, the wind has carved a labyrinth of shallow caves. The walls are covered with charcoal drawings left by travelers over centuries: camels, horsemen, prayers in Arabic and Sanskrit, names and dates. A small Buddhist shrine occupies the largest cave — a clay Buddha painted with cheap gold leaf, surrounded by burnt-out incense sticks and offerings of dried fruit. The monks are gone, but the shrine-keeper, an old Tangut woman with a leathery face, tends the lamps and accepts whatever coins the travelers leave.
ev.lop.shrine.title: The Caves of Lop
ev.maabar.entry.body: When you leave the Island of Seilan and sail westward about 60 miles, you come to the great province of MAABAR which is styled INDIA THE GREATER; it is best of all the Indies and is on the mainland. You must know that in this province there are five kings, who are own brothers. I will tell you about each in turn. The Province is the finest and noblest in the world. At this end of the Province reigns one of those five Royal Brothers, who is a crowned King, and his name is SONDER BANDI DAVAR.
ev.maabar.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.maabar.entry.title: Arriving at GREAT PROVINCE OF MAABAR
ev.maabar.site_gap.body: Cotton threads hang in rows inside the weaving shed. A weaver stretches threads of different thickness over a wooden frame. The warp must be strong; the weft can vary for the pattern. She lets you pull a length to see whether it breaks easily. Years of handling have polished one corner of the frame, and she trusts her fingers as much as her eyes.
ev.maabar.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Coilum
ev.maabar.site_gap.title: A Weaver’s Cotton Knot
ev.maldive.battuta_a.body: The vizier Jamāl Oddīn, husband of the Queen, receives you with honour: a house with a garden, a dress of honour, and a horse, though none but the vizier rides, the nobles going in palanquins or afoot. He asks you to take the office of judge, whose word is obeyed like a king's, and whose right is the revenue of three islands. You accept. Under the island custom a traveller may marry for a very small dowry, on condition of divorce at his departure, for the women never leave their districts; so you marry three wives. Your kin become numerous and powerful, and the vizier, weak in troops and unused to war, begins to fear you, inquiring into your affairs and watching your steps in secret. You take thought to leave the islands.
ev.maldive.battuta_a.choice.flight: Divorce your wives and seek a ship
ev.maldive.battuta_a.title: Judge, Three Wives, and Flight
ev.maldive.entry.body: These isles are a wonder of the world — some two thousand of them, near a hundred ringed so close together that the people of one isle know the people of the next. The cocoa-nut palm is the greatest tree, bearing twelve crops in the year, so that fruit green, ripe, and dry hang together on the same bough; from the nut men make palm-wine, oil, and a strong thread with which the ships of India and Yemen are sewn, yielding against a rock where iron nails would break. The coin of the land is the wada, a sea-shell buried in the earth till the flesh wastes away. A woman, the Queen Khodīja, rules the chief isle; the women keep their own company at table and never leave their districts; and the judge's word is obeyed like a king's.
ev.maldive.entry.title: The Coconut Isles
ev.mecha.entry.body: You approach Mecca across the valley and come upon the signs that part the haram — the sacred territory — from the hill. Within those towers all is haram; beyond, hill. Here pilgrims put on the ihrām and pray at the miqāt before entering the House. Zamzam water issues from the well; men pour it upon weary limbs after the circumambulation of the Ka‘bah. Fresh dates and the fruits of this protected town are praised by every stranger. You must know that this is the direction of prayer for every Muslim upon the earth, and that the road hither is lined with wells, mosques, and the footprints of the prophets.
ev.mecha.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.mecha.entry.title: Arriving at Mecha
ev.mecha.site_gap.body: Clay jars stand by a spring, tiny drops collecting on their sides. A potter taps one: well-fired clay does not leak, and fine sand mixed into it helps prevent cracks while drying. The mouth must be wide enough to draw water and wash the jar. Keep it in shade, he says, and never set it directly on a fire. Water runs through a crack in the rock.
ev.mecha.site_gap.choice.interact: Feel the thickness of a jar wall
ev.mecha.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Medina
ev.mecha.site_gap.title: Clay Water Jars by the Spring
ev.medina.entry.body: Medina — City of the Prophet — lies three days from al-Safrā’ upon the pilgrim road. Mount Uhud stands three miles north; upon its slopes is the mosque of Hamzah and the tombs of the martyrs. Eastward, by Bāb al-Baqī‘, lies the cemetery of al-Gharqad — tombs of Safiyyah, of Mālik ibn Anas under a modest cupola, of Ibrāhīm son of the Prophet under a white one. Men come to acquire blessings at these graves. You must know that after Mecca this is the second city of the Faith, and that no pilgrim from Irāk or Syria passes without visiting the sacred tomb.
ev.medina.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.medina.entry.title: Arriving at Medina
ev.medina.site_gap.body: Outside an inn stands a shared water jar. The keeper turns a copper ladle upside down on its rim. Rinse it before use and turn it over afterwards, he says, so dust does not settle inside. Travellers can drink here. He lifts the lid to show clean water and leaves the ladle handle pointing out for the next person.
ev.medina.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Petra
ev.medina.site_gap.title: Drinking Water at the Inn
ev.melibar.a.body: Melibar faces west upon the sea, a great kingdom that pays tribute to no man. From this coast and from Gozurat, men say, more than a hundred corsair ships put out each summer, sailing in squadrons that spread across a hundred miles of water so no merchant vessel may pass unseen. You stand on the quay where pepper bales are loaded under the watch of men who scan the horizon for sail.
ev.melibar.a.choice.ask-south: Ask the pilots which ports lie along the pepper coast
ev.melibar.a.choice.buy-pepper: Buy Malabar pepper while the harbour watch holds
ev.melibar.a.choice.watch: Watch the harbour and ask how the merchants avoid the corsairs
ev.melibar.a.title: The Pepper Coast and the Corsair Watch
ev.melibar.b.body: At night upon the shore you mark the North Star standing two cubits above the water — higher here than in any land you have sailed. The people of Melibar are idolaters with a tongue of their own, and their mandirs stand open along the bāzār even while merchants trade in fear of the sea. Priests anoint stone images with oil and rice, and pilgrims leave garlands of coconut flowers at the threshold. You watch the rite in silence, the pole-star bright above the temple roof.
ev.melibar.b.choice.buy-pearls: Buy pearls from a diver who prayed at the shrine
ev.melibar.b.choice.measure-star: Measure the North Star against the mast and record what you see
ev.melibar.b.choice.observe: Observe the idol rites from the temple steps
ev.melibar.b.title: The North Star and the Idol Rites
ev.melibar.battuta_a.body: You reach Kalikut, one of the great ports of Malabar, and wait three months for the season when the sea of China is navigable. In the harbour ride the great junks, each like an independent city: six hundred sailors and four hundred soldiers aboard the largest, with houses of wood built on deck, and oars like masts, twenty-five men working standing. They are built nowhere but at El Zaitun and Sin Kilan. One night the sea rises; the junk bearing the Emperor's present strikes the shore, and all on board perish with the wealth. You have stayed on land for the Friday prayer, and are saved.
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.junks: Watch the great junks at anchor
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.prayer: Keep the Friday prayer on shore
ev.melibar.battuta_a.choice.trade: Trade with the richest merchants of the port
ev.melibar.battuta_a.title: The Chinese Junks and the Wreck in the Night
ev.melibar.entry.body: Melibar is a great kingdom lying towards the west. The people are Idolaters; they have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. In this country you see more of the North Star, for it shows two cubits above the water. And you must know that from this kingdom of Melibar, and from another near it called Gozurat, there go forth every year more than a hundred corsair vessels on cruize. These pirates take with them their wives and children, and stay out the whole summer. Their method is to join in fleets of 20 or 30 of these pirate vessels together, and then they form what they call a sea cordon, that is, they drop off till there is an interval of 5 or 6 miles between ship and ship, so that they cover something like an hundred miles of sea, and no merchant ship can escape them. For when any one corsair sights a vessel a signal is made by fire or smoke, and then the whole of them make for this, and seize the merchants and plunder them.
ev.melibar.entry.choice.battuta: Ask of the traveller and the Chinese junks
ev.melibar.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.melibar.entry.title: Concerning the Kingdom of Melibar
ev.merva.entry.body: At Merva, an old canal has silted into a green pond, where ducks swim past a fallen brick wall. An innkeeper repairs his roof and sees you looking at the ruins. “The oasis once watered fields through these channels. Mulberry trees and silkworms made Merva's woven silk known far away. Someone must clear each channel and allot the water; if one household opens its sluice without leave, fields downstream go dry.” He brings you melon soup and taps an old map. “The wells are still there, and so is the road. Stay tonight and decide in the morning.”
ev.merva.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.merva.entry.title: Arriving at Merva
ev.merva.site_gap.body: A copyist dries sheets of paper beneath a mulberry tree, holding them down with thin wooden strips. Before touching one, check that its edges are dry. Thinly spread pulp takes ink well, but folded while damp its fibres stick together. You test a stroke on waste paper; it spreads evenly. He brushes a fallen leaf away from the edge.
ev.merva.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Sapurgan
ev.merva.site_gap.title: Pages Drying Beneath a Mulberry Tree
ev.mien.entry.body: And when you have travelled those 15 days through such a difficult country as I have described, in which travellers have to carry provisions for the road because there are no inhabitants, then you arrive at the capital city of this Province of Mien, and it also is called AMIEN, and is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters and have a peculiar language, and are subject to the Great Kaan. And in this city there is a thing so rich and rare that I must tell you about it.
ev.mien.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.mien.entry.title: Arriving at MIEN
ev.moscovia.birchletter.body:
Before the northern traveller departs, Darya’s son returns with the note he took out of the packet. He has copied it twice in larger letters because he worries the first will be hard for his grandmother to read. Both say that he has learned to mend a net and wants his grandmother to visit when the river opens. The traveller is mending the last strap on his wagon outside.

Darya suggests giving him the clearer copy and keeping the other. Her son asks you to read it aloud first. You can sit with him over the words, or take the note to the traveller yourself and earn a small fee for the errand.

The boy points to a crooked letter and asks whether his grandmother will think it says ‘boat’ instead of ‘net.’ Darya leans over the bark: ‘Read the whole sentence to me.’ He does, slowly. The traveller knocks at the doorway and says his wagon is nearly ready. ‘One more moment,’ Darya calls. You can help the boy choose the clearer copy, or carry it down to the wagon while Darya finishes tying the cloth.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.choice.deliver: Take the note to the traveller
ev.moscovia.birchletter.choice.read: Read the note with the boy
ev.moscovia.birchletter.result.deliver: You place the note in the traveller’s packet and return to tell the boy it is safely tucked away. Darya pays you 0.4 silver for the errand. He keeps the other copy and reads it once more to her.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.result.read: You read each line and let the boy correct his own spelling. He takes the clearer copy to the traveller himself. Darya thanks you; the family will remember your patience.
ev.moscovia.birchletter.title: A Note for Grandmother
ev.moscovia.entry.body:
At the Moscow landing, a woman named Darya is wrapping a packet of cloth for a northern traveller. Her little son presses a birchbark note into the knot. ‘For Grandmother,’ he says. Darya unties the packet, puts the note inside where it will stay dry, and makes him tie it again.

Houses and workshops spread from the river toward the town’s churches and walls. Timber, wax, and furs pass through the landing. Darya tells you where the caravans stop, then calls her son back before he can ask the traveller for a second promise.

The traveller asks the boy, ‘What did you write?’ The boy grips the packet and says it is a surprise. Darya replies, ‘Your grandmother can barely see small letters. Did you make them large enough?’ He takes the note back for a moment, frowns, and promises to check. You ask when the northern party leaves. Darya says it is waiting for a wagon axle to be repaired; there is time to find a bed by the landing before they set out.
ev.moscovia.entry.choice.rest: Rest for a day by the river
ev.moscovia.entry.title: A Letter beside the River
ev.nanghin.entry.body: Nanghin is a very noble Province towards the west. The people are Idolaters (and so forth) and live by trade and manufactures. They have silk in great abundance, and they weave many fine tissues of silk and gold. They have all sorts of corn and victuals very cheap, for the province is a most productive one. Game also is abundant, and lions too are found there. The merchants are great and opulent, and the Emperor draws a large revenue from them, in the shape of duties on the goods which they buy and sell.
ev.nanghin.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.nanghin.entry.title: Concerning the City of Nanghin
ev.nicaea.entry.body:
Nicaea sits beside a lake, its old walls visible from the road. Eleni is washing a blanket at the shore. Her grandson Leon sits on a stone, holding the wooden pegs she uses to dry it. Each time she asks for one, he gives her two.

“One for the blanket, one for the next blanket,” he explains. Eleni tells you that when he was smaller he tried to dry a fish with a peg. The fish escaped into the lake, taking the peg with it. Leon says he no longer does that. He is watching the water carefully now.

Eleni asks whether you have come from the east or the west. She shows you the lane that meets the road beyond the walls and offers a place to rest. Leon points out the easiest place to walk down to the water, then checks whether his grandmother has enough pegs left for the blanket.

You ask Leon how he knew the fish would take the clip with it. ‘I did not,’ he says. ‘I only found out when Grandmother counted the clips and one was gone.’ Eleni says a neighbour returned it a week later, caught in a reed beside his boat. Leon asks if she still has it. She points to the slightly bent one in his hand. He tries it on the thick edge of the blanket; it holds, though he has to press harder than with the others. Eleni asks him to leave that one for the last corner.
ev.nicaea.entry.choice.pass: Thank Eleni and continue beside the lake
ev.nicaea.entry.choice.rest: Stay a day at Eleni's house
ev.nicaea.entry.title: By the Lake at Nicaea
ev.nicaea.figpath.body:
Along the lane above the lake, Irem is packing figs into a shallow basket. Her mother has written a message for Aunt Zoe, who lives across the hills on the road toward Smyrna. Irem folds it three times and tucks it beneath the fruit, then takes it out again because juice has begun to leak through the cloth.

Aunt Zoe taught Irem to graft the tree when she was young. This is the first year it has borne enough fruit to send any away. Irem has learned the southward road from her aunt's letters, including the way toward Smyrna. Her mother is walking with her as far as the caravan stop tomorrow and invites you along. They also have lunch ready if you would rather sit with them and hear why Irem kept the tree alive through its first dry summer.

You ask whether the fruit will last until tomorrow. Irem’s mother presses one gently and says the ripest should stay at home; her sister can wait for the firmer ones. ‘Will Aunt Zoe mind if I choose them?’ Irem asks. ‘She will be pleased you grew them,’ her mother replies. Irem moves the damp letter into a dry cloth and asks you to check that the address is still legible. You can read it, though a corner has curled. She straightens it beneath the basket handle and tells you her aunt always writes back with news of the road and the family’s old garden.
ev.nicaea.figpath.choice.meal: Stay for lunch and hear about the fig tree
ev.nicaea.figpath.choice.walk: Walk with Irem to the caravan stop tomorrow
ev.nicaea.figpath.result.meal: At lunch, Irem tells you how she carried water to the young tree during its first dry summer. Her mother remembers that Irem forgot her own sandals twice but never forgot the tree. They cut open one ripe fig to share, then pack the rest with fresh cloth. You eat with them and set out feeling stronger.
ev.nicaea.figpath.result.walk: You spend the day walking with Irem and her mother. At each turn Irem recalls something Aunt Zoe wrote about the southward road. At the caravan stop they find a traveller bound toward Smyrna and give him the basket, the letter now wrapped in dry cloth. You mark Nicaea, Smyrna, and the route between them on your map. Irem asks the traveller to bring back word when her aunt tastes the fruit.
ev.nicaea.figpath.title: The Figs for Aunt Zoe
ev.ninive.entry.body:
Mosul’s houses stand beside the Tigris, with the old mounds of Nineveh across the water. At the ferry, a father tries to persuade his daughter to let go of a sack of grain long enough to get into the boat.

‘It’s for Aunt Laila,’ she tells you. ‘Last month she sent us a bowl and told us to fill it when the harvest came.’ Her father takes one handle and lets her keep the other. Around them, travellers are finding space for their bundles and deciding which bank they need.

The ferryman calls for people bound across to wait until the animals are aboard. Mariam asks her father whether Aunt Laila will see them from the bank. ‘She always comes early when she knows we are bringing grain,’ he says. You ask if there is room for one more traveller. He glances at the boatman, who holds up two fingers for the places left. Mariam tries to shift the sack without dropping it. Her father tells her to set it on the dry plank first and keep her hand on the tied end. She does, then checks twice that the knot is secure.
ev.ninive.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day resting by the river
ev.ninive.entry.title: Across from Nineveh
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.body:
When the ferry returns, Mariam is carrying Laila’s bowl. It is full of roasted grain. ‘She said I brought enough for her neighbours too,’ Mariam says. ‘Then she filled this so we’d have something for the way home.’

Her father offers to show you the quieter path toward Tabriz after he puts the boat in order. Mariam is happy to share the roasted grain now if you would rather sit with her on the bank.

You ask whether Laila kept the bowl full while they visited. Mariam says her aunt emptied it into smaller cups for the neighbours, then refilled it from the pan before they left. ‘She never lets a dish go home empty,’ her father says. Mariam asks him if he told Laila about the torn sack. He nods; Laila sent back a stronger needle and told him to keep it with the ferry gear. The boatman calls for the next crossing, and her father rises to help move a bundle. Mariam rests the warm bowl on her knees and waits until he has the boat settled.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.choice.eat: Sit with Mariam and share the grain
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.choice.path: Walk with her father to the Tabriz road
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.result.eat: Mariam pours grain into your palm and tells you how Laila roasts it in a shallow pan. You eat slowly while the ferry crosses again. The rest leaves you with more strength for the road.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.result.path: You walk to the turning with her father. He names the next places to stop and waits until you have marked the route toward Tabriz and the city beyond it on your map. Then he turns back toward the boat.
ev.ninive.ferrybowl.title: The Bowl Comes Back
ev.novogardia.barknote.body:
A boatman finds a birchbark note tucked into Anfisa’s wax bundle. It is a reminder from her sister: bring a little wax home for candles and stop working after the evening bell. Anfisa laughs at the second part but folds the note carefully.

Her daughter offers to carry a small parcel to her aunt. You can walk with her and see the town beyond the market, or stay to help Anfisa finish weighing the last bundles before dusk. Anfisa will pay for the work.

‘Did she really write that I should stop at the bell?’ Anfisa asks her daughter. ‘Twice,’ the girl says, showing her the second line. Anfisa tucks a little wax into the parcel and asks you whether it will survive the walk without breaking. Her daughter suggests wrapping it in old cloth. Her father calls that the last bundles are ready for the scales. Anfisa hands the parcel to the girl and says she may go as soon as someone helps finish the weighing.
ev.novogardia.barknote.choice.walk: Walk with her daughter to her aunt’s house
ev.novogardia.barknote.choice.weigh: Stay and weigh the wax bundles
ev.novogardia.barknote.result.walk: You accompany her through the lanes. Her aunt takes the wax and asks after Anfisa. On the way back, the girl shows you a quiet place to sit, and you recover some strength before leaving.
ev.novogardia.barknote.result.weigh: You help Anfisa weigh the last bundles, then spend the night nearby. At dawn she pays you 0.5 silver for the day’s work. Her daughter returns with a candle her aunt made from last year’s wax.
ev.novogardia.barknote.title: The Note in the Wax Bundle
ev.novogardia.entry.body:
At Novgorod’s river market, a woman named Anfisa counts bundles of wax while her father argues with a boatman over space. Her daughter carries a birchbark note from one stall to another: a neighbour has borrowed their scales again.

‘Tell him to bring them back before noon,’ Anfisa calls. Then she turns to you and explains where travellers gather for the road south. The city’s churches and trading yards stand close to the water; the river makes it easy for news to arrive with the cargo.

Her father asks whether they can use another trader’s scales. Anfisa shakes her head: ‘I promised the buyer I would weigh it on ours, so he can check the mark himself.’ The girl returns without the scales and says the neighbour has found one pan bent and is coming to apologize. Anfisa asks her to help lay out the bundles in order. You ask where to find a bed after the market closes; she points to a house behind the landing, then reminds her daughter that the small bundles go first.
ev.novogardia.entry.choice.rest: Rest for a day near the river
ev.novogardia.entry.title: The River Market
ev.ormus.a.body:
At the harbour customs table, a clerk is weighing a sealed bundle while a pearl sorter waits with a shallow basket. Her son has written the shell count on a scrap, but the ink ran when he set it beside the water jar. ‘The shells have not changed,’ he says. His mother asks him to count them again anyway.

You ask whether the basket came from the near shore. She points across the water and names Calatu, where she knows people who handle boats and divers. The clerk says his charge for entering cargo is 3 silver. The pearl sorter asks whether you have paid it before she lets you through the working yard; the boy rolls his eyes but carries the basket back into the shade.

A watchman on the wall calls down the names of the boats coming in. The clerk checks the next bundle, while the boy makes fresh marks for the shells. His mother hands him a dry board to write on this time.
ev.ormus.a.choice.pearl_diver: Ask the pearl sorter about Calatu
ev.ormus.a.choice.watch_ships: Spend a day watching the boats from the wall
ev.ormus.a.title: The Customs Scale and Pearl Basket
ev.ormus.astrodice_tide.body:
At the landing, a captain has set his cargo by the boat but has not given the order to load. The pilot checks the tide mark on the wall, and his niece counts the water jars. One of the crew asks whether you will cast the three dice you learned or simply ask the captain when he is ready.
