The eldest daughter, who has watched them all week, presses the frayed end into her father’s hand. “This was cut with a blade.” Her younger brother asks the neighbouring camps whether anyone heard hooves; one woman remembers a rider leaving after the fires died. Their father has read an old account of harsh penalties for horse theft among the Ghuzz, but he tells the children to find the animals first. “We need their tracks before more riders pass,” the daughter says. She and her brother can search if someone watches the horses still tied at home; staying to help adds a day to your journey. Your party is also preparing to leave, and the father asks you to wait until he has moved the remaining animals inside the rope ring. The daughter takes a water skin and starts toward the first hoofprint.
ev.road.fadlan_23.choice.press_on: Travel with your party after the camp is secured
ev.road.fadlan_23.choice.stand_watch: Watch the remaining horses while the family searches
ev.road.fadlan_23.title: Three Horses Missing Before Dawn
ev.road.fadlan_24.body: A woman invites passing travellers into her tent while her son repairs a saddle strap by the hearth. She offers you a bowl of fermented mare’s milk. “Have some if you like,” she says, setting a second cup beside it. “My son knows which well still has water.” Another visitor has brought raisins and pepper. The host thanks him and puts the gift on a high shelf until the children have eaten. Her youngest asks whether the raisins are for him. “After supper,” she says, and hands him a piece of bread. The son tests the repaired strap by pulling it over his knee. “Which way are you going?” he asks you. “One track is firm by the low ground, and the other has fresh wheel holes.” You can sit with the family and hear his directions while you share the offered drink, or bring a gift from the nearby stall before joining them. The host moves a stool closer to the fire so you can look at the route he draws.
ev.road.fadlan_24.choice.accept_bowl: Accept the bowl and ask the family about the next well
ev.road.fadlan_24.choice.bring_gift: Buy raisins and pepper for the host
ev.road.fadlan_24.title: The Bowl at the Roadside Tent
ev.road.fadlan_25.body: At dusk, a shepherd counts his goats beside a roadside camp and notices wolf tracks at the outer tether. His younger sister has brought the smallest animals inside the rope ring. “Three followed us from the far grass,” she tells him. “One stopped when the carts came through.” The shepherd carries dry wood to the drivers and asks who can watch the side of camp away from the fire. He hands you a bundle. “If the watchers stand together, the goats may settle enough to rest.” His sister asks for a second lantern where the tether bends. Staying to share the watches and then travel on adds two days to your journey. Leaving with the loaded carts at first light adds one day; the drivers will have to keep their animals close while the wolves are still near. A driver asks the sister which side the wolves approached, and she points beyond the last cart. The shepherd counts the goats once more before putting the wood down.
ev.road.fadlan_25.choice.keep_fires: Stay for the night watch, then travel to the next halt
ev.road.fadlan_25.choice.press_on: Leave at first light while the wolves remain nearby
ev.road.fadlan_25.title: The Shepherd's Night Watch
ev.road.fadlan_26.body: At a family’s roadside camp, a child lies under a blanket while her mother cools a cloth in a bowl of water. The mother’s brother has gone to meet the healer expected at tomorrow’s gathering. “He rides a grey horse,” the mother tells a passing driver. “Did you see him on this road?” The driver saw a grey horse but could not tell who rode it. The child asks for a little water. Her mother lifts the bowl and checks that the cup is clean before giving it to her. You have clean water with your party, and the cooking fire needs tending while the mother watches the child. Staying until the healer arrives adds a day to your journey. The family also needs its brother told that they are still at this camp if you travel on; carrying that word to the next stop adds a day. The mother sets a spare cup by the fire and asks whether you can leave some water in it.
ev.road.fadlan_26.choice.help_child: Stay the day with water and help the family wait
ev.road.fadlan_26.choice.press_on: Share water and carry word to the next stop
ev.road.fadlan_26.title: A Child Waiting for the Healer
ev.road.fadlan_27.body: A salt merchant has set a balance on a box beside the road. One pan keeps sinking; a hook bent when the cart jolted yesterday. His sister is unloading larger salt blocks from a camel, while he must weigh a small parcel for the cook at the next camp. “If I guess, she will have to weigh it again,” he says. His sister brings out a list of wells their family used years ago when buying salt near the Aral shore. “This load came from closer by,” she says, tapping a different mark, “but Father kept the old route in case we went north again.” The merchant asks you to hold the scale steady while he straightens the hook. His sister offers to show you where the two journeys part on the list. His sister finds a second hook in the tool bag and asks if they should use that instead. A driver waiting for the parcel calls from the road, and the merchant tests the empty pans once more before adding salt.
ev.road.fadlan_27.choice.ask_the_shores: Ask the family to show you their Aral route list
ev.road.fadlan_27.choice.press_on: Leave the merchants to their scale and travel on
ev.road.fadlan_27.title: The Salt Merchant's Broken Scale
ev.road.fadlan_28.body: At a water stop, a young rider shows her brother a drawing their aunt made years ago. The sun is a narrow crescent on the page. “That was an eclipse,” the aunt says. “The horses moved against their ropes when the daylight faded. I held them until it brightened.” The boy turns the page over. On the back she copied an older traveller’s account, with marks for the passing time. “How long did yours last?” he asks. “I did not mark it,” she says. “I remember who held the second horse.” The keeper brings out a bowl with measured lines and offers to show the boy how it can mark intervals. Comparing the drawing, the aunt’s memory and the copied account will add a day to your journey; travelling on with the party also takes an extra day by the longer road around the stop. The boy sets the bowl on level ground before anyone fills it.
ev.road.fadlan_28.choice.press_on: Thank the family and make the day's journey
ev.road.fadlan_28.choice.record_omen: Stay the day and compare the eclipse accounts
ev.road.fadlan_28.title: The Rider's Eclipse Drawing
ev.road.fadlan_29.body: At a roadside well, a guarded group waits while their water skins are filled. Their wrists are tied. One woman holds up her younger brother’s hand. “This knot has rubbed him raw,” she tells the guard. He loosens it, then turns back to a buyer asking about the next market. A traveller beside you hears the woman name her home village. “My mother’s sister lives there,” he says. The woman asks him to remember that she and her brother passed this well alive. He repeats both their names once, but he will leave by another road before noon. She looks at you. “Could you write my brother’s name too? He is shy with strangers.” Staying to learn the group’s names and route adds a day to your journey. Your party is ready to leave after the animals drink; travelling with it also uses an extra day on the road. The woman keeps her brother close while the skins are tied to the guard’s pack.
ev.road.fadlan_29.choice.look_away: Continue the day's road with your party
ev.road.fadlan_29.choice.witness_record: Stay a day to hear their names and where they were taken from
ev.road.fadlan_29.title: The Names Beside the Road
ev.road.fadlan_30.body: The sky darkens while a family is still pitching its tent beside a steppe road. Their youngest child carries one peg at a time until thunder rolls across the grass. His father calls him back under the half-raised cloth. “Hold this corner where I can see you,” he says. A neighbouring driver points to a dry rise and offers to move the heavy bundles there. The mother asks whether the canvas will reach the higher ground. “It will if we loosen that side first,” the driver says, taking one rope. Wind pulls the tent before the last peg is in. Staying to secure the camp and waiting for the softened ground adds two days to your journey. Another group of drivers means to travel between the squalls; joining them adds one day but leaves less time to dry the gear. The child brings his last peg to his father and waits for someone to hold the canvas still.
ev.road.fadlan_30.choice.halt_tents: Help secure the tents and stay until the ground firms
ev.road.fadlan_30.choice.press_on: Join the drivers travelling between the squalls
ev.road.fadlan_30.title: The Tent Pegs Before the Storm
ev.road.fadlan_31.body: Someone has opened an old burial mound beside the road, and shards of pottery have slid from the cut onto the path. An elder from the nearest camp is gathering them in a cloth. Her grandson brings a spade. “If rain gets in, the whole side will fall,” he says. “First show me where you picked each piece up,” she answers. He lays down the spade and points out a small fragment still wedged near the top. The elder remembers her grandmother saying a horse was buried here, though she never learned who made the mound. “That bit of story belongs to her,” she tells the boy. “This broken pot is what we can see.” She asks you to help sketch the open side and the stones still in place before they refill the cut; the work adds a day to your journey. The boy asks whether the drawing should show the pottery as well. His grandmother nods and points out the pieces still lying in the cut. He holds a corner of the cloth so the wind does not scatter the fragments again.
ev.road.fadlan_31.choice.press_on: Leave the family to its work and take the road
ev.road.fadlan_31.choice.survey_mound: Help the family survey the mound before they close it
ev.road.fadlan_31.title: The Opened Mound
ev.road.fadlan_32.body: At a river crossing, a clerk for the local ruler is registering baggage and animals before people use the guarded ferry. He has a stamped ledger and asks a toll for the crossing. The ferryman’s daughter calls from the bank, “When the morning carts are through, I can bring the animals over.” A driver waiting alongside you has counted his sacks twice. “Write the number on my receipt before I pay,” he tells the clerk. The clerk does so and asks the next traveller to read the line back. The ferry and the queue add a day to your journey. Upstream lies a shallow reach that avoids this post, though reaching it and taking the animals across adds three days. The driver asks if his written count will travel across with the sacks. The clerk hands him the stamped receipt. The daughter asks everyone to keep the first bags above the water while she checks the boat’s fastening.
ev.road.fadlan_32.choice.detour: Spend three days reaching the upstream crossing
ev.road.fadlan_32.choice.pay_toll: Pay the toll and take a receipt for the guarded ford
ev.road.fadlan_32.title: The Ford Clerk's Ledger
ev.road.fadlan_33.body: At a roadside camp, a bootmaker is repairing felt boots for a traveller whose soles have worn thin. Her apprentice has sewn the outer layer so close that it will not fit over the horse-hide sole. “Pull that seam out two fingers’ width,” she tells him. “He will want another pair of socks in winter.” A traveller who has read Ibn Fadlan’s older account of bitter cold among the Turks asks whether felt alone kept people warm. The bootmaker presses the dry sole with her thumb. “This part kept one customer’s feet off wet ground,” she says. “He crossed a river in the same pair and came back with water inside.” The apprentice asks how she dried them without making the leather hard. She moves the boot away from the hearth to show him. Learning the fitting and drying work adds a day to your journey; continuing with the departing party also adds a day on the road. The apprentice sets the loosened seam beside the sole to check it again.
ev.road.fadlan_33.choice.learn_lacing: Spend the day learning to fit and dry the boots
ev.road.fadlan_33.choice.press_on: Thank the bootmaker and travel on today
ev.road.fadlan_33.title: The Bootmaker's Winter Pair
ev.road.fadlan_34.body: A pale stretch of ground shines ahead like a pool. A guide’s daughter goes out on foot and tests its edge with a stick; when she returns, salt clings to the tip. “The crust holds near the marked track,” she tells her father. “Farther out, the stick went through.” A cart driver has already turned his animals toward the gleam. “I thought that was water,” he says, pulling on the reins. The guide leads him back and opens his list of wells. “Here is the one they can drink from. It lies after the next turn.” The daughter asks you to walk with her around the salt ground and help move a marker onto dry soil. That circuit adds two days to your journey. Her father’s marked route along the firm edge adds one day. The cart driver asks his youngest helper to remember the real well’s name. He offers the animals the last of their water while they wait for the guide to point out the turn.
ev.road.fadlan_34.choice.circle_wide: Circle the salt ground with the guide's daughter
ev.road.fadlan_34.choice.press_on: Follow the marked track beside the salt ground
ev.road.fadlan_34.title: White Ground Ahead
ev.road.fadlan_35.body: At a frozen river, a deep sound moves under the ice while the first sled is still close to the bank. The driver checks the lashings on his load. His daughter holds the horses back and asks the guide, “Did that come from where the sled is?” The guide listens, then takes a pole and feels for the edge of the safe ice. “I have heard it when colder air comes,” he says. “We still test this crossing each time.” He sets branches along a line and asks the driver to send the sleds over in small groups. Waiting while he checks all the way to the far bank adds a day to your journey. Going with the first group along the marked line also adds a day, with less time to find thin patches. The driver asks her to watch the rear runner as the sled starts, so its load will not swing toward the branches. She passes him a spare rope and keeps her horse beside her until the guide calls the next group.
ev.road.fadlan_35.choice.press_on: Cross with the first group on the marked line
ev.road.fadlan_35.choice.wait_for_sound: Wait for the guide to test the whole crossing
ev.road.fadlan_35.title: The Sound Beneath the Ice
ev.road.fork_tarot.body: Two post-roads split. You may lay a choice-gate and compare gain against cost.
ev.road.fork_tarot.title: Cards at the Fork
ev.road.geomancy_counsel.body: The road offers a moment to cast geomancy. Great fortune and great ill omen are both spoken here without shame.
ev.road.geomancy_counsel.title: Counsel of geomancy
ev.road.jiaobei_counsel.body: The road offers a moment to cast jiaobei. Great fortune and great ill omen are both spoken here without shame.
ev.road.jiaobei_counsel.title: Counsel of jiaobei
ev.road.runes_counsel.body: The road offers a moment to cast runes. Great fortune and great ill omen are both spoken here without shame.
ev.road.runes_counsel.title: Counsel of runes
ev.sachiu.entry.body: After you have travelled thirty days through the Great Desert, you come to a city called SACHIU, lying between north-east and east. It belongs to the Great Kaan and lies in a province called Tangut. The people are for the most part Idolaters, though there are some Nestorian Christians and some Saracens. Those who are Idolaters have a peculiar language and are no traders, but live by the fruits of the earth. They have many abbeys and minsters, all full of idols of divers fashions, to which they pay great honour and show reverence. The city lies on the edge of the Desert, where caravans restock after the terrible crossing; the farmers grow excellent melons and wheat in the irrigated fields.
ev.sachiu.entry.title: Arriving at Sachiu
ev.sachiu.site_gap.body: A station hand mixes dry grass with beans. A horse on a long journey needs strength, he says: beans add energy and grass gives it bulk. The amount depends on the distance. A horse fed too heavily just before departure may be harmed. He spreads the feed to dry before bagging it, since wet grass heats and spoils on the road.
ev.sachiu.site_gap.choice.interact: Help pick thorns from the grass
ev.sachiu.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Etzina
ev.sachiu.site_gap.title: Horse Feed at the Posting Station
ev.saianfu.a.body: Saianfu is a very great and noble city that rules over twelve other large and rich cities, and is itself a seat of great trade and manufacture. In the weaving quarters you hear shuttles clacking from dawn until lamp-light, and the magistrates' lists name every subject town upon the plain.
ev.saianfu.a.choice.magistrates: Ask the magistrates which towns owe tribute
ev.saianfu.a.choice.silk: Buy fine silken stuff from a weaver's stall
ev.saianfu.a.choice.weavers: Watch the silk weavers at their looms
ev.saianfu.a.title: Twelve Rich Cities
ev.saianfu.b.body: They have much silk here, and also a quantity of game, for the woods and marshes round Saianfu abound in beasts and birds. Hunters bring pelts to the market beside the armourers, and the city holds all that behoves a noble seat — workshops, granaries, and deep waters on three sides.
ev.saianfu.b.choice.ginger: Buy ginger from a victualler's stall
ev.saianfu.b.choice.market: Walk the hunters' market beside the workshops
ev.saianfu.b.choice.walls: Walk the northern approach where the host once lay siege
ev.saianfu.b.title: Game and Manufacture
ev.saianfu.entry.body: Saianfu is a very great and noble city, and it rules over twelve other large and rich cities, and is itself a seat of great trade and manufacture. The people are Idolaters (and so forth). They have much silk, from which they weave fine silken stuffs; they have also a quantity of game, and in short the city abounds in all that it behoves a noble city to possess. Now you must know that this city held out against the Great Kaan for three years after the rest of Manzi had surrendered. The Great Kaan’s troops made incessant attempts to take it, but they could not succeed because of the great and deep waters that were round about it, so that they could approach from one side only, which was the north. And I tell you they never would have taken it, but for a circumstance that I am going to relate. You must know that when the Great Kaan’s host had lain three years before the city without being able to take it, they were greatly chafed thereat.
ev.saianfu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.saianfu.entry.title: Concerning the Very Noble City of Saianfu, and How Its Capture Was Effected
ev.samara.entry.body: Samara — a kingdom on the northern coast of Sumatra, with its own king and its own language. The people eat rice and fish; the forests are full of elephants and rhinoceros. Ships from China and India call here for fresh water and fruit. The king claims descent from Alexander the Great; his palace is built of teak and decorated with Chinese porcelain.
ev.samara.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.samara.entry.title: Arriving at Samara
ev.samara.site_gap.body: A shipwright hangs hemp rope beside a mast, with three strips of different colours tied to it. They show sailors changes in wind direction, though clouds and waves must also be checked before sailing. Small boats furl their sails offshore. He hangs the wet rope in moving air: saltwater left in its fibres makes it brittle.
ev.samara.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the sea route to Mien
ev.samara.site_gap.title: The Shipwright’s Monsoon Markers
ev.samarcanda.a.body: In Samarcand, the turquoise dome glows in the sun. A scholar steps from the arcade and asks whether you came to see it or to hear a lesson at the madrasa. He points out the school by the square and a quiet garden reached along the canal. Students under the arcade sing a question-and-answer poem about blue roofs, mountain water, and watching the stars for the hour. The scholar says that reading the sky, tracing the canals, and learning the roads all belong to a traveller’s education.
ev.samarcanda.a.choice.dome: Stand beneath the turquoise dome of the Gur-i-Mir
ev.samarcanda.a.choice.gardens: Walk the canal-lined streets and greet the scholars
ev.samarcanda.a.choice.madrasa: Visit the madrasas of the Registan
ev.samarcanda.a.title: The Blue City
ev.samarcanda.b.body: At a Samarcand paper workshop, a maker polishes a pressed sheet against a smooth stone. “Let it dry before you touch it,” he says. Scholars and merchants buy this paper because ink holds its line on the polished surface. His apprentice sings the steps as he works: soften and beat the linen, mix the pulp with water, lift a thin layer on a screen, press, dry, and polish it. The maker asks you to feel a half-dry sheet and judge whether its fibres are even. A calligrapher has brought an illuminated manuscript; you may watch him write, buy paper, or choose a book.
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.learn: Watch the paper-makers at their craft
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.manuscript: Buy an illuminated manuscript from a calligrapher
ev.samarcanda.b.choice.paper: Buy a sheaf of Samarcand paper
ev.samarcanda.b.title: The Paper-Makers' Quarter
ev.samarcanda.c.body: At a mosque in Samarcand, people speak of a stone that gathers drops of water before disaster. The mullah opens an old chronicle and points to the years when it was said to have wept. “Look for yourself whether those years brought trouble,” he says. He offers no certain reading of the stone. You may pray, touch it, or ask when it last gathered water.
ev.samarcanda.c.choice.pray: Pray in the great mosque for the road ahead
ev.samarcanda.c.choice.touch: Press your forehead to the weeping stone
ev.samarcanda.c.choice.watch_pilgrims: Ask the mullahs when the stone last wept
ev.samarcanda.c.title: The Miraculous Stone
ev.samarcanda.entry.body: Samarcan is a great and noble city towards the north-west, inhabited by both Christians and Saracens, who are subject to the Great Kaan’s nephew, CAIDOU by name; he is, however, at bitter enmity with the Kaan. I will tell you of a great marvel that happened at this city. It is not a great while ago that SIGATAY, own brother to the Great Kaan, who was Lord of this country and of many an one besides, became a Christian. The Christians rejoiced greatly at this, and they built a great church in the city, in honour of John the Baptist; and by his name the church was called. And they took a very fine stone which belonged to the Saracens, and placed it as the pedestal of a column in the middle of the church, supporting the roof. It came to pass, however, that Sigatay died. Now the Saracens were full of rancour about that stone that had been theirs, and which had been set up in the church of the Christians; and when they saw that the Prince was dead, they said one to another that now was the time to get back their stone, by fair means or by foul. And that they might well do, for they were ten times as many as the Christians. So they gat together and went to the church and said that the stone they must and would have. The Christians acknowledged that it was theirs indeed, but offered to pay a large sum of money and so be quit. Howbeit, the others replied that they never would give up the stone for anything in the world. And words ran so high that the Prince heard thereof, and ordered the Christians either to arrange to satisfy the Saracens, if it might be, with money, or to give up the stone. And he allowed them three days to do either the one thing or the other. What shall I tell you? Well, the Saracens would on no account agree to leave the stone where it was, and this out of pure despite to the Christians, for they knew well enough that if the stone were stirred the church would come down by the run.
ev.samarcanda.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the bājgāh (toll-house)
ev.samarcanda.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.samarcanda.entry.title: Of the Great City of Samarcan
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.body: Before you leave Samarcanda, the old student of the blue-tiled college asks what you have learned from Samarcanda. The lesson is not a spell or a bargain; it is a way of noticing which detail will matter after the road turns.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_1: Ask what the road will demand
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_1_re: The old student of the blue-tiled college answers without evasion: patience, and the weighing of words, will be asked of you. His lesson is offered, and what you make of it lies with you.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_2: Stay for a day and listen to the whole account
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_2_re: You stay a day at the college with the old student, and he gives you the whole of his learning at leisure. What you take away is a book no copyist has yet made.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_3: Thank the guide and keep moving
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.choice_3_re: You thank the old student of the blue-tiled college and take the road. He lets you go with a blessing, and the lesson of Samarcanda remains unwritten.
ev.samarcanda.mentor_closure.title: The Guide of Samarcanda
ev.sapurgan.entry.body: On leaving the Castle, you ride over fine plains and beautiful valleys, and pretty hill-sides producing excellent grass pasture, and abundance of fruits, and all other products. Armies are glad to take up their quarters here on account of the plenty that exists. This kind of country extends for six days’ journey, with a goodly number of towns and villages, in which the people are worshippers of Mahommet. Sometimes also you meet with a tract of desert extending for 50 or 60 miles, or somewhat less, and in these deserts you find no water, but have to carry it along with you.
ev.sapurgan.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.sapurgan.entry.title: Concerning the City of Sapurgan
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.body: A coppersmith sets two weights on a wooden tray. For valuable goods, he says, a stamped mark is not enough: compare a weight with a standard one first. Copper wears, and rounded corners may change its measure. They feel almost identical in your hands. He wipes away verdigris and hangs them beside the scale.
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Taykan
ev.sapurgan.site_gap.title: Copper Weights at the Market
ev.semenat.entry.body: Semenat is a great kingdom towards the west. The people are Idolaters, and have a king and a language of their own, and pay tribute to nobody. They are not corsairs, but live by trade and industry as honest people ought. It is a place of very great trade. They are forsooth cruel Idolaters.
ev.semenat.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.semenat.entry.title: Concerning the Kingdom of Semenat
ev.semenat.site_gap.body: Coconut-leaf baskets hang beneath a pavilion roof. A basket maker flattens the leaf ribs and weaves them across one another. Every few rows he folds a rib back to spread the load, keeping the mouth from stretching wide. He lets you hold an empty basket. Newly made ones must dry under the eaves before storage, or green leaves may grow mould.
ev.semenat.site_gap.choice.interact: Try weaving a row around the rim
ev.semenat.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Tana
ev.semenat.site_gap.title: Weaving Coconut Leaves at the Road Pavilion
ev.siju.a.body: When you leave Piju and travel two days south through districts abounding in game, you reach Siju, a great and rich city flourishing with trade and manufactures. The southern road brings in grain and harness, and the workshops here finish what the northern towns begin.
ev.siju.a.choice.grain: Walk the grain market on the fertile plain
ev.siju.a.choice.sugar: Buy sugar from a refiner's stall
ev.siju.a.choice.workshops: Tour the manufactures brought down from Piju
ev.siju.a.title: Manufactures from Piju
ev.siju.b.body: The people of Siju are idolaters who burn their dead and use paper-money, and you see funeral parties pass toward the cremation grounds outside the walls. They lay out paper offerings beside the pyre, and the smoke rises all day above the southern road.
ev.siju.b.choice.ask: Ask an elder why they burn rather than bury
ev.siju.b.choice.observe: Stand at a respectful distance and watch a funeral rite
ev.siju.b.choice.paper-money: Buy paper-money at a stall near the cremation ground
ev.siju.b.title: Burning the Dead
ev.siju.entry.body: When you leave Piju you travel towards the south for two days, through beautiful districts abounding in everything, and in which you find quantities of all kinds of game. At the end of those two days you reach the city of SIJU, a great, rich, and noble city, flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are Idolaters, burn their dead, use paper-money, and are subjects of the Great Kaan. They possess extensive and fertile plains producing abundance of wheat and other grain. But there is nothing else to mention, so let us proceed and tell you of the countries further on. On leaving Siju you ride south for three days, constantly falling in with fine towns and villages and hamlets and farms, with their cultivated lands. There is plenty of wheat and other corn, and of game also; and the people are all Idolaters and subjects of the Great Kaan. At the end of those three days you reach the great river CARAMORAN, which flows hither from Prester John’s country.
ev.siju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.siju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Siju, and the Great River Caramoran
ev.sindafu.entry.body: When you have travelled those 20 days westward through the mountains, as I have told you, then you arrive at a plain belonging to a province called Sindafu, which still is on the confines of Manzi, and the capital city of which is (also) called SINDAFU. This city was in former days a rich and noble one, and the Kings who reigned there were very great and wealthy. It is a good twenty miles in compass, but it is divided in the way that I shall tell you.
ev.sindafu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.sindafu.entry.title: Concerning the Province and City of Sindafu
ev.sinju.a.body: Sinju stands on the greatest river in the world, which men call Kian. Though the city is of no great size, the waters before it are black with vessels, and boatmen swear that more wealth passes here than on all the rivers and seas of Christendom together.
ev.sinju.a.choice.count: Stand at the bank and count the moored vessels
ev.sinju.a.choice.tea: Buy tea from a river bargeman
ev.sinju.a.choice.toll: Ask the toll clerks how many vessels pass in a year
ev.sinju.a.title: The Greatest River
ev.sinju.b.body: The people are idolaters subject to the Great Kaan, and they use paper-money in every transaction on the quay. For all its modest walls, Sinju sees a very great amount of shipping and trade, and the revenue the Khan draws here is something marvellous.
ev.sinju.b.choice.harbour: Walk the harbour and note how small the city is for such traffic
ev.sinju.b.choice.porcelain: Buy porcelain from a river trader
ev.sinju.b.choice.quay: Watch merchants pay tolls in paper-money
ev.sinju.b.title: Paper-Money Port
ev.sinju.entry.body: You must know that when you leave the city of Yanju, after going 15 miles south-east, you come to a city called SINJU, of no great size, but possessing a very great amount of shipping and trade. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and use paper-money. And you must know that this city stands on the greatest river in the world, the name of which is KIAN. It is in some places ten miles wide, in others eight, in others six, and it is more than 100 days’ journey in length from one end to the other. This it is that brings so much trade to the city we are speaking of; for on the waters of that river merchandize is perpetually coming and going, from and to the various parts of the world, enriching the city, and bringing a great revenue to the Great Kaan.
ev.sinju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.sinju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Sinju and the Great River Kian
ev.sinjumatu.entry.body: On leaving Tadinfu you travel three days towards the south, always finding numbers of noble and populous towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. There is also abundance of game in the country, and everything in profusion. When you have travelled those three days you come to the noble city of SINJUMATU, a rich and fine place, with great trade and manufactures. The people are Idolaters and subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and they have a river which I can assure you brings them great gain, and I will tell you about it. You see the river in question flows from the South to this city of Sinjumatu.
ev.sinjumatu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.sinjumatu.entry.title: Concerning the Noble City of Sinjumatu
ev.smyrna.entry.body:
The road reaches Smyrna beside a wide bay. Aysel is rinsing a basket at the water's edge while her daughter Mina keeps a smaller one out of reach of the waves. They brought figs down from the hillside this morning; Mina insists the small basket was full too, though only three figs remain.

“I gave two to the boatman,” she says. Aysel asks about the other three. Mina admits she ate them on the way. The boatman calls from his boat that he received only one. Mina looks at her mother and begins counting again.

Aysel offers you a fig and points out the lane toward the houses above the water. She asks which way you are travelling. Mina adds that the boats know the bay better than anyone, but her mother knows which footpath is shortest. Both wait to see which one you ask.
ev.smyrna.entry.choice.pass: Thank Aysel and continue along the bay
ev.smyrna.entry.choice.rest: Stay a day at Aysel's house
ev.smyrna.entry.title: At the Bay of Smyrna
ev.smyrna.grapes.body:
On a terrace above the bay, sisters Esma and Lale are turning grapes that have lain on woven mats for several days. Their older brother sails with a small boat and asked for dried grapes he can keep in a bag. Esma wants to send him the largest bunches. Lale says the small ones are nearly ready, and he leaves in two days.

Their mother comes out with bread and asks why one mat has not been turned. The sisters explain at once, each talking over the other. Their mother takes a grape from each pile, tastes them, and says they can send both. Esma turns the large bunches; Lale shows her how to leave space for air between them.

The family sells some of its dried fruit to travellers. They will sell you a small packet today, or welcome another pair of hands to turn the grapes for the rest of the day and tomorrow morning.

You ask whether their brother knows they have saved him the first dried batch. Esma says she told him to bring a clean bag; Lale says he will forget it and use his cap. Their mother hears both and brings out a cloth pouch she has already sewn. ‘He can keep the cap on his head,’ she says. Lale asks whether the pouch should be tied tight before they finish drying. ‘Not while the fruit is warm,’ their mother answers. Esma holds up a handful for you to feel; it is still soft in the middle. The sisters spread it back on the mat and make room for the breeze.
ev.smyrna.grapes.choice.stay: Stay until tomorrow and help turn the grapes
ev.smyrna.grapes.result.buy: You pay for a packet. Lale checks that the grapes inside are dry and ties the cloth closed. Esma says their brother will get a larger bag, with both sorts mixed together. You eat a few on the road and regain strength. The sisters go back to their mats, now both full.
ev.smyrna.grapes.result.stay: You spend the day helping Esma and Lale turn the grapes. Their mother feeds you supper and gives you a place to sleep. At dawn Lale tests a small bunch and decides it is ready; Esma fills the bag for their brother. He comes by on his way to the boat, tastes one grape, and says he hopes the voyage lasts long enough to eat them all. You leave after breakfast. The family remembers your help when you pass this terrace again.
ev.smyrna.grapes.title: Grapes for the Brother at Sea
ev.suju.a.body: Suju is a very great and noble city with a circuit of some sixty miles, and the people possess silk in great quantities from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs. You walk a weaving quarter where the shuttles never rest, and the master tells you the city's name means Earth in our tongue.
ev.suju.a.choice.brocade: Watch the gold brocade looms at work
ev.suju.a.choice.circuit: Ride part of the city's sixty-mile circuit
ev.suju.a.choice.silk: Buy a length of gold brocade
ev.suju.a.title: Gold Brocade and Sixty Miles
ev.suju.b.body: The city hath merchants of great wealth and an incalculable number of people, though they are accomplished traders and not soldiers at all. Between the canals you find gardens where wealthy men keep fishponds and plant ginger and rhubarb in the shaded plots.
ev.suju.b.choice.bridges: Stand on a stone bridge and watch the canal traffic
ev.suju.b.choice.gardens: Walk the canal gardens with a merchant's clerk
ev.suju.b.choice.rhubarb: Buy rhubarb from a garden stall
ev.suju.b.title: Merchants and Canal Gardens
ev.suju.entry.body: Suju is a very great and noble city. The people are Idolaters, subjects of the Great Kaan, and have paper-money. They possess silk in great quantities, from which they make gold brocade and other stuffs, and they live by their manufactures and trade. The city is passing great, and has a circuit of some 60 miles; it hath merchants of great wealth and an incalculable number of people. Indeed, if the men of this city and of the rest of Manzi had but the spirit of soldiers they would conquer the world; but they are no soldiers at all, only accomplished traders and most skilful craftsmen. There are also in this city many philosophers and leeches, diligent students of nature. And you must know that in this city there are 6,000 bridges, all of stone, and so lofty that a galley, or even two galleys at once, could pass underneath one of them. In the mountains belonging to this city, rhubarb and ginger grow in great abundance; insomuch that you may get some 40 pounds of excellent fresh ginger for a Venice groat.
ev.suju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.suju.entry.title: Of the Noble City of Suju
ev.taican.a.body: After twelve days' journey you come to a fortified place called Taican, where there is a great corn market. It is a fine place, and caravans from every quarter stop here to buy grain before the high passes and the salt mountains to the south.
ev.taican.a.choice.ask_balc: Ask the caravan masters which road leads toward Balc
ev.taican.a.choice.buy_cotton: Buy cotton cloth for the road ahead
ev.taican.a.choice.walk_market: Walk the corn market and hear what the caravans pay
ev.taican.a.title: The Corn Market
ev.taican.b.body: The mountains that you see towards the south are all composed of salt. People from all the countries round, to some thirty days' journey, come to fetch this salt, which is the best in the world, and is so hard that it can only be broken with iron picks.
ev.taican.b.choice.ask_sapurgan: Ask which caravan road runs on toward Sapurgan
ev.taican.b.choice.buy_salt: Buy a block of Taican salt for the high passes
ev.taican.b.choice.watch_miners: Watch two days while the miners break the hard salt
ev.taican.b.title: The Mountains of Salt
ev.taican.entry.body: After those twelve days’ journey you come to a fortified place called TAICAN, where there is a great corn market. It is a fine place, and the mountains that you see towards the south are all composed of salt. People from all the countries round, to some thirty days’ journey, come to fetch this salt, which is the best in the world, and is so hard that it can only be broken with iron picks. ’Tis in such abundance that it would supply the whole world to the end of time. [Other mountains there grow almonds and pistachioes, which are exceedingly cheap.] When you leave this town and ride three days further between north-east and east, you meet with many fine tracts full of vines and other fruits, and with a goodly number of habitations, and everything to be had very cheap. The people are worshippers of Mahommet, and are an evil and a murderous generation, whose great delight is in the wine shop; for they have good wine (albeit it be boiled), and are great topers; in truth, they are constantly getting drunk.
ev.taican.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.taican.entry.title: Of Taican, and the Mountains of Salt. Also of the Province of Casem
ev.tana-azov.entry.body:
The Don spreads out before it meets the Sea of Azov. Near a landing place, Zoya has set a pot over a small fire. Her grandson Murad is trying to keep a bundle of reeds from rolling into the water. Each time he leans over to catch one, another slides free.

“Sit on the bundle,” Zoya tells him. He does, and the reeds stay put. She says his father had the same trouble when he first brought a load downriver. Murad asks if his father really lost an entire bundle. Zoya says only half, and he had to explain it to the family that ordered it.

Zoya welcomes travellers when they stop beside the river. She points out where the bank is firm enough to approach the water. Murad wants to know the name of the place you came from; he is collecting names his father might recognize when he returns.
ev.tana-azov.entry.choice.pass: Thank Zoya and continue by the river
ev.tana-azov.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day at Zoya's shelter
ev.tana-azov.entry.title: The River Landing at Tana
ev.tana.entry.body: Tana is a great kingdom lying towards the west, a kingdom great both in size and worth. The people are Idolaters, with a language of their own, and a king of their own, and tributary to nobody. No pepper grows there, nor other spices, but plenty of incense; not the white kind however, but brown. There is much traffic here, and many ships and merchants frequent the place; for there is a great export of leather of various excellent kinds, and also of good buckram and cotton. The merchants in their ships also import various articles, such as gold, silver, copper, and other things in demand.
ev.tana.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.tana.entry.title: Concerning the Kingdom of Tana
ev.tana.porridge.body:
Zoya has set out bowls of barley porridge for passing travellers. Murad sits beside her with a cord full of knots. His father tied one knot for every place on a journey toward Kiovia; Murad is trying to put the names back in the right order.

“He remembers the road better than his own birthday,” Zoya says. Karim corrects her from the fire: he remembers both, and it was Zoya who once forgot to send him a birthday letter. She says the letter was written, just left beneath the pot. Murad laughs and points to the last knot, which his father says marks the place where the family received it.

Zoya sells a warm bowl to travellers. If you want to hear the road story, Karim will untie the knots with Murad while you take notes. He has travelled the route himself and can name the stops toward Kiovia.

You ask whether the birthday letter ever reached Karim. He says it did, because his mother tucked it into the food bundle after she found it. Zoya asks Murad to show you the knot that marks the place where he read it. He feels along the cord, stops, then chooses the next knot instead. ‘That one,’ Karim says, ‘where we waited for the rain to ease.’ Zoya ladles another bowl for a boatman and tells Murad to wash his hands before touching the bread. He holds up both palms, dusty from the rope, and goes to the water jar.
ev.tana.porridge.choice.meal: Buy a warm bowl of barley porridge for 0.8 silver
ev.tana.porridge.choice.road: Follow the knots and copy the Kiovia route
ev.tana.porridge.result.meal: You pay Zoya for a bowl. Murad brings you a spoon, then asks if you can remember the name of the first place on his father's route. You eat while he tries the knots again. The porridge warms you and gives you strength for the road. Zoya finds the old birthday letter and shows Murad where she signed it.
ev.tana.porridge.result.road: Karim unties the cord one knot at a time. Murad says each name before his father does; twice he gets it wrong and starts again from the river mouth. You copy the sequence onto your map, marking Tana, Kiovia, and the road between them. At the last knot Zoya admits that she did send the letter in the end. Karim says he still has it.
ev.tana.porridge.title: Zoya's Road Names
ev.tana.site_gap.body: A sugar maker watches coconut sap bubble in a wide pot. He skims it with a wooden spoon. Too fierce a fire drives off the water quickly and makes the sugar bitter. When the syrup coats the back of the spoon, he pours it into moulds to cool. He scrapes a thin crust from the rim for a child to taste, sweet with a hint of char.
ev.tana.site_gap.choice.interact: Try judging when the syrup is ready
ev.tana.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Melibar
ev.tana.site_gap.title: A Pot of Coconut Sugar by the Shore
ev.tanpiju.a.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day's journey south-east through a plenteous region, you pass a succession of dwellings and charming gardens before you reach Tanpiju. Peach and mulberry plots line the road, and the air smells of turned earth and canal water.
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.gardens: Walk the garden road from Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.mulberry: Ask which gardens feed the silkworms
ev.tanpiju.a.choice.tea: Buy tea from a gardener's stall
ev.tanpiju.a.title: Gardens a Day from Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.b.body: Tanpiju is a great and rich city under Kinsay. The people burn their dead as elsewhere in Manzi, use paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts, with all necessaries in great plenty and cheapness. Carts from the Heaven City arrive each morning with goods for the local market.
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.funeral: Watch a funeral party pass toward the cremation ground
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.lacquer: Buy lacquerware from a Kinsay trader's stall
ev.tanpiju.b.choice.market: Walk the market where Kinsay goods are sold
ev.tanpiju.b.title: Under Kinsay
ev.tanpiju.entry.body: When you leave Kinsay and travel a day’s journey to the south-east, through a plenteous region, passing a succession of dwellings and charming gardens, you reach the city of TANPIJU, a great, rich, and fine city, under Kinsay. The people are subject to the Kaan, and have paper-money, and are Idolaters, and burn their dead in the way described before. They live by trade and manufactures and handicrafts, and have all necessaries in great plenty and cheapness. But there is no more to be said about it, so we proceed, and I will tell you of another city called VUJU at three days’ distance from Tanpiju. The people are Idolaters, &c., and the city is under Kinsay. They live by trade and manufactures. Travelling through a succession of towns and villages that look like one continuous city, two days further on to the south-east, you find the great and fine city of GHIUJU which is under Kinsay. The people are Idolaters, &c. They have plenty of silk, and live by trade and handicrafts, and have all things necessary in abundance.
ev.tanpiju.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.tanpiju.entry.title: Of the City of Tanpiju and Others
ev.tarsus.entry.body:
A river runs beside the road into Tarsus. Under an awning, Hadiya is tying a roll of cloth to a cart. Her son Yusuf holds the rope while she pulls it tight. He has put the knot on the wrong side, and each time the cart moves the loose end brushes his ear.

“Let me try once more,” he says. Hadiya lets him undo it. She says that when she was young, her mother made her pack the cart for a journey into the hills. She tied everything so tightly that nobody could get the food out at supper. Yusuf asks whether his grandmother still remembers. “She tells that story every time she sees me with a rope.”

Hadiya offers you a place in the shade and points out where the road crosses the water. Yusuf has finally moved the knot to the right side. He asks you to watch the cart while he rolls it a few steps to test his work.

You ask whether the load is meant for the market today. Hadiya says a neighbour is waiting for two rolls, while the rest will leave with a caravan tomorrow. Yusuf pushes the cart a short distance; the knot stays clear of the wheel. ‘Now it works,’ he says. Hadiya checks the lower roll, then asks him to tell the neighbour exactly which cloth is hers. He reads the mark on the wrapping aloud. A ferryman calls from the bank that the crossing is open, and Hadiya points out where you can reach it without bringing the cart through the narrow lane.
ev.tarsus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Hadiya and continue along the river road
ev.tarsus.entry.choice.rest: Spend a day at Hadiya's awning
ev.tarsus.entry.title: The River Road at Tarsus
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.body:
Near the river, Hiba is weaving a basket from reeds. Her grandson Aman has made the handle. It is wide enough for his hand but too short for the basket, and he keeps trying to force it into place.

The basket is for his aunt, who carries bread to relatives outside Tarsus. She lost her old one when a donkey stepped through it. Aman wants to give her a new basket before her next trip. Hiba tells him to soak another reed and make the handle longer. “You can tell her the donkey helped with the design,” she says.

Hiba has several baskets to finish for neighbours and offers a day's pay if you stay to weave with them. You can also sit for a while, share the bread Aman's aunt brought, and hear how the family learned to work by the river.

Aman asks whether the donkey will step on the new basket too. Hiba says his aunt has moved the feeding place since last time, and the animal now stands farther from the door. You ask how they know the handle is long enough. Hiba puts two loaves inside and tells Aman to lift it without squeezing the rim. He tries, then takes out one reed and weaves it back through the handle. ‘Now Aunt can carry it with her arm,’ he says. Hiba checks the knot and asks him to set the basket in the shade until it dries.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.choice.meal: Sit with Hiba and share the bread
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.choice.work: Stay a day and weave baskets for a wage
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.result.meal: You eat bread beside the river. Hiba says her daughter learned to weave baskets as a child, though she now spends more time carrying bread than making them. Aman listens, then quietly removes his short handle and starts a longer one. His aunt arrives while you are still there and promises to return for it tomorrow. The meal leaves you ready for the road.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.result.work: You spend the day soaking reeds and holding the basket frames while Hiba and Aman work. Aman makes a new handle. His aunt arrives before dusk, puts six loaves inside, and lifts the basket without straining it. Hiba pays you the promised wage. You leave the next morning as Aman is showing the neighbours how he made the longer handle.
ev.tarsus.reedbasket.title: The Basket for the Journey
ev.tauris.a.body: Tauris is the greatest commercial city of the Ilkhanate — a crossroads where Persian, Turkish, Armenian, Georgian, and Frankish merchants trade the goods of two continents. The city has outgrown every set of walls ever built around it, and its suburbs now stretch for miles across the plain, a patchwork of orchards, workshops, gardens, and caravanserais. The Ilkhan's summer palace stands on a hill to the south, surrounded by gardens of cypress and rose watered by qanats that bring snow-melt from the mountains. From the palace rooftop, the whole plain of Tauris is visible — a green island in the brown Persian plateau, dotted with the smoke of a thousand cooking-fires.
ev.tauris.a.choice.merchants: Ask the foreign merchants about the roads ahead
ev.tauris.a.choice.pearls: Buy a Tabriz pearl in the Great Bazaar
ev.tauris.a.choice.view: Climb the hill to see the whole city
ev.tauris.a.title: The Ilkhan's City
ev.tauris.b.body: Every nation has its own quarter in Tauris and nearly every foreign merchant-house keeps an agent here. The Genoese fondaco stands near the Great Bazaar, a fortress-like building where the Latin merchants store their goods, sleep, and pray. The Armenian caravanserai by the east gate receives the overland caravans from Trebizond and the Black Sea. The Moslem traders occupy the covered market, selling silk from China and Cathay, pearls from the Gulf, and cloth of gold from Baghdad. A merchant who knows four languages — Persian, Turkish, Arabic, and Italian — can make his fortune in Tauris in a single caravan season. Every bale that passes through pays a tax to the Ilkhan.
ev.tauris.b.choice.browse: Walk the covered market and listen
ev.tauris.b.choice.dragoman: Hire a dragoman and learn the Persian tongue
ev.tauris.b.choice.latin: Speak with the Genoese merchants in their fondaco
ev.tauris.b.title: The Merchant Quarters
ev.tauris.c.body: Outside the city, the gardens of Tauris stretch for miles along the qanats that bring water from the mountains. The great lords of the Ilkhanate — Persian viziers, Mongol noyans, Armenian merchants, and Turkish amirs — have their summer pavilions here: open halls with tiled fountains, shaded by plane trees and cypress, surrounded by orchards of apricot, pomegranate, almond, and pistachio. The air smells of jasmine, rose, and watered earth. The fruit is the finest in Persia, and the gardeners have a saying: 'A man who drinks the water of Tauris and eats its apricots will never want to leave.' Many foreign merchants have found this to be true.
ev.tauris.c.choice.fruit: Buy dried apricots and pistachios for the road
ev.tauris.c.choice.rest: Rest a fortnight in the gardens among the jasmine
ev.tauris.c.choice.wander: Walk the qanats and learn how the water comes
ev.tauris.c.title: The Garden Suburbs
ev.tauris.entry.body: Tauris is a great and noble city, situated in a great province called YRAC, in which are many other towns and villages. But as Tauris is the most noble I will tell you about it. The men of Tauris get their living by trade and handicrafts, for they weave many kinds of beautiful and valuable stuffs of silk and gold. The city has such a good position that merchandize is brought thither from India, Baudas, CREMESOR, and many other regions; and that attracts many Latin merchants, especially Genoese, to buy goods and transact other business there; the more as it is also a great market for precious stones. It is a city in fact where merchants make large profits. The people of the place are themselves poor creatures; and are a great medley of different classes. There are Armenians, Nestorians, Jacobites, Georgians, Persians, and finally the natives of the city themselves, who are worshippers of Mahommet. These last are a very evil generation; they are known as TAURIZI. The city is all girt round with charming gardens, full of many varieties of large and excellent fruits. Now we will quit Tauris, and speak of the great country of Persia. [From Tauris to Persia is a journey of twelve days.]
ev.tauris.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the tamghā-khāna (tax-house)
ev.tauris.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.tauris.entry.title: Of the Noble City of Tauris
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.body: Beside the card table, another reader keeps three dice for the hour of departure.
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.choice.ask: Ask what the houses mean on the road
ev.tauris.mentor_astrodice.title: Star-dice in Tauris
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.body: A Frankish widow teaches spreads that weigh gain, cost, and the rule of choice at forks.
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.choice.learn_astr: Pay and learn the star-dice as well
ev.tauris.mentor_tarot.title: Cards at Tabriz
ev.tenduc.a.body: Tenduc is governed by Christians of the Nestorian faith, and its king George claims descent from Prester John, whom the Great Kaan confirmed in this province though his realm is less than the priest-king once held. You enter the church where the cross stands beside tablets in Syriac script, and the priests tell you how the kings of this line have long taken the Kaan's daughters to wife — a custom older than any living man remembers.
ev.tenduc.a.choice.ask-cambaluc: Ask the priests what road leads to the Great Kaan's city
ev.tenduc.a.choice.attend: Attend the Nestorian service and listen to the Syriac psalms
ev.tenduc.a.choice.offer: Leave a coin offering at the church door
ev.tenduc.a.title: The Nestorian Church and Prester John's Line
ev.tenduc.b.body: The market of Tenduc brings together Christians, idolaters, and Saracens who worship Mahommet — all under the eye of the Kaan's darughachi, who takes his tenth and keeps the peace. Camel-hair cloth of many colours hangs beside blocks of azure stone and sacks of grain from the pasture lands. You hear three tongues in a single alley, and no quarrel breaks out before the overseer's staff.
ev.tenduc.b.choice.ask-north: Ask the Saracen merchants which road leads north to the steppe
ev.tenduc.b.choice.buy-cloth: Buy a roll of coloured cotton cloth from a Nestorian weaver
ev.tenduc.b.choice.walk: Walk the market and listen in three tongues
ev.tenduc.b.title: The Mixed Market of Three Faiths
ev.tenduc.entry.body: Tenduc is a province which lies towards the east, and contains numerous towns and villages; among which is the chief city, also called TENDUC. The king of the province is of the lineage of Prester John, George by name, and he holds the land under the Great Kaan; not that he holds anything like the whole of what Prester John possessed. It is a custom, I may tell you, that these kings of the lineage of Prester John always obtain to wife either daughters of the Great Kaan or other princesses of his family. In this province is found the stone from which Azure is made. It is obtained from a kind of vein in the earth, and is of very fine quality. There is also a great manufacture of fine camlets of different colours from camel’s hair. The people get their living by their cattle and tillage, as well as by trade and handicraft. The rule of the province is in the hands of the Christians, as I have told you; but there are also plenty of Idolaters and worshippers of Mahommet.
ev.tenduc.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.tenduc.entry.title: Concerning the Province of Tenduc, and the Descendants of Prester John
ev.tiju.entry.body: When you leave Cayu, you ride another day to the south-east through a constant succession of villages and fields and fine farms until you come to TIJU, which is a city of no great size but abounding in everything. The people are Idolaters (and so forth). There is a great amount of trade, and they have many vessels. And you must know that on your left hand, that is towards the east, and three days’ journey distant, is the Ocean Sea. At every place between the sea and the city salt is made in great quantities.
ev.tiju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.tiju.entry.title: Of the Cities of Tiju, Tinju, and Yanju
ev.trapezus.entry.body:
Trebizond stands where the mountains meet the Black Sea. Tamar has spread two wool cloaks over a low wall above the water. Her daughter Ana takes one down because the wind keeps lifting its corner. The other belongs to her younger brother Davit, who has left it outside since morning.

“He says it needs more air,” Ana tells you. Tamar says he forgot it when he went to watch boats. She has been repairing both cloaks before her children travel inland, and she wants Davit back to try his on before she finishes the hem.

Tamar asks where you are bound and points out the lane down to the boats. Ana can show you the places where travellers wait for a crossing. If you have a day, Tamar will walk with you through the streets and ask the sailors which boats have gone toward Caffa.

You ask Anna whether Davit knows which cloak is his. ‘He knows,’ she says, ‘but he will claim mine is warmer.’ Tamar calls toward the ships, and he appears carrying a small coil of rope for his pack. He tries on the cloak she kept for him; one sleeve sits too high. His mother asks him to stand still while she loosens the seam. Davit says he can wait, then points to a boatman below who has promised news of the Caffa passage. Anna reminds him to ask about the departure day as well as the fare.
ev.trapezus.entry.choice.look: Spend a day with Tamar above the harbour
ev.trapezus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Tamar and continue through the town
ev.trapezus.entry.title: Above the Water at Trebizond
ev.trapezus.tworoads.body:
Tamar has laid two travel bags by her door. Ana is going south toward Aleppo, where an aunt who taught her to weave has asked her to visit. Davit is taking their father's old spindle southeast toward Edessa; a friend there promised to repair its bent shaft.

Ana thinks Davit's bag is too heavy. He says she packed all the food into his, and empties it onto the floor to prove his point. Tamar divides the bread between them. Ana slips an extra piece back into his bag when he is not looking.

They leave by different inland roads in the morning. Tamar can walk with one child as far as the first rest place; she asks whether you will accompany the other. Both know the stopping places from family journeys, so you can choose which road to learn as you go.

You ask why Davit carries the old spindle all that way. ‘Father used it before I was born,’ he says. ‘My friend knows a turner who may straighten it.’ Anna asks whether he has written the friend’s address where he can find it. Davit pats one pocket, then another, and finally takes a folded note from the bread cloth. Tamar tells him to put it in his belt before the food stains the ink. Anna laughs, but checks her own letter to the aunt too. Their mother gives each of them a small packet of salt for the road and asks them to meet the family again when they can.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.choice.ana: Walk one day with Ana toward Aleppo
ev.trapezus.tworoads.choice.davit: Walk one day with Davit toward Edessa
ev.trapezus.tworoads.result.ana: You spend the day on the road with Ana. She points out the turns her aunt taught her and names the places where the family has stayed on earlier journeys. At the first rest place she opens her bag and finds a small packet of dried fruit that Tamar slipped in beside the bread. You mark Trebizond, Aleppo, and the route between them on your map. Ana thanks you and sets off again in the morning.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.result.davit: You spend the day with Davit on the eastern road. He shows you the places where his father once stopped with the spindle in his pack. At the first rest place he finds the extra bread Ana gave him and smiles; he saves it for breakfast. You mark Trebizond, Edessa, and the route between them on your map. Davit takes the spindle out once more to check that its shaft has survived the day.
ev.trapezus.tworoads.title: Two Roads from Tamar’s Door
ev.tripolis.entry.body:
After reaching Tripolis, you follow a cart carrying goods for a ship down to the harbour. It stops beside the quay. The bottom of a wooden crate has split, leaving sugar stuck to a wheel. Hassan and another porter lift it onto an old piece of sailcloth.

"My sister packed this one," Hassan says. "She draws a little moon on the side. When I find it, I'll know whose account it goes on."

His sister is writing on the next batch of crates under a shed. She runs over, sees the crack, and says she will fetch a carpenter. Hassan starts to lift the crate again. "Gather the corners of the cloth first," she tells him. "We can still get the sugar back in."

A ship is waiting for its cargo. The coastal road leads south; people here also travel north to Antioch. For now the brother and sister are trying to get this one crate aboard.
ev.tripolis.entry.choice.pass: Ask them for the southern road and keep travelling
ev.tripolis.entry.choice.rest: Help gather the sugar and rest in town for a day
ev.tripolis.entry.title: The Sugar Crate at the Harbour
ev.tripolis.oven.body:
The communal oven is hot. People wait with dough on wooden boards as the baker loads one batch after another. An old man arrives last with three rounds covered in sesame seeds. "For my grandson's ship," he says.

The baker asks when it sails. The man only knows that his grandson asked him to come before noon. Two women ahead of him move their boards aside to make room.

The man thanks them, scattering sesame seeds from his sleeve. His grandson is sailing to Alexandria for the first time. Before leaving he complained that the bread was too hard; now he has asked for three rounds and seems to be in a hurry for them.
ev.tripolis.oven.choice.bake: Help carry the bread to the harbour
ev.tripolis.oven.choice.damascus: Wait for this batch and ask the baker about the road to Damascus
ev.tripolis.oven.result.bake:
The bread is hot when it comes out. You and the old man carry the board between you to the quay. His grandson sees him from the ship and runs down the gangplank. "Share them on the way," the old man says. "Don't eat them all at once." The young man takes a bite and says this batch is just right.

Back in town, the baker is making room for the next batch. The old man collects his board and says he will come tomorrow to keep an eye on his neighbour's dough.
ev.tripolis.oven.result.damascus:
As he loads the oven, the baker tells you that caravans for Damascus gather east of town. Before leaving, their drivers often bake thin loaves to carry for several days. He points to the long boards against the wall; they are used to slide the dough into the oven.

The old man hears where you are headed and offers you a piece of fresh sesame bread. You remember where the caravan gathers.
ev.tripolis.oven.title: Bread for the Ship
ev.tripolis.quay.body:
At the quay, a young woman looks from one boat to another. She holds a short length of blue rope tied with three knots. Her father ties its match to the family boat's oar so that she can recognise it when he comes in.

"The boat is here, but the oar isn't," she says. "Father says he lent it to the next boat. They say he didn't. I need to find it before they leave."

A porter overhears her. "Your father went to buy a new oar this morning. Ask him before you search every boat in the harbour." She blushes but still wants to know what happened.
ev.tripolis.quay.choice.help: Help her ask about the oar on both boats
ev.tripolis.quay.choice.road: Ask the porter for the coastal road to Tyre
ev.tripolis.quay.result.help:
The other boat's master takes you to the stern. The old oar is there, with its blue rope still tied to the handle. He says he borrowed it that morning while her father went into town to buy a new one. He had promised to return it by noon. She remembers that her father spoke in a hurry that morning; she caught only the words "the oar is next door."

They carry the old oar back together. The master grins. "Next time, tell your father to write it down. It'll save you a walk round the harbour." She offers you some water and remembers your help.
ev.tripolis.quay.result.road:
The porter takes you to the end of the quay and points south along the coast. "For Tyre, follow those mule carts. They leave through the south gate this afternoon."

The young woman comes over. "Father sails to Tyre in a few days. If you meet him, tell him I found the old oar. Next time he lends something, he can tell me the whole story." The porter laughs, and so does she.
ev.tripolis.quay.title: The Blue Rope on the Boats
ev.tyrus.entry.body:
The road reaches the sea at Tyre. Beside some old stonework, Salma has spread a cloth over a low shelter. She is mending her younger brother's sandal with a thick needle. He holds the other sandal against his foot and announces that this pair will last until he is grown.

“You said that about the last pair,” Salma tells him. “It lasted six weeks.” He says the stones near the shore are unusually sharp. She gives him the needle to hold while she tests the new stitching.

Salma offers you water and asks where you came from. Her brother supplies three guesses before you can answer. She knows which stretch of the coastal road stays clear after rain, and draws it with her finger in the dust. When you take out your map, she asks you to mark the shelter too. “Travellers bring their sandals to me. My brother asks each one where they came from, then draws their roads in the dust.”
ev.tyrus.entry.choice.pass: Thank Salma and continue along the coast
ev.tyrus.entry.choice.rest: Stay by Salma's shelter for a day
ev.tyrus.entry.title: Arriving at Tyre
ev.tyrus.fishrack.body:
Farida is tying a new crosspiece to a drying rack. Her daughter Lina holds it up from below. A strip of salted fish hangs from the old side of the frame, just out of the reach of a cat that has been following the work.

Lina says her uncle taught her the knot before he went inland to work as a carpenter. She has tied it twice, and it still slips. “He used to pull the rope with his teeth,” she says. Farida makes her take it out of her mouth. “He also lost a tooth. Use both hands.”

Farida sells small packets of fish to people on the road. The rack needs another crosspiece before she can hang today's catch. She asks whether you would like food for the journey or have time to stay and work with them. The cat sits beneath the unfinished side, waiting for an answer of its own.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.choice.buy: Buy Farida’s salted fish for 0.8 silver
ev.tyrus.fishrack.choice.stay: Spend the day helping them finish the rack
ev.tyrus.fishrack.result.buy: You pay Farida for a packet. Lina wraps it in a clean scrap of cloth and ties the knot her uncle taught her; this time it holds. On the road, you eat the fish with bread and feel stronger. Farida counts the coins into the small pot she keeps for new rope. The cat receives one tiny piece that fell from the rack.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.result.stay: You hold the frame while Farida fastens the crosspiece. Lina tries the knot again with both hands. It stays tight, and she hangs the first fish on the new side. By evening the rack is full. Farida gives you supper and a place beneath the shelter for the night; you leave the next morning. She tells the nearby families who helped build it, and they greet you when you pass.
ev.tyrus.fishrack.title: The Fish Rack by the Shore
ev.yarcan.entry.body: Yarcan is a province five days’ journey in extent. The people follow the Law of Mahommet, but there are also Nestorian and Jacobite Christians. They are subject to the same Prince that I mentioned, the Great Kaan’s nephew. They have plenty of everything, [particularly of cotton. The inhabitants are also great craftsmen, but a large proportion of them have swoln legs, and great crops at the throat, which arises from some quality in their drinking-water.] As there is nothing else worth telling we may pass on.
ev.yarcan.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.yarcan.entry.title: Of the Province of Yarcan
ev.yarcan.site_gap.body: An orchard keeper cuts a branch to a smooth sloping face. To graft it, he says, align the bark layers while the tree is growing and bind them with cloth. A dry cut will not take. Unripe fruit hangs above an irrigation channel. He keeps the cuttings in damp cloth until the afternoon cools so they do not dry too quickly.
ev.yarcan.site_gap.choice.route: Ask about the road to Cascar
ev.yarcan.site_gap.title: A Grafting Knife at the Orchard
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.body:
In a Yazd lodging house, the keeper, Hamid, is mending a torn mat. His daughter brings bread to two travellers who came from Isfahan and had earlier crossed the Fars hills. They tell her how small lodgings along that mountain road keep food ready for people who arrive late.

‘Do they know who is coming?’ she asks. ‘Usually not,’ one traveller says. ‘That’s why your father keeps an extra loaf, isn’t it?’ Hamid smiles and asks her to set the bread beside the guests. The travellers also pass on a story they heard in Shiraz about a religious elder who welcomed strangers. You can stay overnight, join the evening prayers, or ask them about the road they took from Isfahan to Yazd.
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.choice.cell: Stay overnight at the lodging house
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.choice.shiraz: Ask how they travelled from Isfahan to Yazd
ev.yasdi.battuta_a.title: A Lodging Keeper’s Tale
ev.yasdi.entry.body:
In a Yazd workshop, a weaver named Roya cuts a loose thread from a length of silk. Her younger brother holds the cloth up to the light and points to a place he thinks she has missed.

‘That one belongs to the pattern,’ she says, turning the fabric over for him to see. A merchant waiting by the door will take this piece with him when it is ready. He tells you that Yazd silk travels far; for the road beyond the town, he is filling every water skin he has. Roya’s brother wants to know where you are headed so he can tell you which courtyard still has a well.

You ask the merchant why he is waiting instead of collecting the cloth. He says Roya promised to check the edge in daylight; last time a folded corner hid a loose stitch, and his buyer noticed first. Roya tells him that was another order and asks her brother to bring the whole length outside. The boy balances it across both arms. ‘This one is for your buyer with the blue border, yes?’ she asks. The merchant confirms it, then asks if the courtyard well is open. Her brother says it is, though the keeper has a queue of potters waiting. Roya promises to finish the edge while he fills a skin.
ev.yasdi.entry.choice.look: Spend a day looking around and taking notes
ev.yasdi.entry.title: The Weavers of Yazd
ev.yasdi.threadwell.body:
Roya’s brother has promised to bring water for the workshop, but the shared jar at the well is cracked. Water keeps leaking onto his sandals. Roya needs the silk rinsed before the merchant returns.

The well keeper lends him a sound jar now and asks him to help repair the broken one when the potter arrives. He looks at the workshop, then at you. ‘I need to get water to Roya. Could you help with the old jar later?’ The keeper sets the sound jar between them and tells the boy to carry it to Roya first. The potter will look at the cracked one after she finishes a neighbour’s order.

You ask whether the cracked jar has served the well long. The keeper says her father left it there years ago; everyone knows its blue rim and brings it back after use. Roya’s brother asks if a repair will hold. The potter, passing with another customer’s bowl, says she needs to see the crack dry before promising anything. He reaches for the borrowed jar, then stops because his sandals are wet and his hands are slippery. The keeper wipes the handle with a cloth and asks him to hold it by both sides. He takes two careful steps, glances back at you, and says his sister will worry if the water is late again.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.choice.carry: Carry water back to Roya now
ev.yasdi.threadwell.choice.repair: Spend a day helping mend the jar
ev.yasdi.threadwell.result.carry: You take a smaller jar back to the workshop. Roya rinses the silk and hangs it where the air can reach it. Her brother brings you a cup of cool water before going back for the next load. You feel refreshed.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.result.repair: The potter shows Roya’s brother how to seal the crack, then lets the repair dry. You spend the day helping him and carrying water in another jar. By evening the caretaker knows your name and thanks you for keeping the workshop supplied.
ev.yasdi.threadwell.title: Roya’s Water Jar
ev.zayton.battuta_a.body: The traveller's tale is borne out as you walk the quay: in China you buy and sell with paper. A palm-sized sheet, stamped with the king's stamp, is money: twenty-five such notes make a nashhat, a dinar of the place, and torn notes are exchanged at the mint for new ones, without interest. No one will take a dinar or a dirhem until it is changed for these notes. The painters are the most skilful in the world: every stranger who passes through their towns finds his likeness upon the walls and on papers stuck up in the streets. When a vessel leaves China, the names and forms of the men aboard are written down, and when it returns the magistrates' servants board it and compare; if a man is missing, the commander of the vessel is seized, and goods not entered in the register forfeit ship and cargo to the king — an oppression seen nowhere else.
ev.zayton.battuta_a.choice.change: Change your coin for the king's paper
ev.zayton.battuta_a.choice.registry: Watch the registry of the junks
ev.zayton.battuta_a.title: Paper Money, Painters, and the Registry of Ships
ev.zayton.entry.body: Five days south-east of Fuju, through valleys of camphor trees and a constant succession of towns, the road brings you down to the water, and you see why men speak of this place as they do. The haven of Zayton is frequented by all the ships of India, which bring hither spicery and every kind of costly ware; and you must know that for one shipload of pepper that goes to Alexandria for Christendom, there come a hundred such to this haven, aye and more too. The masts stand so thick along the water that a man might take them for a burnt forest. At the head of the quay the Great Kaan's clerks keep their tables, and there is no coming ashore with goods that does not pass beneath their brushes.
ev.zayton.entry.choice.ask_ships: Ask a boatman what all these ships are
ev.zayton.entry.choice.battuta: Ask of the traveller who marvelled at the king's paper money
ev.zayton.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods to the Kaan's clerks
ev.zayton.entry.choice.slip: Go up by the fishermen's steps instead
ev.zayton.entry.title: The Haven of Zayton
ev.zayton.fanfang.body: The merchants of India and of Persia and of the Arab lands have their own street here, and their own houses of prayer, and they have had them long enough that their grandsons are buried in this soil. Persian and Arabic and the local tongue are bargained in under one roof, and a man who has none of the three will find his purse lighter than his understanding. Nobody in the quarter finds any of this remarkable, which is itself the most remarkable thing about it.
ev.zayton.fanfang.choice.interpreter: Pay a lad of the quarter to interpret for a season
ev.zayton.fanfang.choice.persian: Ask the Persian traders about the sea road
ev.zayton.fanfang.choice.silk: Buy a bolt of silk from a Manzi weaver
ev.zayton.fanfang.title: The Foreign Quarter
ev.zayton.harbour.body: The quay runs the length of the water and is never quiet. Pepper comes ashore in sacks the height of a man; there are pearls weighed out in little brass scales, and lignaloes and sandalwood stacked like cordwood. You must know that the merchant pays dearly here: the Kaan takes a tamghā on everything, ten in the hundred, and the ship's charge on top of it — thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper. Between the freight and the Kaan's due a man pays out a good half of what his cargo is worth. And yet on the other half he makes so great a profit that he is always glad to come back with more.
ev.zayton.harbour.choice.monsoon: Stand the pilots a drink and ask about the winds
ev.zayton.harbour.choice.pepper: Buy a sack of pepper at the quayside price
